#4143. Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

Stalker 2’s first add-on isn’t far off, and it may just be the thing to bring you back to post-apocalyptic Chornobyl in 2026.

One of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the new Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the big news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two new regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two new regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

The developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.

#4142. Bandai Namco Shuts Down Unknown 9: Awakening Developer Reflector Entertainment

Bandai Namco has announced it is shutting down Reflector Entertainment, the Montreal studio behind 2024’s Unknown 9: Awakening.

Reflector, founded in 2015, is a subsidiary of Bandai Namco that was acquired in 2020. Unknown 9: Awakening is the studio’s only released title, which was first revealed at Gamescom 2020 and released on October 17, 2024. The third-person action game is set within the broader Unknown 9 transmedia franchise, which includes a book trilogy, comics, and a web series, and stars Haroona, a woman able to traverse a separate dimension called the Fold. Haroona, played by The Witcher actress Anya Chalotra, uses this ability and other supernatural powers to battle a hostile secret society across India and other global locations.

Upon release, Unknown 9: Awakening didn’t make much of a critical splash; it currently has a 59 Metascore and "Mixed" Steam reviews. In November 2024, a month after Unknown 9's launch, Reflector laid off 18 percent of its staff.  More layoffs were announced in January 2025 as Reflector canned an unannounced project while confirming Unknown 9 failed to meet expectations. With Reflector’s dissolution, Bandai Namco expects to post “an extraordinary loss” of approximately €21 million on its Q3 financial results for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027.

#4141. Gallery: Hollow Knight & Silksong's Switch 2 Physicals Are A Delight For Map Fans

Fangamer announced earlier this year that it had two swanky new Switch 2 physical releases in the works for both Hollow Knight and Silksong, each complete with a couple of bonus goodies inside the box.

With the release date finally upon us, the good folks over at Fangamer have sent us a copy of each, and let it be known, they are both really rather sexy.

Both boxes boast wrap-around cover art (for some particularly detailed spines) and reversible sleeves so you can opt for a design without all of the Switch 2 T&C text down at the bottom.

All of the DLC for the first game is included on the cart, too, and while Silksong's Sea of Sorrow expansion obviously isn't on there at the moment (we're still waiting for a firm release date on that one), it will come as a free download to all those with a copy when it eventually drops.

Inside, both copies contain some bonus booklet goodies, too. Each has its own instruction booklet, containing introductions for everything from both the Knight and Hornet's movesets and upgrade abilities, to points of interest in the world. Gosh, we didn't realise how much we had missed physical manuals.

A physical copy of each game's map is included in the box as well, which folds up into a little wax-stamped envelope — a very neat touch, if we've ever seen one. This gives you a detailed rundown of each location for both games, and could prove as a valuable route tracker for those still trying to uncover Hallownest/Pharloom's secrets.

Both the Hollow Knight and Silksong Switch 2 physicals are now available on the Fangamer website.

#4140. PlayStation Cancels In-Development Live-Service Shooter, Fairgames, At Jade Raymond's Former Haven Studio

PlayStation has reportedly canceled Fairgames, the long-in-development live-service shooter being made by Haven Studios, which Jade Raymond founded in 2021. Sony acquired Haven in 2022, and in 2025, Raymond left the studio, though it remained dedicated to developing Fairgames without her. It seems the story of Fairgames is now over, according to a new Bloomberg report.

The publication reports that PlayStation will not enforce any job cuts or layoffs as a result of Fairgames' cancellation, which comes as a surprise, and the studio will instead shift to support other first-party teams under the PlayStation umbrella. According to Bloomberg, this cancellation comes after a recent test of the game that allowed "thousands of players" to check it out did not deliver the results PlayStation wanted.

"While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," PlayStation executives Sean Decker and John Doyle wrote in an email to employees today, according to Bloomberg. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

This doesn't necessarily come as a surprise. PlayStation announced Fairgames back in 2023 and hasn't shown much since, leaving many to assume development has been struggling behind the scenes. Since then, PlayStation has pulled back heavily on its live-service plans, which originally included launching more than 10 live-service games by March of this year. Naughty Dog's Last of Us multiplayer game was canceled, Bungie ended active development on Destiny 2, and live-service Horizon spin-off Hunters Gathering is reportedly being overhauled following poor playtest feedback, amongst other stories. Reading between the lines, many fans were waiting for news like today's cancellation of Fairgames to drop.

Still, in an era where games are canceled and entire teams are laid off (sometimes even after releasing a successful game), it's nice to see Haven employees are not facing layoffs.

#4139. Xbox Series X25 Getting A Limited Restock On Release Day

Despite its price, the Xbox Series X25 sold out almost immediately when its pre-orders went live in August. Now its release date is less than 24 hours away, and Xbox has confirmed that those who didn’t place their order before the limited edition console was completely sold out will have a second chance to buy one tonight.

Xbox confirmed on Twitter that a “limited number” of X25 consoles and matching controllers will be available on November 12 through the Microsoft Store and other third-party retailers. It didn’t mention which retailers, but it's worth keeping an eye on the usual suspects - Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, Target, and GameStop - if you arrive at the Microsoft Store tonight and get placed in a queue, or make it through and find the restocked console has already sold out for a second time.

The restock will happen at midnight EST in the US, so as soon as November 11 becomes November 12, which means staying up for those of you who really want one of these consoles. This will, almost certainly, be the last chance you have to buy one, barring resorting to resale sites. I’d really not recommend taking that route, both because it rewards scalpers and because after X25 pre-orders sold out in August, scalpers were listing the consoles for almost $3,500.

Xbox does imply that the restock won’t necessarily be exclusive to the US, although all that note adds is that the console’s availability will vary by region and retailer. There will likely be a lot of people in the UK hoping to bag one tonight, if they can, after high street retailer Argos canceled pre-orders long after the consoles had already sold out everywhere else.

Even though the X25 getting one last restock is good news, it’s still hard to believe so many people are willing to pay its MSRP that it has become one of the most highly sought-after consoles in recent memory. The translucent green X25 costs $899.99. That’s $400 more than a standard Series X cost when the console launched six years ago.

To try and sweeten the deal, Xbox threw in a free copy of Halo: Campaign Evolved with X25 pre-orders. That deal will still apply with the restocked consoles, as all X25s will come with a matching controller and the Halo remake.

The email targets those who haven't turned on their Xbox in a while.

#4138. Never one to lag behind HSR and ZZZ, Genshin Impact will introduce its own new pink-haired animal-themed girl in Version Luna 6

Plus Mondstadt is expanding yet further north in Genshin Impact's Luna 6 update.

Today’s Genshin Impact Special Program has wrapped up, and it’s brought us some big news about the next major update. Luna 6 is the next phase in the action RPG’s story, titled Song of the Welkin Moon: Rondo - Augured Homecoming.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of new content, including a big expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

As part of this new update, Mondstadt’s northern parts expand with new areas. The new Dornman Port is one thing, but the most exciting is the Temple of Space. This floating structure is home to Asmoday fragments, and is made up of different realms inspired by Liyue, Sumeru, and various other civilizations from around Teyvat. Launching with the update is a new mechanic that lets you manipulate the space to reveal hidden paths containing secrets.

If you take the time to explore, you’ll find a lot to there to learn about Asmoday, Ruler of Space. There’s a new boss to take on in the temple, too: Watcher: Fallen Vigil.

The only new character in Luna 6 is Linnea, who continues the current trend within HoYoverse games of focussing heavily on cute pink-haired animal-themed girls. Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her big gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

This update will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no new characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other new arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

#4137. Beloved Co-Op Adventure Big Walk in Hot Water After Failing to Disclose AI Usage

Big Walk, one of the most highly-rated games of 2026, has suddenly found itself in a spot of bother, and it's all thanks to those controversial AI tools.

This story stems from the Independent Games Festival Awards (IGF); some of the jurors have taken a hard stance against usage of generative AI or LLM technology.

These jurors recently put out a statement in which they condemn the tech, and in the aftermath of this, it's come out that developer House House did in fact use gen AI, albeit in a minor capacity, when making Big Walk.

On the game's official website, this is now addressed directly in a new FAQ page.

In the statement, House House says LLMs were used "sparingly" near the end of the game's production "to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs."

"In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

The statement goes on to provide an example of how and why the tech was used.

Ultimately, it seems the team has utilised AI very minimally, but that its use was not previously disclosed has rubbed people the wrong way.

Usually, generative AI usage is declared on a game's Steam page, but House House says it didn't do so because "the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage" but has made it public information in light of IGF's actions.

It opens up the debate about gen AI once again. Whether you like it or not, more and more games are being built with the tech to varying degrees, and I expect the number will only grow bigger over time.

However, its ubiquity doesn't safeguard it from criticism, especially when it comes to generating in-game assets, writing, or other creative aspects.

In Big Walk's case, an LLM was used to help with specific technical issues, which I think is relatively harmless, but others may still feel any gen AI is too much.

#4136. Caleb's third Myth has finally arrived in Love and Deepspace, and it's good news for all the husbandbro fans out there

Love and Deepspace has kicked off a new event, squarely built around Caleb's new Memory Pair.

Love and Deepspace’s latest update is here, adding a new Memory Pair for Caleb. The event is dubbed Ghosts' Final March, and it’s available now as part of a new Limited Wish Pool, as it has always worked.

The new Memory Pair is a 5-Star Solar-Slot, which can be obtained through the aforementioned Wish Pool. Doing so will unlock the Netherlord Companion for Caleb, and there’s even more for you to explore in this one.

Alongside the big new Memory Pair, Ghosts' Final March also offers the opportunity to earn a new 4-Star Solar-Slot Memory Pair, alongside ten Deepspace Wishes, 500 Diamonds, and other freebies. The event ends on April 11, so you have some time to get in and play.

If you’re only interested in the 5-Star variants, you’ll be happy to know that Infold is sticking with 150 pulls as the absolute maximum to guarantee earning Netherlord. This will be automatically unlocked after you pull both Nether Yearning and Nether Parting through the Wish Pool.

Obtaining either of the two will give you access to all chapters for the new Myth that’s also available as part of this event: Yin Yang Sundering. You can read all the lore once either of the two Memories have been unlocked, and you won’t even need to upgrade either of them.

The Lost Souls event has also kicked off alongside the new update. You can take part to claim a 4-Star Solar Slor Memory Pair for Caleb: Duskshard Dreams and Duskshard Lotus. You can also earn the 3-Star Memory, Lotus Bond, alongside some other freebies like more Wishes, Diamonds, Photo Poses, and an event-exclusive title.

After you unlock Caleb’s Netherlord Companion, you may want to fight alongside him to get another 4-Star Memory for free. You’ll need to challenge the the Rehearsal Stage to do so, and your first clear is guaranteed to get you the Duskshard Lotus Memory.

If you’re new to Love and Deepspace, or you simply want a refresher, we’ve put together a guide to help you wrap your head around Myths; how they work and how to unlock them. Banners are also an important part of any gacha game, Love and Deepspace included, so here’s how banners work, and what the current and next banners are.

And, as ever, it’s worth checking if you’re missing any of these Love and Deepspace codes to get some in-game freebies.

#4135. The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Is Nintendo's Fastest-Selling Switch 2 Game Ever

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Nintendo's second remake of the original N64 game that first launched way back in 1998, is the fastest-selling Nintendo-published game on the Switch 2 ever. That accolade comes after the game sold more than 5.2 million copies in just four days following its November 5 launch last week.

This remake is already the Switch 2's second-best-selling Nintendo game at 5.2 million units sold, behind Mario Kart World's impressive 16.48 million copies sold to date. If The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time keeps this pace up, it could one day overtake Mario Kart World, though the Mario Kart series typically holds onto that top spot. Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is still far and away the best-selling game on Switch.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the crown jewel of Nintendo's 40th Zelda series anniversary celebration, which also includes other games, products, and even an upcoming worldwide orchestral tour. Plus, a live-action Legend of Zelda film will debut in theaters worldwide on April 30, 2027.

Game Informer gave The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time a 9.25 out of 10 in its review, with our reviewer Kyle Hilliard writing, "For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve the original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn't expect to be so moved."

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launched last week exclusively on Nintendo Switch 2.

For more, read this interview with the remake's producers about changes to the original game, easter eggs, the Bombchu bowling alley operator, and more, then check out this feature breaking down the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time easter eggs that did and didn't make it into this 2026 remake. After that, read about how the Switch 2 Pro controller can make The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time even better, then check out this interview with award-winning composer and musician Jon Batiste about the Ocarina of Time score.

Did you pick up The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time last week? Let us know what you think of it so far in the comments below!

#4134. Talking Point: With Big Walk, The AI-In-Game-Dev Debate Just Got A Lot Murkier

"The line must be drawn here! This far, no further!"

Please forgive the Captain Picard First Contact quote (it's been a couple of weeks since Patrick Stewart's death and only now can I mention his most famous character without welling up) - I promise it's relevant as an illustration of an admirable, principled stance.

In the Borg, good ol' Jean-Luc had a well-defined enemy to engage, with the threat of humanity's assimilation providing a pretty clear line between good and bad. There are larger philosophical questions about the hive mind and our aversion to Star Trek's cube-riding automatons, but for the purposes of this article, let's assume we're all in agreement: Borg=baaad.

Back in the real world, though, that line between right and wrong often isn't so easy to define. Today there'll be a lot of commentators in the video game space, players and developers alike, longing for a better understanding of another encroaching, all-consuming entity.

House House's belated disclosure that LLMs were used during the development of indie hit Big Walk pours fuel on an already raging debate and brings questions over permissible AI use in game dev right back into the discourse - specifically the differences between generative AI for player-facing audio-visual assets and writing versus coding and other less obvious uses.

News Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

This latest flashpoint followed a statement released by a subset of IGF Award jurors explaining why they won't be voting for games developed using any form of generative AI.

Last year, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — which swept The Game Awards with nine wins from 13 nominations — raised similar questions after the Indie Game Awards disqualified Sandfall Interactive's game upon discovering AI had been used in the development pipeline.

I've voiced my distaste for GenAI, and it remains a massive no-no - professionally and personally. I'm fortunate to not have corporate overlords mandating its use around these parts, which certainly isn't the case for some other outlets, nor for many creatives in the gaming space. The gulf in quality between the human-written word and generated bilge is still enormous and easily identifiable, and for now, the same is broadly true of GenAI visual artwork, too.

What this Big Walk situation highlights, however, is how difficult it can be to discern in other places, and the increasing pull it has on even the most principled developers.

Talking Point Does It Bother You That Big Games Companies Are Using GenAI?

The phrase gets bandied around a lot, but it's fair to call Big Walk a proper 'critical darling'. It garnered "Universal Acclaim" back in August, with an impressive 91 Metascore. Alex gave it a "Great" 8/10 after reviewing the Switch 2 version for us - technical hiccups took the shine off it for him, but he still loved the co-op experience. And by September it was already Nile's GOTY.

As someone who didn't play Big Walk at launch, its place in my GOTY-catch-up priorities may have shifted, but wherever you land on the GenAI spectrum, the consensus among critics and players is as unanimous as it gets: Big Walk is an excellent video game.

There are many issues to consider — not least where AI use crosses from tool to theft — but an important one relates to how this game in particular has had a profound effect on many players. Rejecting something flagged as 'suspicious' on principle is easy, especially with so many brilliant games releasing each week. But something you've played already and internalised and loved? From a dev team you respect?

For some, this revelation will feel like when a beloved artist/actor/writer/musician is revealed to be problematic, but we're not talking about illegal behaviour or allegations here.

If House House's statement is to be taken at face value, the team used a chatbot to find a solution to a coding issue with Unity, the third-party engine the game is built on. People online with real chops have already investigated the specifics of House House's single example:

took me 3 hours but I figured out the “URP culling shadowcasters behind the camera” issue House House cites in their disclosure. This culls immediately when the object is off-camera, but modifying the culling params with a custom frustrum is straightforward

this needs cleaning up but is basically the gist

This was a terrible use of 3 hours, but I know just a bit more about how to do something cool. I’m sympathetic to them wanting to ship something good but AI rots your damn brain

That's the one example the devs offer in their statement, and the language around further usage feels vague. The impression it gives is of a team searching for a solution to a specific problem using common tools, as opposed to vibe-coding huge swathes of the game.

Now, I've never programmed anything in my life, but I can appreciate that efficient code must be an art in itself. Is it any less of an art because that code is invisible to players? Then again, to me, generating great chunks of game code feels very different from using an LLM to squash a bug or find a solution when third-party documentation fails. Is one usage as 'bad' as the other, or is this slippery slope, gateway-drug territory?

(Perhaps if any programmers are reading, they'd like to share thoughts in the comments - as the headline says, this is very much a talking point and I'm keen to explore with as much nuance as the internet will permit.)

My point is that seeing exactly where to draw that line is increasingly difficult when AI tools of all types become ubiquitous. A blanket rejection of anything inevitably now means excluding not just an increasing number of games, but also artistically significant, important ones.

And with executives like former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser advocating the use of AI for indie teams to improve workflow, it's also easy to understand how a developer might turn to the tech. The whole topic is getting greyer by the day, much to the pleasure of evangelists, I'm sure.

Like it or not, this situation forces AI sceptics to reconcile their positive feelings for the game. House House estimates "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code" has any trace of generative AI, but to paraphrase a certain Starfleet captain again, "How much does it take before it becomes wrong, hmm?" That is the question.

For some players who simply don't care, it's a non-issue. Some may reluctantly cut the game from their lives and GOTY lists. I suspect that others, though, disappointed or otherwise, will start reconsidering where they personally draw the AI line.

And if House House hadn't disclosed this, would anyone have ever known? I'd guess not. And if a celebrated indie team turned to AI as a problem-solver, how many other devs aren't disclosing similar usage? And how many sure-as-hell won't do so after this?

Lots of questions, no clear answers, just murk. How unsatisfying. I've heard 'ends-justify-means' sentiments online — 'hey, if the game is good, does it matter?' — which feel unsavoury given the documented, quantifiable damage AI is doing to the games industry and the wider world. It's that damage which has IGF jurors abstaining from voting for Big Walk this year: an understandable, admirable stance.

Which leads us to one final question: What would Captain Picard do?

Naturally, he'd call everyone into the Observation Lounge for a big old meeting in a calm, civilised manner, that's what. Conference.

Let us know below if this revelation changes your relationship with the game or where you draw the line when it comes to generative AI in its various forms.

I’m not a game dev but a software engineer with over 15 years of end-to-end more than just full stack software development experience who helped build up 2 successful startups with my own hand written code, no matter the coding language, backend, front end, infrastructure as code.

I’ve started to increasingly use AI because in today’s world it would burn you out to do anything without AI with all the pressure coming from needing to survive as a business.

My own rule is simply to use AI only to the capacity that ensures you have full control and AI doesn’t take over, and not in a way that replaces Human Resources but improves efficiency. In art this is difficult to achieve, but for coding it is simple.

1) If it’s some quick one-time tedious type of work (e.g. migrating to a new system), AI can be immensely helpful, you only need to review the end-result/output. I find the use of AI okay if you are capable of ensuring quality output and review it.

I had AI write scripts to do several types of migration work where it would take me weeks to learn all the tiny bits and unknowns, then write all the code. I used to do it all by hand and it is thankless work where you learn a lot of things you will never apply again in your life. Perfect scenario for AI to just do it. It can research everything needed and think of unknowns you couldn’t think of. Once the work is done, throw the scripts away because migration is done. Weeks of work reduced to a mere few hours. Instead I can focus on more fun parts of my job.

2) if its production level code that impacts user experience, I feel you should only use AI for assistance to improve and not to build. You need full control. We had an instance in the company somebody wrote the entire microservice via AI in a way he was incapable of debugging without AI. One part of it I had to rewrite completely by hand to fix it. They had no clue what they were doing and it could have been a disaster.

Unfortunately, I personally have come across too many lazy developers that make me prefer AI written code over their code, because AI simply codes better, more structured, can follow design patterns properly.

If you are unable to clearly envision the expected logic you intend to write, the expected design patterns used, don’t use AI. Learn first.

This brings me to 3) using AI to improve your skills is an extremely powerful tool. I told a friend to have AI teach him design patterns since I have no time for doing that, but he can always cross check with me. He has never improved so fast in his own hand-written creations before AI.

— Now I’ve tried using AI in various ways for coding and one thing for sure is that you need to be extremely good in giving boundaries and directions. Basically the correct “prompt”, and you can only do that if you have enough experience and skills yourself to control AI in that way. And you can never get there if you just let AI do all the work. It makes a lot of mistakes.

Now if I had to not worry about money, I would use AI far less and only for code reviews or learning, basically jsut as “feedback”, not a producer. But that’s not something I can afford, especially in a world where all employers now expect you to use AI to improve cost-efficiency.

Maybe not a common take, or a popular one, but I'm not a developer, yet I've been able to do amazing things with AI that I never could have without it. I have always had ideas and never been able to do anything with them because I lack the skill to code, and the time/desire to learn.

Since picking up Claude Code less than a year ago I've made several small games for myself that were terrible and I abandoned, but I've also been able to make some great stuff:

All of these projects are open source, on my github, and I will never charge for them, so I have the luxury of saying if you don't like it, don't use it. But I can sympathize with people who CAN code and are being forced to work faster not smarter on commercial projects, or losing their jobs altogether because 1 developer can do the work of 3, with the quality of none.

At work I've been able to (with my CEO's blessing) teach an AI agent how to fix 80% of the issues we see regularly to the point where over half of my daily work is done now with fully deterministic code, written by an AI agent, and the rest is triaged and investigated before I ever see it. Our time to resolution has gone down, and customer satisfaction has gone up, and we still send every communication by hand. None of the code is user facing, and none is supported by our dev team, so it's only to benefit our support staff.

I'm absolutely against using AI to replace people, whether it's in development, design, art, writing, communication, or anywhere else, but I'm a huge proponent of using it to enable your team to hand-off the time consuming, repetitive tasks to agents and focus on the things that the love about their job instead.

I'm very anti AI. I also turn my TV against the wall in case it steals my soul.

@Slowdive I think your blanket statement is at odds with the nuance the article is calling for.

"Do you use Google search? Then you are BAD. EVIL. NO GOOD."

See how ridiculous that sounds? I'm not pro-AI by any stretch but I do think we need to come to terms with the fact that technology will indeed advance, and AI tech is never going to go away. Let's call out bad USES of it instead! I think there's a lot of tools that are going to stick around that will enable tiny, small indie teams who use it PURPOSEFULLY to make some really lovely experiences.

One of the most common defenses of AI is that it's just a tool. This is, technically, true.

A hammer is also a tool. You can use a hammer to make a beautiful birdhouse. You can use it to make an ugly birdhouse. Or you can use it to bash in the brains of someone who criticized your birdhouse.

The difference is that there are already well established rules/laws in place about ethical hammer usage. With AI, we're really only getting started, and it's probably going to take a long time to figure out all the nuances, especially with a technology that will only continue to evolve.

I am also aware that there are environmental concerns, but I don't know enough to comment.

@OrangeSoda I mean, those laws haven't stopped hammers from being used wronfully.

Also, any actual illegal use of AI has already had people prosecuted. People generating pics that harm others have been jailed.

Of course when it's about copyright and whatever about protecting IPs, where it's a more grey issue about what is or isn't fair use, no one has faced actual consequences.

Y'know, I've struggled with my own thoughts on AI, a thing that describes the ultimate plagiarism machine approved by the dumbest and worst people in the entertainment industry but also completely normal shortcuts used in various aspects of tech that were fine to good before renamed the same thing as the plagiarism machine as a marketing tool.

And my main thought is to think of how people will bring up the most logical extreme to try to get a less extreme thing to happen. This is a compromise in many places, but the one that comes to mind is when the creator of a family friendly show wants to do anything that isn't just the safest, made for 6 year olds only story possible. So they'll put something with zero chance of making it past the censors, so that they can sneak in something more reasonable because its less extreme.

I think that's my stance. I am as anti-AI as reasonably possible, because I only want the reasonable examples of AI (much of which we did not call AI 10 years ago, always keep that in mind) to exist. And the only way to do that is to push against AI entirely, because that is likely, the only way to prevent the bad parts of AI to happen.

Though part of it is also that the bad parts of AI are so obviously terrible that this is the level of nuance you need to present for any of it to be remotely tolerable. Which is admittedly, unfair. But in that case, the blame for that is on the people that (sometimes quite literally) poisoned the water. If this is just a new tool, it is a new tool. But when you make it AI vs. artists, the only correct opinion when you are forced into an all or nothing choice is to burn it all down to save artists. And at the end of the day, this is maybe the most obviously, corporate approved, forced trend of my lifetime. Being anti-AI is just being against the extreme of corporate destruction and replacement of art, because there's not much of a choice otherwise.

I feel bad for people stuck in the middle, and I hope someday we can have a more nuanced look at all this. But while I wouldn't say people should or need to or that even necessarily I would refuse to buy a game for this exact scenario (I'm almost certainly gonna buy E33 someday and that had its own weird AI controversy), if someone did, I would not blame them. It is not difficult, even in this scenario, just be like "no thanks", and move on to the many games where you don't have to even think about this nonsense.

Also for me personally, sometimes I'd just rather not waste my time thinking about such things at all. Being annoyingly controversial and nuanced is not something that makes me want to buy a game, sounds like a pain. I think way too much about way too much bad stuff, I don't need to spend my time on being conflicted about a game choice when I could play countless other games.

@dartmonkey I'm an embedded software engineer who has dabbled a bit in AI-assistent use in the context of my work. I'd say at the moment I have a "middle of the road" stance on AI usage in this form. I've seen the advantages and disadvantages of using AI for code generation/fix/support and I acknowledge both the opportunities and threats that AI present.

In my experience, the code that an engineer writes is a means to an end, a way to implement a certain logic concept into something that actually works. As such, I consider my core work to be the conceptual logic I think of, whereas the actual coding part is merely a necessary task to fulfil that logic. It's no surprise then that code generation has been used for decades already in software engineering, be it model-based or low-code or whatever that I'm not even aware of. Though most of those solutions were not very smart, the generation works based on a very strict logic and it's the engineer task to make sure that logic translates into correct code. In this context, using AI to generate code seems merely a new iteration of the same concept, but now it's smarter. It uses the experience of thousands of software engineers to try and generate the correct code based on the prompt. A different way to achieve the same result.

Now, some would say that writing the most optimized, efficiently running and easily maintainable code is also an art in itself. That may be true, but history has also shown that humans engineers are phenomenally bad at achieving that result consistently (which explains why code generation is even a thing). We're reliant on other, more experienced engineers to show us how to achieve those code quality goals, the best design patterns and the best practices. And that in turn makes the code we write only as good as the teachers that taught us. Now compare that with using AI, which will eventually (MAJOR caveat there, "eventually" is doing a lot of heavy lifting) be trained on the best quality code, best design patterns and best practices of hundreds of thousands software engineers. That's a huge win. It's a good result, especially in the context of "just writing the code". If the engineer creates the correct design, the AI only needs to generate the best possible code to make that design a reality. Based on this view, I do not consider AI use to generate, fix or optimize code an issue.

@dartmonkey But I'd like to reframe the concept to something you as a writer can better relate to. How do you feel about the following scenario. A writer is struggling with a paragraph in a certain text, even after multiple drafts they are not satisfied. Eventually, they contact a fellow writer and ask the very simple question "how would you write this part"? Perfectly normal, right? But how about that writer uses an AI to ask the same question. Instead of getting one suggestion from a known source, they get the combined response of over thousands of writers. Sure, these are anonymous sources and might not have given this response explicitly, but the end result is much the same, I think.

This is similar to the coding scenario, I believe. The question becomes, what is your core output as a writer. The message you want to convey, or the way you present that message. Now, I can see how for writing that presentation is much more important that the coding is for achieve a logic result; calling the actual writing of a text "a means to an end" for a message is going too far. But, I think considering this view has merit.

And so, with the use of AI in any context, I think the way AI is utilized is very important in determining the "morality" of its use. There's a huge difference between asking an AI to "write a positive review about this game" and "reword this paragraph to make it sound more neutral". Same as there's a huge different between asking an AI to "make a game where an electrician jumps on platforms" and "make the physics of this jump routine more natural".

#4133. The Petit Planet beta is coming back with new updates, but you still need to hope for an invite

If you've been missing Petit Planet since it was last available to play, you'll be happy to know that HoYoverse is hosting another test soon.

It’s been quite a while since we’ve heard anything about Petit Planet, the upcoming game from Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail developer HoYoverse. By most accounts, Petit Planet is the studio’s take on Animal Crossing, though with a few interesting ideas of its own.

The game’s most recent test took place all the way back in November, but its next big test isn’t far off.

HoYoverse announced today that Petit Planet’s Stardrift Test is scheduled for April 21. This latest build will be available on PC, Android, and iOS. The beta will include new Neighbors, an updated Starsea Voyage, and more for you to do at the Galactic Bazaar.

Seeing as interacting with Neighbors is a core part of this life sim RPG, the confirmation that new faces will be available in this test is big news. Each Neighbor in Petit Planet is a character, with their own personalty and life story.

The Starsea Voyage now includes a map, too, which you can use to take you to other Islets. If you played any of the previous tests, you should already be familiar with this feature.

The only bit of bad news here is that this remains a closed beta. You’re still encouraged to sign up on the official website, but you’re not guaranteed access. HoYoverse said that only a portion of players who sign up will be invited to the upcoming beta.

Petit Planet remains without a release date. If nothing else, it’ll be interesting to see the progress the game has made since last November’s beta.

#4130. Heartopia celebrates 30 million downloads with new outfits, permanent price cuts

Heartopia's rise has continued since its launch earlier this year, and the game's developer isn't slowing down with updates.

Heartopia has kicked off a new event to celebrate passing 30 million downloads. Just a couple of weeks after delivering the vintage Hollywood-themed Dreamlight Cinematics event, developer XD Games has revealed The Whimsical Tea Party, a limited-time Gilded Acorn Exhibition.

The event kicked off on Saturday, bringing some new themed content to the game.

Whimsical Tea Party’s biggest addition are the new outfits, including the Wandering Traveler, and the Duke Bunny outfits. Each outfit is available in three different colours. Another thing Heartopia events bring are building materials sets.

This one adds the Labyrinth furniture building materials set, the Hedgehog & Flamingo mallet, and the Cheshire Cat pet costume. Speaking of outfits, XD Games is dropping the in-game prices for a number of items permanently.

All original pet outfits now cost 66.7% less. Those of the Common variety will now cost 10 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, instead of the previous 30. Rare pet outfits will cost 5 Souvenir Ticket Stubs, down from 15.

If you happened to buy Common or Rare original pet outfits between July 17, 2024 and March 22, 2026, you’ll be refunded the difference. This will automatically show up in-game the next time you log in. If you instead purchased those pet outfits between March 23 and April 4, you should look forward to your refund before April 10.

Keeping with the theme of freebies, Heartopia is also celebrating surpassing 30 million downloads worldwide by giving all players a small gift package in-game. This freebie is available until May 29, so you should have enough time to claim it.

For comprehensive guidance on where to find birds, bugs, and fish, check out our Heartopia bird locations, Heartopia bug locations, and Heartopia fish locations guides. If you’re instead looking to find some wild vegetables for those cooking recipes, hit those links. And, as ever, it doesn’t hurt to see if you missed out on any Heartopia codes.

#4129. Honkai: Star Rail players are eating good, with Version 4.2 and third anniversary celebrations kicking off later this month

Honkai: Star Rail will be celebrating its third anniversary just days after it delivers a major update, and there's quite a bit to chew on in this one.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a stacked Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, delivering the one-two punch of revealing the game’s next major update, and detailing what you can expect from its third anniversary celebrations.

First off, Version 4.2, dubbed So Laughed the Masses, arrives April 22, making two characters playable, and bringing back a host of beloved characters for re-runs. The new update continues the Phantasmoon Games arc, as the story takes an especially suspect new development.

The big inciting incident of this new chapter is the reveal that whoever wins the Phantasmoon Games will also become the permanent Aeon of Elation. Meanwhile, Fulwish has invited all Supplicants to the Fulwish TV HQ to announce their intention to host a TV debate about the ultimate goal of the Phantasmoon Games.

Naturally, you’re invited, and you’ll have to overcome the challenges that await to gather more Wishpower.

Our first new arrival is Silver Wolf LV.999, with whom you should already be familiar from her Version 1 form. The difference now, of course, is that she’s getting a brand-new alternate kit, since — true to her new name — she's evolved into a Godmode Player upon reaching Level 999. Silver Wolf LV.999 is a 5-Star Imaginary character on the Path of Elation.

Her main combat trick is the ability to rack up Hidden MMR, which is what allows her to eventually activate her Cartridge and settle into the aforementioned Godmode state. While in that form, she shifts the entire battle into the virtual world, pulling in both teams into her gaming domain.

This is essentially a world under her control, which is why she can unlock a Reward Stage at the start of her turn, which lets her spawn in-game items. When picked up, these items can turn the tide of battle.

Keeping up with the ultra-gamer persona, Silver Wolf's Aha Instant strike blasts all enemies with a laser cannon, dealing massive damage. Perhaps her most interesting ability is being able to hack into the battlefield when she’s not actively on the team, something she can do when a teammate falls under enemy control.

Evanescia is the other newly-playable character, who has thus far only been an observer of the Phantasmoon Games, as well as one of the most prominent new characters we've met so far on Planarcadia. V4.2 sees the girl join the roster as a 5-Star Physical character who’s likewise on the Path of Elation. As she fights, she always accumulates Certified Banger, when she earns the title she’s able to simultaneously regenerate Energy and maintain her damage.

Evanescia’s damage continues to increase the more Certified Banger she accumulates, triggering an attack from Master Fox upon reaching a certain threshold, which deals damage to all enemies and regenerates Energy for herself. Her Elation Skill adds a bit of a performance to her kit, and is capable of hitting all enemies.

You may have noticed the Path of Elation theme in this one, so you won’t be surprised to learn that the Elation Trailblazer variant on the main playable character is also joining the team in 4.2. There’s a new weapon that starts off as a glow stick but can transform into a lightblade as you deal damage, and, yes, gain Certified Banger.

It can also turn into nunchucks, which delivers a unique flurry of attacks on all enemies surrounding the character, dealing multiple instances of damage. You can also use it to cheer for a teammate, hyping them up.

Version 4.2 Warp Events will bring back six characters. The first half will see reruns of The Dahlia, Castorice, and Firefly. The second half will give you another shot at unlocking Tribbie, Sunday, and Feixiao. What’s more, four of the game’s characters will be buffed in this update, so you may want to reconsider putting them them back on your team. They are Firefly, Huohuo, Seele, and Welt.

As part of the same update, you can expect the debut of the Cosmic Data Roaming event, which goes live alongside the anniversary celebrations. The event lets you live the life of a streamer.

Currency Wars is getting a big expansion, too. Likewise, the Cosmicon Collective is getting its version 2.0 update, adding new decks, dice as well as a new team challenge game mode.

As for the big third anniversary celebration, it will kick off in-game on April 26, bringing back Festive Gifts. The event will only be available during these celebrations, and it will once again be gifting players who log in regularly a total of 20 pulls.

You’ll also be able to a select a blessing card from a companion of your choice to receive a special gift of 1,600 Stellar Jades. The same celebrations will also seeHuohuo and Robin permanently added to the Stellar Convergence store. You’ll have another chance to exchange a Golden Companion Spirit for any companion you like in that store, too — and all you need to do is log in anytime between Versions 4.2 and 4.4. This being a new year for Honkai: Star Rail, the top-up double bonus is resetting, meaning anyone who tops up their wallet will get a hefty bonus.

Elsewhere, you’ll find new items in the Gift of Stardust Store, including a new outfit for Castorice. Between the time 4.2 launches and when the celebrations begin, you’ll be able to try your luck in Aha's Chosen: Spreading Elation Everywhere, an online event where you can leave a message for a chance to win various prizes.

#4128. Guide: Xbox Game Pass Essential: Full List Of Games (November 2026 Update)

Here's everything you can play on Game Pass Essential

Back in 2023, Microsoft finally phased out Xbox Live Gold, replacing it with Xbox Game Pass Core as a new entry-level tier to its subscription service. Since then, it's been renamed to Xbox Game Pass Essential as of October 2025.

We've gathered together the full Xbox Game Pass Essential list of titles down below, and we'll continue to update this guide as Microsoft adds more games to the library. Microsoft says all Essential titles are "fully playable" on both console and PC (despite the Xbox website suggesting only around half are PC-enabled), and a lot of them are supported as part of Xbox Cloud Gaming too.

"Our revamped Essential plan now includes unlimited cloud gaming, online multiplayer, in-game benefits, and Rewards with Xbox, plus a curated catalog of 50+ games playable on both console and PC. The Essential library is now fully playable on PC, featuring standout titles like Hades, Cities: Skylines – Remastered, Stardew Valley, and Warhammer 40,000: Darktide. You also get unlimited cloud gaming, allowing you to play games, including select games you own, on the devices you choose — giving you more freedom to play your way."

Before we get into it, we should mention that Xbox classes various free-to-play games as part of the Xbox Game Pass Essential library (because they feature in-game benefits as part of the service), but we're just going to focus on the paid titles that are included with the program.

Here the list of every Xbox Game Pass Essential title so far (as of November 2026):

#4127. Mouse Work, The Switch 2 Game Using Joy-Con Mouse Controls, Arrives This December

Prepare for your shift by pre-ordering today

Update [Tue 10th Nov 2026, 11:35pm]: Nitrome has now officially announced Mouse Work will be arriving for Switch 2 on 7th December 2026.

It's described as the ultimate showcase for the system's mouse controls, and will include a "massive 8-10 hour campaign solo" or you can bring a crew with you for a co-op experience. This includes 1-4 players locally and online via GameShare.

"In Mouse Work, players take on the role of adorable mice that are just trying to earn some cheddar. Fortunately for them, the local Job Centre has a wealth of offerings available, each testing our mice with new and innovative cursor-based gameplay."

This title will set you back $19.99 / £15.99 and pre-orders are now live on the eShop. Nitrome has also shared a new trailer, which you can check out above.

Original Story: Remember Mouse Work? It was announced by developer Nitrome for the Switch 2 just a few months before the system's launch and requires you to use mouse controls to complete all sorts of fun and challenging jobs.

We've not got an update about this title since last year, but it looks like it's finally on the way. According to a listing that has recently appeared on the Japanese Nintendo Store and eShop, it will be arriving this holiday season on 7th December 2026 for 2,200 yen.

The translated description notes how the campaign is 10 hours across more than 50 unique stages. You'll also be able to participate in local and online multiplayer, including GameShare support. When we hear more about the local release, we'll provide an update.

Nitrome has previously released games such as Bomb Chicken and Shovel Knight Dig on the original Switch. Are you excited for its new game on Switch 2? Let us know in the comments.

#4124. Animal Crossing: New Horizons gets a new item to celebrate 25 years of the series

The allegedly finished game might finally, truly be feature complete with the addition of an anniversary item.

Animal Crossing: New Horizons has received a surprise patch today to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the life sim series. The update, version 3.0.2, is available across the Switch and Switch 2 versions of the game.

The patch brings a single new addition to New Horizons - a leaf item. Everyone gets it, too, so you don’t have to do anything special to acquire it.

After installing the patch, simply head to your in-house mailbox to claim it. The mail includes a hearty message to fans who supported the series for years, featuring an appropriate Nintendo N64 stamp.

The Leaf Statue, as it’s referred to in-game, lights up when placed.

April 14, 2011 marks the release of the original, lesser-known version of Animal Crossing in Japan. The game was initially released as Animal Forest (Dobutsu no Mori) on the Nintendo N64, before later making its way to the Nintendo GameCube in December of the same year as Dobutsu no Mori+ with some extra features.

That same, original design of the package is also available for display in your game. The rest of the patch notes are entirely about various bug fixes, so not much more there. You can see the full change log on Nintendo’s support website.

#4123. Metro 2039 goes back to its Metro underground roots, with a story shaped by the war in Ukraine and the people who suffer it

Metro 2039 takes us back to the tunnels of the Moscow Metro where, fittingly, Nazi ideology never died.

The Metro series is finally, officially back with a new installment. 4A Games has just unveiled Metro 2039 to the world, the follow-up to the outstanding Metro Exodus, released all the way back in 2019.

2039 takes an unusual route with its scope, however. Rather than build on the semi-open-world structure of Exodus, the upcoming sequel instead brings the focus back to where it all began: the Metro.

What won’t be changing is the kind of game that it is. Metro 2039 remains, like its predecessors, a story-driven, single-player game. Returning to the confined spaces of the Moscow Metro brings the focus back to the claustrophobic, uneasy atmosphere of the original games.

The game’s protagonist is, for the first time, going to be voiced throughout. From what we’ve been able to see, the psychological horror in this installment will be driven more by the very real effects the apocalypse has had, and continues to have, on denizens of the Metro.

2039 has been in development for years, but 4A Games has been rocked by two considerable events: the 2020 Covid pandemic, and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, where the developer is based. The game’s darker story has changed in response to that.

The team’s Ukrainian perspective is molded into the narrative, and more prominently represents the toll the events of the last several years has taken on members of the team, their families and communities.

According to the developer, you can expect a bigger emphasis on choice and consequence, with Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky returning to co-write a narrative that explores the compromised morality of a post-war society.

The new protagonist’s return to the Metro comes with the reveal that the different underground factions are now united under one banner, the not-so-subtly named Novoreich. Lead by a former Spartan, the Novoreich is an authoritarian regime which offers what it believes to be the only path to salvation.

4A Games remains majority Ukrainian, with teams based in Kyiv, and Malta. Unlike most AAA projects today, the studio continues to rely on its own engine tech. The 4A Engine is given a major upgrade for 2039: ray tracing is now a core component of the rendering pipeline, but the tech has been rebuilt to run better on modern hardware.

Today’s reveal sadly didn’t feature much gameplay - only a brief first-look with a mix of gameplay and cinematics. The developer, however, emphasised that creating cluttered, believable and lived-in environments remains a key focus.

Metro 2039 is set for release sometime this winter on PC, Xbox Series X/S, and PS5.

#4122. Halo 2 Is 22 Years Old Today, And I'm Gutted The Remake Isn't Happening

Pure Xbox is listening to: Blow Me Away - Breaking Benjamin 🎶

It feels like only yesterday that Halo: Campaign Evolved teased a remake of Halo 2, something I've been hoping for more and more as time went on. After all, it's been 22 long years now. Yep, that's right - Halo 2 launched on November 9, 2004 for the original Xbox, and has often been credited as the game that put Xbox Live on the map.

As the years slip by, anniversaries for OG Xbox titles have a habit of making me feel my age. Still, what a privilege it was to be there for the inception of Xbox Live, to play both co-op and PvP with friends across the globe in the second entry of Bungie's incredible run of Halo games.

Admittedly, it's been a hot-minute since I last booted up Halo 2 in the Master Chief Collection. But visits to retro gaming bars like Manchester's NQ64 reminded me just how good this FPS still is. I recall sitting down for a few games of Slayer, only for the muscle memory to kick in and humble a good number of Hookshot staff - Fraser included. Oh boy, it never gets old.

In fact, just sit back and listen to 15 minutes of Halo 2's main menu music and ponder the good old days of dual-wielding SMGs in Beaver Creek.

Halo 2 took Master Chief's fight against the Covenant to Earth, selling more than 8.4 million copies before its servers shut down in 2010, following the discontinuation of the original Xbox Live services. The game was later ported to PC and remastered for Xbox One as part of Halo: The Master Chief Collection.

Xbox's 25th anniversary is just round the corner: in fact, it's this Sunday! We'll be here, keeping an eye out for any and all announcements from Xbox throughout the week. Understandably, we've been feeling pretty nostalgic, hence this Halo 2 feature. In fact, I'm reinstalling the MCC as we speak.

I was a big fan of Halo Studios' Campaign Evolved. Like, I really, really enjoyed it. So, it's bittersweet knowing that their teased Halo 2 remake in Unreal Engine will never happen.

Sure, the devs fumbled modern Halo multiplayer, but perhaps a Halo 2 remake could have been a case of history repeating itself. Y'know, a remade return of Halo 2's iconic online multiplayer?! Ah, well.

#4121. PSA: Nintendo Ending Google And Apple Sign-Ins On Nintendo Accounts In 2027

You'll need a Nintendo Account from here on out

If you currently use a Google or Apple account to sign in to your Nintendo Account, Nintendo has got some news. In an official notice, it's announced the discontinuation of Google and Apple account sign-ins on Nintendo Accounts.

This will take place on 26th January 2027, so we're just a few months out. "As of" this date, it will no longer be possible to link a Google or Apple account. Nintendo notes this exact end time "may be delayed depending on the progress of the system change work".

Nintendo: "We apologise for any inconvenience to those who used a Google or Apple account to sign in to their Nintendo Account."

Here's what this means when it does come into effect:

And "if you are already logged into your Nintendo Account on a device, you may not have to sign in again". If the sign-in page does appear, you'll need to sign in using the email address or sign-in ID and your password for your Nintendo Account, or a Passkey.

If we hear any updates about this, we'll let you know. What are your thoughts about this announcement? Let us know in the comments.

Liam is a news writer and reviewer on Nintendo Life. He's been writing about games for more than 15 years and is a lifelong fan of many iconic video game characters.

#4120. PS Store Adds PS5 Hardware Tab, But It's Extremely Limited

Sony has begun advertising PS5 hardware and accessories directly through the console's PS Store via a new Hardware tab at the end of its horizontal scroller.

The new page promotes PS5 consoles, controllers, the PS Portal, headsets, PSVR2, and PS5 Covers. There's then a part below it that details the sort of benefits you get by ordering through PlayStation Direct.

Here's how the new Hardware tab on the PS Store looks on a PS5 system:

I've taken a look through the tab, and while all the visuals are indeed neat and eye-catching, the actual implementation is extremely limited. These sections are essentially just landing pages that want you to scan the QR code from your phone, which directs you to the relevant section of PlayStation Direct in your web browser.

From there, you can buy PS5 systems and accessories.

I suppose this works well as an advertisement for the more casual gamers who may not be aware of the latest PS5 accessories, controllers, and console covers. However, the more tuned-in fans will already know to simply head to PlayStation Direct for those peripherals.

Liam grew up with a PlayStation controller in his hands and a love for Metal Gear Solid. Nowadays, he's found playing the latest and greatest PS5 games as well as supporting Derby County. That last detail is his downfall.

#4119. Splendid Junji Ito-inspired RPG World of Horror is now 20% more horrible, thanks to a free PC update with extra gods, locations, and wounds

This hole was already made for me, but now it's a fair bit wider and deeper

Excellent apocalypse RPG World of Horror has just received a sizeable free update, As Below So Above, adding no less than two Old Godly invasions for you to identify and thwart. One of these additional cosmic disasters involves four cults summoning their fave abominations at the same time. I picture them forming a shaky barbershop quartet on the skyline, while stamping the streets to mush. Damn it, Ath-Yolazsth – you're leading again!

Also in As Below So Above: more "enemies, mysteries, characters, items, spells, curses, and injuries", together with "a large batch of quality-of-life features and bug fixes". I can only applaud the vicious disconnect of listing "injuries" alongside "quality-of-life". These will be the most polished and ergonomic grievous wounds you've ever had! The experience will flow like your gushing blood!

This is the Junji Ito-inspired game's largest update yet, according to developers panstasz and publishers Ysbryd. It makes the game 20% bigger, though surely no mere percentage can ever encapsulate the creatures and forces that slumber on the other side of the mortal veil.

"Two never-before-seen manifestations of the Old Gods raise the stakes," explains the press release. "IKT-YOSIS, THE FIRST NIGHTMARE, sleeps in a gargantuan chamber beneath the mountains. With each ritual performed to wake him, the world above slowly reshapes itself and brings strange weather with it." You'll need to keep tabs on forecasts, if you want to get ahead of the elements. As for "THE WAR FOR SHIOKAWA", this "adds an extra level of terror, with four cults summoning their eldritch masters simultaneously to plunge the town into pure evil."

It's just as well there are three new puny human protagonists to continue the battle against these cyclopean trouble-makers: Kiriko, who knows her way around a Tarot deck, Satoshi, a seasoned hiker, and Makoto, a school AV club member. You'll also be able to enlist 10 additional allies and learn about them care of a reworked conversation system, which trips at random between investigations.

There's a new location, the Mountains, alongside 60 extra events, 19 enemies, three challenges, and 30 items. And let's not forget the Scenario Mode, which plays host to self-contained yarns set before the main game. The first of these Worldlets of Horror is a hunt for three students lost in the woods, with a variety of endings.

Lots of numbers! And while much of this may break your mind, none of it will break your mods. There's a new modding system that's backwards compatible with everything made for the 1.0 version.

Unfamiliar with World of Horror? Here is Alice Bee's review (RPS in peace): "Repetitive combat in World Of Horror can't entirely mar a unique, stylish and layered horror adventure that makes you want to play more the more that you play."

#4118. Blizzard will talk about Diablo 4: Lord of Hatred one last time before the expansion's launch next week

We're well under two weeks from the launch of Diablo 4's next expansion, Lord of Hatred, but there's more yet to be said.

Diablo 4 is mere days away from the launch of its biggest expansion yet, and Blizzard wants to make sure it got one last chance to tell you about it. Lord of Hatred is the follow-up to 2024’s Vessel of Hatred, and it’s set to arrive on April 28.

Next week, however, we’re getting an updated look at the new content as part of a livestream. This is the Developer Update kind; the meaty, information-dense show anyone who follows Diablo’s livestreams should be familiar with.

The next Developer Update is set for Thursday, April 23. It’ll kick off at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 6pm GMT. The show will, naturally, focus on Lord of Hatred. In particular, we’re getting another look at the expansion content that hasn’t been given the same level of coverage as the bigger features.

Everyone knows about the new Skovos region, the Warlock class (and the Paladin before that), but we haven’t seen much from the other gameplay-altering features that affect a lot of the core flow.

In next week’s showcase, Blizzard will show off the updated and expanded skill trees - which come to all classes, the Talisman system, and the gear-altering Horadric Cube. War Plans, the new make-your-own-endgame feature will be discussed, too.

More interestingly, we’re also going to hear about the new season kicking off right alongside the launch of Lord of Hatred. A short, in-betweener season is currently live in Diablo 4, and it’s going to end right as the next one/the expansion launch.

And, of course, the show won’t end before the team takes a few questions from chat, as is tradition. If you want to catch it live, you’ll be able to do so on Diablo’s official YouTube, Twitch, Twitter, and TikTok channels.

#4117. EA execs choosing Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 was the main factor in BioWare's demise, according to report

Corporate chair shuffling and the Mass Effect studio's recent struggles may also have played roles

The postmortem on BioWare, following their shuttering by EA this month, points to the publisher's preference to back Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 as the main factor in the demise of the beloved RPG developer. That's according to Bloomberg, who also report that a couple of other factors likely also had some influence.

The Bloomberg report paints EA's position as being one of a company caught between spending a bunch of money on a Star Wars shooter-shaped rock and a hard place with a sign that read Mass Effect 5. Disney reportedly swooped in to offer the publishers the opportunity to make Star Wars Battlefront 3 around the time EA were, as a result of being saddled with debt as part of the leveraged buyout which saw the Saudi government and private equity take them over, looking to not to spend as much cash.

So, Star Wars and Mass Effect became a decision of whether Star Wars or Mass Effect would be the better bet to stick projected hundreds of millions of dollars on. The suits, quelle surprise really, went for the series that currently sits just below powerhouse money-maker Winnie the Pooh on Wikipedia's list of the highest-grossing media franchises. Battlefront 3's development reportedly hasn't even kicked off yet, but it's got that safe and predictable big name to it, and will be a shooter to nestle among EA's treasured flotilla of gun and ball games, rather than an RPG.

Bloomberg add that that BioWare's well-documented up and down record with game releases since Mass Effect: Andromeda began a skid which Anthem only made worse and Dragon Age: The Veilguard couldn't arrest also played a role. Potentially also in the mix was some corporate chair and nameplate switching among EA's execs this summer, which saw EA Sports-linked suits David Tinson and Cam Weber promoted while reported BioWare advocate Laura Miele was sidelined via promotion from overseeing EA's non-sports studios to a gig based around helping big boss Andrew Wilson pursue "strategic growth opportunities beyond EA's core business".

For what it's worth, an EA spokesperson told Bloomberg the company "collectively" decided to shoot BioWare into space "following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities".

And so, BioWare's body has been sent to the stars, while Respawn and DICE look set to make Battlefront 3. There is a bit of depressing irony in EA deciding to go for the perceived safe bet of a big name licensed game over taking some risk on a game that'd come without Disney as a rights-holding middleman. This is, after all, the company which in 2022 ditched governing body Fifa as the namesake and licensing partner of their very successful football games, choosing the risk of going it alone with a lesser brand EA would have more direct control over and ownership of rather than sticking with an established big name juggernaut.

Then again, you could probably call EA's soccer games something like 'Hey, you, person reading this: the (insert year here) football game you're looking at thinks your face is ugly and your haircut's stupid' and they'd still fly off the shelves.

#4116. The Sims 4's much maligned paid mods have made it to consoles, but Kits are coming back to PC

The Sims 4's Marketplace and user-created content have officially arrived on consoles, a little over a month after their debut on PC.

The Sims 4 players on PlayStation and Xbox have now caught up to their friends on PC, at least when it comes to the game’s Marketplace. This new feature is essentially a hub for paid mods and other user-created content.

As often happens when long-established games introduce paid mods, The Sims 4’s wasn’t especially well-received, in part because of the introduction of a new premium currency - Moola - that is the only way to purchase any of that content.

The Moola denominations and prices are similar to many other in-game currencies, and the criticism around them is the same: they obfuscate the true value of items, and because of the way those denominations are structured, you’ll never be able to buy exactly what you need.

For most games, the subject of paid mods has always been fraught, and that's certainly true for The Sims 4. In the announcement blog post, Maxis said that the launch on consoles will work similarly to what PC players have seen, in that Kits will no longer be available to buy directly with real money on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores. While Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs will remain, you’ll need to buy Moola if you want to acquire Kits going forward.

Interestingly, however, EA seems to have changed its mind somewhat on the Kits situation. A recently leaked memo (via SimsCommunity), appears to show that the publisher intends on making Kits available for purchase directly again, without the need for Moola.

Unfortunately, this only appears to affect the PC version, with the reversion reportedly forthcoming on both the EA App as well as Steam. Indeed, according to the same report, the change has already taken place on the former, with the latter following on April 20.

Considering the Marketplace only just launched on consoles, the company may wait to see if the decision to remove Kits from console platform marketplaces will be as poorly received as it has been on PC.

If you’re looking to jump back into The Sims 4 to check out all the new paid content, make sure you’re well-equipped with our list of Sims 4 cheats and debug options, or this one specifically for the Royalty & Legacy expansion cheats.

#4115. Unknown 'Mega Man Legends' Project Surfaces Online

As Capcom gears up for Mega Man's 40th anniversary next year, more findings related to the long-running IP are surfacing online.

As reported by Mega Man fan site Rockman Corner, a production titled 'Mega Man Legends' has appeared on ACTRA Toronto's "What's Shooting" database (a public listing of production registered with the Canadian performers' union) this week.

It's filed under "new media" and the production start date was in September, with it scheduled to wrap up by December. Casting is apparently in house, but that's all that's known about the mysterious project.

As the source notes, "new media" could be everything from "video games to television and film". It's also mentions how Capcom "could be looking to Canadian voice talent as an alternative to SAG-AFRA Actors" after "Mega Man: Dual Override became the subject of a SAG-AFTRA 'Do Not Work' order" earlier this year.

Mega Man Legends was originally released as a 3D video game in 1997 and was followed by a second game in 2000. There was also a prequel spin-off in 1999, and a cancelled third entry for the 3DS.

This latest finding also follows a rating board classification in Korea at the end of last month. It featured various classic Capcom console titles, including multiple Mega Man games.

#4114. How To Preload GTA 6 In Full On Xbox Series X|S (Even If You Haven't Bought It)

All 200GB+ goes live in just a few hours' time

The official preload for GTA 6 is literally just a few hours away at the time of writing, and it means everyone will be able to install all 200GB+ of the game on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S ahead of launch on November 19th.

Here are the official preload / preinstall times for GTA 6 on Xbox Series X|S, as we recently highlighted on Pure Xbox:

News GTA 6 Download Size & Preload Times Officially Revealed For Xbox Series X|S

So, there are two ways to preload GTA 6 on Xbox Series X|S depending on whether you have or haven't bought it yet. If you've pre-ordered the game, payment should have now been taken out of your account, and you'll be able to preload it by going to the Microsoft Store app on your Xbox console and searching for Grand Theft Auto VI.

The page you're looking for is the one in the image at the top of this article, although instead of a "pre-order" button, you should see the ability to install the game if you've bought it already. This will install a 300MB placeholder file until 12am GMT on November 10th, after which time the full 200GB download will become available as an update.

If you run into any issues with this, it's worth doing a restart of your console after the full preload goes live.

"On XBOX Series X|S, pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12 a.m. GMT. Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12. The pre-load file will require up to 212 GB depending on your device, so make sure you've got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible."

If you haven't bought GTA 6 yet but still want to preload it on Xbox Series X|S, you can do so by opening up the Xbox mobile app, going to the "Store" page (represented by a bag icon) and searching for Grand Theft Auto VI. You're specifically looking for "Grand Theft Auto VI" - not the Bundle version, but the standalone version.

In our case, it showed up as the fourth option down - you should see a variant of the following page when you open it:

Again, hitting the install button prior to 12am GMT on November 10th will install a small placeholder file, and then the full 200GB+ download will become available when the full game preload goes live.

That means everyone (except Xbox One owners, of course) has the ability to download GTA 6 on their Xbox consoles later today, so be sure to clear some room ahead of time - it's going to take up a heck of a lot of storage space!

#4113. GTA 6 on PS5 Is PS Store's Most Pre-Ordered Digital Game in History

It was always going to be big, but with a week until release, Rockstar has now confirmed that GTA 6 is the most pre-ordered digital game in PS Store history.

Confirmation comes courtesy of the PS Blog, in a post from Sony’s Tim Turi.

“GTA 6 is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of PS Store. Given this unprecedented demand, we’ve joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start pre-loading the game nine days early, so they’re ready to play on launch day. We’ve also adopted a rolling midnight launch by country, beginning at 12:00AM NZDT in New Zealand and running across the globe as respective countries hit midnight on 19th November.”

You can learn more about when you’ll be able to play in our dedicated GTA 6 release times guide, so keep that bookmarked for 19th November.

Digital pre-orders for GTA 6 have been available since 25th June, so Rockstar has had a long time to build up numbers.

It’s worth reiterating that physical versions are following a “code-in-box” format, so there’s less incentive to purchase at retail, too.

(Although in a recent Push Square poll, a remarkable 23% of our readers did say they’d be plumping up for the boxed version.)

Record-breaking pre-orders like this are significant as the PS Store has been selling digital games for over a decade now; that it’s set a new record with over a week to spare and hype still building is remarkable.

While we don’t have actual numbers, Rockstar’s said they’re “exceeding” its external expectations.

Analyst firm Sensor Tower predicts 9.69 million pre-orders have been placed, with an astonishing 75% of those sales commanded by the PS5 version.

It’s worth noting that this milestone comes at a time of deep unrest among PS5 players, who’ve continuously spammed the platform holder with proclamations of ‘No Disc, No Buy’ in the aftermath of its decision to stop shipping physical games in 2028.

Sony recently reported year-over-year increases to its monthly active users, during a period in which enthusiasts mobilised a “blackout” of its platform.

Irrespective of fan frustration, it looks like Rockstar’s latest open world is days away from registering the biggest digital launch in industry history.
