#4112. Naval warfare, an actual server browser and more on the way to Battlefield 6 this year as BF Studios reveals 2026 roadmap

2026 is looking very exciting for Battlefield 6, even if much of what's coming is based on things we already know, and some we've long been asking for.

It took Battlefield Studios over four months to tell Battlefield 6 players what they can actually expect from the game over the course of this year, in terms of content - but we’re glad to see a plan laid out nonetheless.

The developer unveiled a grand 2026 roadmap, covering three more seasons currently in the works, and a wealth of new additions across the entire game, including new maps and the introduction of a new theatre of combat.

In a wide-ranging new video dubbed The Year Ahead, members of the Battlefield 6 development team have revealed a lot of new information about the future of the multiplayer shooter, going over plenty of the features and new content coming over the course of this year.

The video confirmed that BF6 has at least three other seasons in the works. Season 3, which begins in May, will be followed by Season 4, and Season 5 later in the year. Season 5 is the most mysterious, which is understandable.

We’ve known about some of what’s coming in Season 3, such as the remake of Golmud Railway (now called Railway to Golmud), but the video also revealed that a remake of Battlefield 3’s Grand Bazaar - now Cairo Bazaar - will also arrive later in the same season. Other exciting additions, such as battle royale solos and ranked play for Redsec are also on the agenda for Season 3.

Season 4, set for July, looks to be the biggest so far, with the introduction of naval combat, which will be available across two maps. Tsuru Reef, which is said to be even larger than Golmud, the largest map in BF6. The Pacific-set map won’t be the only one, as later in the season, another remake will arrive, this time of the iconic Wake Island.

The introduction of naval combat will bring with it a new dynamic wave system, aircraft carriers with operational flight decks, and new naval vehicles. Custom lobbies and Spectator Mode are also planned for Season 4.

Season 5 will bring three maps to BF6, rather than two, but all of its content remains under wraps.

Perhaps a sour note is that almost all of the maps referenced and shown in the video are remakes of maps from other Battlefield games, or reimagined at the very least. The Battlefield series is no stranger to remaking its own maps, but Battlefield 6 appears to be leaning on it much more than past entries.

If it’s any consolation, however, the map remakes we’ve played so far in Battlefield 6 have gone through major changes that have contributed to giving them a different flow and feel from their classic versions, or even remakes in other BF games.

Over the course of 2026, you can also expect the return of persistent servers, as well as a server browser to find them all - just like the good ol’ days. This includes the ability to host your own, though it’s unclear quite how this is going to work.

Season 3 is set to revealed in the coming days, so you’ll be hearing back from BF Studios in the near future.

#4111. Diablo 4's next season won't have any new mechanics or a new theme because all the focus is on Lord of Hatred

If you don't intend to buy the Lord of Hatred expansion, the next season in Diablo 4 won't be as exciting as you'd expect.

Diablo 4 is gearing up for its biggest post-launch event yet: the upcoming release of the Lord of Hatred expansion. As was the case with Vessel of Hatred before it, expansion releases alter the seasonal flow in a few ways, and Blizzard has now explained how.

The game’s next season - its 13th - has been officially revealed as Season of Reckoning. The new season will kick off alongside the expansion’s release next week, and will be available to all players, just like all previous seasons.

Although Season of Reckoning will roll out as normal, the season itself won’t be as meaty, at least when it comes to the sort of gameplay mechanics and themes players have come to expect from each new season.

You’ll still find the normal Season Rank chase, Smoldering Ashes, and various rewards at each chapter. Season Blessings will also return, but that’s about it for progression outside of the game itself. If it’s any consolation, there are more goals and objectives to tackle this season.

The even better news is that, according to Blizzard, future seasons will follow the classic format, which makes sense. The new season will come with a battle pass, of course, featuring four Reliquaries, as usual. The first Reliquary is free, while the others are paid.

Blizzard has also confirmed the the pre-load for Lord of Hatred is available now on all platforms. Even if you’re not getting the expansion, patch 3.0.0's pre-load includes all expansion content regardless, so you may as well pre-download it to be ready for April 27/28. On launch day, you’ll also need to download a smaller patch, version 3.0.1.

In case you missed it, we published our Lord of Hatred review earlier in the week. Give it a read if you’re curious about the expansion’s impact on the narrative, and how it changes core Diablo 4 gameplay.

#4110. Wooshy wuxia actioner Phantom Blade Zero is sharp enough on the Steam Machine, if blunted on the Steam Deck

It would appear that Phantom Blade Zero (Phantom Blade 0? Zero? Let’s go with Zero) demanding more gigs than a mismanaged stadium is doing little to stop people playing the thing. It therefore stands to reason at least some folks will want to run S-Game Studio’s lightly Soulsy sword-em-up on the Steam Machine, so let us now examine how said GabeCube stands up to its effects-heavy martial artistry. With some settings proposals, natch.

Two signs boded poorly, before I got to testing the Machine. The first was a comment on Oisin’s day one patch piece, warning of heavy glitching on a Linux system. The second was my Steam Deck OLED, also a Linux system, being incapable of running Phantom Blade Zero at even close to a steady 30fps; even with the Low preset and some nasty-looking Ultra Performance upscaling, the game’s flashy moves and jerking (apologies – cinematic) camera shifts made for regular framerate drops into the teens.

Fortunately, the Steam Machine is much more resilient, even if it does benefit from a few quality cuts (and, realistically, will struggle if pushed beyond standard 1080p.) The Medium preset and Quality-level FSR are enough for 45-60fps in what I’ve played so far, and the High preset – while a touch susceptible to sub-40fps dips for my liking – is at least playable without major bugs or stuttering.

Strangely enough, the only major technical problem I’ve had wasn’t caused by graphics, or the Linux-based SteamOS, but the Steam Controller I was playing with. Despite being assured during the boot process that I was being treated to the Official Gamepad Configuration – cor! – an unresponsive map-opening button left me immobile during a prompt tutorial. Immobile and, I suppose without a map, lost. It turns out this this is a common bug with the Steam Controller specifically, and can be fixed by remapping the Select button, in SteamOS’s controller settings, to emulate the effect of clicking the touchpad of a PS5 pad. PC gaming.

With that sorted, Phantom Blade Zero seems to work fine? If I was nitpicking I’d point out that some high-drama sequences are visibly less buttery than the slower, roaming sections, which can exceed 60fps on Medium. Same for a lot of cutscenes, which aren’t hard-locked to 30fps like prerendered scenes often are, but do cause heavy framerate drops for little apparent reason. Still, it’s reasonable when actually playing.

Settings-wise, that Medium preset (with FSR on Quality) works well if you’re lazy. But a few of Phantom Blade Zero’s individual quality options aren’t terribly performance-sapping by themselves, and than thus be tuned upwards for a slightly nicer-looking wuxia tale with minimal drawback. Have a crack with the following:

Don’t miss those Dynamic Resolution Quality and Super Resolution Output Scale tweaks; on their defaults, they both make the game uglier than it needs to be. And on the subject of Super Resolution, FSR upscaling does leave a bit of roughness on certain edges, but then at 1080p, so does FSR even when it’s on its Native Resolution setting. You might as well get the extra frames.

#4109. Round Up: The Reviews Are In For Pikmin 4 - Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy

Following the anticipated return of Zelda: Ocarina of Time last week, Nintendo has now released Pikmin 4 - Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy. The critic reviews have now gone live. If you haven't already seen ours, we gave it seven stars, calling it a pleasant but perplexing piecemeal.

"Overall, £8/$10 is a small price to pay for some minor new features and a fun little mode that'll keep me entertained over the coming year, but it's more of a budding shoot right now than the full-bloom upgrade."

Mini Review Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy (Switch 2) - Pleasant But Perplexingly Piecemeal

And here's what other critics had to say:

"For late-bloomers who have yet to experience the magic that is Pikmin 4, the Nintendo Switch 2 Edition is the best place to start. Not only is native 4K resolution a significant improvement that allows the colourful world of Pikmin to shine brighter than ever before, Dandori Academy brings some worthwhile new content, held back only by Nintendo’s puzzling monthly stage distribution method. While not quite as extravagant as some of the other Nintendo Switch 2 Editions we’ve seen in recent memory, the lower-end $10 for the Upgrade Pack is an appropriate price point for what Pikmin 4 has to offer on Nintendo Switch 2; with the base game being in a class of its own."

"The main takeaway is that Pikmin 4 is still excellent, and I was grateful to transfer my save file from the Switch version (and I was tempted to start a new game + save), but Dandori Academy is not a strong incentive to return if you already played the game. It is a nice bonus and an interesting concept that reimagines the familiar time trial mode featured in plenty of video games, but the original campaign is still the main attraction."

"Pikmin 4 still remains one of my favourite titles released on the original Nintendo Switch, but unfortunately this update has left me feeling more than a little underwhelmed. While the game has seen a visual upgrade and the Oatchi commands are certainly a novel addition, the drip-feeding of its major new Dandori Academy content proves more frustrating than anything. More Pikmin is never a bad thing, but having to wait months to see it all, well… that’s a drag."

"Pikmin 4 is already a great time; Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is just the 4K cherry on top. If you don’t own the original Switch version, then this is an easy recommendation; if you’re here for the upgrade/additions, then the visual upgrade will help. Dandori Academy won’t be for everyone, but over the next year it will continue to add extra challenges. The cheaper upgrade price point helps make it an easier recommendation."

#4108. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.8 is refreshing your team comps with a new mechanic, and the game is coming to Steam

Zenless Zone Zero will soon become the first HoYoverse game to make its way to Steam, though we wish we had more details.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a pretty exciting Zenless Zone Zero Special Program that not only delivered all the details on the next big update, it also came with the unexpected announcement that the action RPG is on its way to Steam.

Previously, all HoYoverse games with PC versions have always been directly available from the developer’s website, or through the Epic Games Store. In other words, Zenless Zone Zero will soon mark the massive company’s debut on Valve’s platform.

The main focus of the livestream, of course, has been Version 2.8, otherwise known as New Eridan Sunset. This upcoming release is scheduled for May 6, though the Steam version does not yet have a date.The new release sees the release of two new Agents, as well as the brand-new Wind attribute enemy.

The release also acts as the last chapter of Season 2, and it sees Ramiel becoming the main target of different factions in the Outer Ring. The two new arrivals, together with Proxies and Cissia will embark on a quest to learn the new identity of Ramiel.

The first new Agent is Promeia, the executioner of Krampus. She’s an S-Rank Ice Anomaly Agent who can consume Trial by Cold to trigger Abloom on enemies. This is done by converting Corrosive Chill.

By using her EX Special Attack, she can enter the Bound Absolution state, which allows her to automatically Perfect Dodge any attack that targets her. If you have another Anomaly or Support Agent on the team, Promeia can further boost the entire squad’s Abloom damage.

The second addition in 2.8 is Starlight - Billy, also an S-Rank Agent, though wielding Physical Rupture instead. This is the upgraded form of Billy, and he arrives on a combat motorcycle to bring his signature Starlight Knight to the fight. Through it, he can deliver big Physical burst damage.

The higher Billy’s health, the more Sheer damage he deals. In fact, all Physical damage he deals lands as Sheer damage. Further building on his tank-like role, his skills can also restore his own health.

Re-runs in Version 2.8 will be Lucia in the first half, and Orphie & Magus in the second. The other exciting addition coming with this update is the new Wind attribute enemy, and the accompanying Vortex mechanic.

When an enemy is inflicted with the Wind Attribute Anomaly, any other Anomaly attack type that gets applied will trigger Vortex, rather than Disorder. This deals AoE Anomaly damage of the type that matches the corresponding element.

Throughout the version’s runtime, you’ll be able to take part in the Marcel Bootopia-themed event, which gives you control of Eous and lets you explore a Bangboo resort island. The island has been closed due to an outbreak of Hollows, and you must rescue Bangboos and find treasures.

If you do, you’ll earn Booltergeist and its Bangboo core for your troubles. This is an A-Rank Bangboo that can float around and fire lasers in combat. Its damage is further boosted whenever certain teammates are present.

The Ultimate Verdict Trial is another event you can check out that lets you fight alongside newcomer Promeia, or take part in other mini-activities that all reward Polychrome. Finally, you can look forward to a new Hoshimi Miyabi outfit: Dignified Blossom, which will be available in the store.

Before you jump back in next month, it always helps to catch up on the latest Zenless Zone Zero codes to make sure you’re not missing out on any freebies.

#4107. Warframe's fantasy-pilled sister Soulframe finally goes open to all this November, though Digital Extremes are "nervous" about certain changes

They're celebrating the end of closed alpha by poisoning the world

Warframe creators Digital Extremes have announced that their free-to-play fantasy RPG Soulframe will be available for everyone to download on 6th November, after two years in closed alpha. Finally, you serfs without "prelude" keys will be able to fire up Soulframe.com and make sense of my ranting about the sleeping animals on the lobby screen.

The new "open prelude" will land shortly before the game's 17th major update, Verse of the Veilands, which lets you grow your Omen wolfpup allies into rideable adult wolves by finding the ingredients for a special biscuit. More importantly, prelude 17 violently rearranges the game's wistful world, adding an Ubisoft-esque region purging system that is designed to guide new players a bit more emphatically towards the game's "votives". Aka, missions. Yes, Digital Extremes sort of have a bespoke term for every game feature in Soulframe. I find this can be either charming or maddening, depending on how much sleep I've had.

Here's how the region purging will work: after completing the game's Tormented Stag quest, you'll find that the landscape is being corrupted by siphons deployed by the villainous star-faring Ode faction. You have to complete votives to build energy and learn the sacred song of each region, allowing you to cleanse it and restore the environment.

In a roundtable preview session last week, creative director Geoff Crookes and lead designer Scott McGregor expressed a certain amount of anxiety about deliberately polluting Soulframe's fairytale ambience. "Scott and I were just talking yesterday about, aesthetically, how nervous we are about this change," Crookes commented, "because the game has gotten a lot of really great feedback on how cosy it is, how beautiful the world is, and you're going to enter a game that is much more unforgiving and harsh at first glance."

That said, he thinks the shift "pairs really well with going into open alpha, because it is a much stronger breadcrumb [trail] for the player, to pull them into the world and give them a bit more ownership of what they're doing." Once rinsed of Ode siphons, regions will appear more like how they are in previous versions of Soulframe, with activities such as fishing and new resources to snaffle.

McGregor added that hitherto, a lot of Soulframe players have gotten lost and put the game down after completing the opening "Fables", or story quests. "It's a really big change to the structural flow of the game, you know," he told the assembled journorabble. "We're very open and discoverable, and we had a lot of player feedback that was basically 'what do I do next? What do I do next? I don't know what to do next'.

"So [it's] taking that and mashing it with the votive system, which is our mission system for the game, and making that more of a directed experience," he went on, "and then once they get through that directed experience, they can go back to that open world." Prelude 17 will also let you accept votives more straightforwardly from the world map, after finding the local representative or mission giver.

Digital Extremes have a new Soulframe "pact" or character loadout on the boil, the Ode Shrike. It's a dastardly poacher class who specialises in spike traps and throwable bolas. The Shrike's standout ability is a balloon dart that lets you hoist enemies into the sky, as in Metal Gear Solid V.

You can read more about Soulframe's on-going reinventions on the official site. While you won't need a key to get access as of Nov 6th, the game's paid Founders program will remain the same. Digital Extremes will likely still run closed preview builds alongside the "open prelude", testing out features with a smaller group of players. They're also looking into giving you the ability to reset your character, so you can check out any new material added to parts of the game you've finished.

I'm not sure I've ever been exhilarated by Soulframe, but I like the poise, flamboyance and gentle complexity of its combat. I also really enjoy its faded tapestry aesthetics, though I think it's yanking on the goo-goo glands too avidly with all these fluffy forest animals. Enough photogenic wolfpups, Digital Extremes - let's see you make, I don't know, a blobfish look adorable.

It's also very interesting as a new live service project from a company defined by the success of Warframe. I spoke to the Soulframe developers earlier in the year about the challenge of borrowing Warframe's thunder without getting lost in its shadow.

#4106. 'The Best RPG I've Played This Year' - Queen's Domain Is A Low-Key GOTY Contender On Xbox

Back at the end of last month, a little-known RPG launched on Xbox in the form of Queen's Domain, which we highlighted in our October 30th new releases roundup alongside 14 other titles that arrived that day.

Ever since then, we've been hearing various bits of praise for the game across multiple platforms, and it's gotten to the point where it's definitely a Game of the Year contender - albeit a very low-key one.

Officially, what you're getting here is a "retro-fantasy action RPG with brutal combat and traversal-focused exploration", and Queen's Domain is being compared to loads of legendary franchises including King's Field, Zelda and Dark Souls.

Here's what just a few people are saying about it on Steam, for example:

cautious asparagus on Steam: "It's the kind of game that keeps surprising you with the sheer scope and creativity. You know the first time in Elden Ring where you find the elevator that brings you down to Siofra River, and you're just in awe of how much more there is to the game? There are multiple times in Queen's Domain where you feel that same way. This is the best RPG I have played this year, and it might even be my game of the year."

Huell Babineaux: "Everyone says this is one of the best kings field successors out there and it probably is, but ive never played those games, so to me this game feels more like a dark and gritty first person legend of zelda, and it pulls this off exceptionally well. Combat is brutal and unforgiving, but also learnable. Exploration can be daunting and overwhelming, but always rewarding.

Powersteve on Steam: My game of the year. Not just the best King's Field imitator but a genuine improvement on the formula. Better combat, better variety of combat options and a massive world with some of the best level and secret design I have ever seen. Also remains engaging and balanced for the whole duration and doesn't turn into Doom with lightning bolts half way through like Lunacid. So good that I can't wait to get all the endings just so I can use those secrets to do a fresh run with sequence breaks which is something that I almost never do.

So, why haven't we mentioned this before? Well, the Xbox version of Queen's Domain was actually getting a bit of flack at launch, as people were pointing out a stuttering issue that seemed to be plaguing the Series X and S versions.

Looking at the reviews on the Xbox Store now though, the issue seems to have been addressed in a recent patch, and Queen's Domain is currently rocking a 4.7/5 rating on the US version of the Xbox Store as things stand.

In other words, this might well be worth picking up for your Xbox console! It's £16.74 / $19.99 if you fancy taking a punt in the near future, and we'll leave you with more details and screenshots for it down below.

Queen’s Domain is a retro-fantasy action RPG. Washed up on the shores of the Isle of Neasied, you set out to find your father and uncover the dark heart of this mysterious isle. Wield the Legendary Holy Sword Endu to take flight from platform to platform, and discover an interconnected, labyrinthine world where secrets and dangers lurk around every corner.

Fight action-oriented battles with a classic stamina meter, powerful charge attacks, weapon specific special attacks, and secondary throwing weapons. Level up, accessorize, and choose from a huge catalogue of melee weapons on your quest to fight your way through the hordes of monsters and powerful bosses awaiting you in the darkest depths of the isle.

#4105. PS Plus Pulls Plug on PC Streaming After Fewer Than 1% Used It

Members of the manufacturer’s most expensive tier can currently stream and play titles from the PS Plus Premium catalogue using a PC app, which will be discontinued next month.

Curiously, this service has always been limited to PS4 and PS3 titles – it never expanded support to the PS5 library.

The pages on PlayStation.com where you used to be able to download the software have already been removed in anticipation.

Writing on the PS Blog, Sony’s Adam Michel said:

“PlayStation believes in providing high-quality experiences to our players, and we regularly review offerings to ensure we are focusing on experiences our members value most. With a very small number of eligible PS Plus Premium members (less than 0.4%) using the PS Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use. As a result, the PS Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available.”

Once upon a time, I did temporarily use PS Now streaming on my laptop when I went through a period where I didn’t have access to my consoles. But I haven’t used the feature since.

I don’t think Sony promoted this particularly prominently, so I expect many fans may only be finding out about it now.

But I think this is probably part of a broader push by the Japanese giant to move its software off PC. Internally, it’s pivoted away from porting its first-party single player games to the platform. Now it’s ceasing streaming as well.

It should be stressed that PS Plus Premium cloud streaming will remain available on the PS5, PS4, and PS Portal. There will also be no changes to Remote Play functionality.

Will you be affected by this at all? Given the numbers touted in Sony’s article, I can’t imagine many of you will have used this.

#4104. Genshin Impact Luna 7 brings us the first playable Hexenzirkel as things take a turn in Sumeru

Genshin Impact's Luna 7 update will kick off a new Archon Quest chapter, and deliver some interesting new additions to the playable roster.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a new Genshin Impact Special Program, where the developer revealed everything there is to know about the game’s next major update. Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana, or as its friends call it, Luna 7, was unveiled as part of the showcase.

This next update has a lot going for it, and it will be in players’ hands everywhere on May 20.

Luna 7 will take us back to Sumeru for its new Archon Quest, where a new crisis that threatens to plunge the nation into chaos is brewing. Nahida is out of the picture, and someone who looks suspiciously like Il Dottore has emerged.

If you complete this chapter at launch, you’ll earn up to 560 Primogems, as well as Nicole's Ascension Materials. Nicole is the first of three playable characters arriving with this update. Something else you’ll unlock if you finish the chapter quickly is a new Weekly Boss that HoYo says has “unpredictable abilities.”

And if you haven’t played in a while, don’t worry, you can refer to the Guiding Notes feature to catch you up on what’s been going on in the world. This is part of a larger effort from the team to make story progression more seamless, and also includes improved quest autosave prompts.

Nicole Reeyn is highest-profile and most interesting, being the first playable member of the Hexenzirkel. The mage is a 5-Star Pyro Catalyst wielder intended as a support member of the team. She can boost the ATK of all party members, even those not currently on the field. She also generates a shield while doing so.

Her Elemental Burst allows her to summon an Arcane Projection that follows the active character, sending out Coordinated Attacks that match their Elemental Type. Outside of combat, Nicole can help you find treasures by calling upon a Seelie to guide you to them. Quite fitting, as you’ll be exploring in the inside of the Witch's Lodge in Nicole’s Meeting Point in Luna 7, so bring her along.

Lohen, the Vice Captain of the Knights of Favonius' Fifth Company, is the second new character. Also a 5-Star addition, he is instead a Cryo Polearm wielder designed for aggressive combat. His main use is dealing massive Cryo DMG, and he can do that by managing two resources unique to him: Joy, and Will to Win.

Through his Elemental Skill, he can enter the Masterstroke state, allowing him to build up (and consume) Joy to unleash enhanced skills. The more his teammates fight, the more Will to Win he biulds, which can later be used to boost his effectiveness further. For an even more powerful display of force, bring along a Hexerei character when he’s on your team.

Prune is the third and final addition. Prune is a 4-Star Anemo Catalyst wielder, and her kit is inspired by her Witch Hunter aspirations. Using a bell and a hammer, she can deal DMG of several elements at once, and trigger Swirl reactions.

Nicole, and Lohen will debut in Luna 7’s first half, while Prune will follow in the second. The first half will also see a Durin rerun, with Mavuika returning in the second half. You can look forward to a new limited-time event as part of Luna 7, with a focus on Klee's Little Hexenzirkel.

You’ll find a series of mini-games you can play alongside Prune, as well as Qiqi, Yaoyao, and Sayu. If you play, you could earn the Super Awesome Magic Key, an exclusive weapon skin. Miliastra Wonderland is doing its thing, too, with a new sports festival for you to take part in.

One new gameplay addition worth calling attention to is that Manekins can now perform actions in Teyvat. The Kamera, which you can use to capture moments with Manekins, is getting upgraded, too, with new editing tools and assets.

Before you pick the game back up, be sure to check out our recently-updated Genshin Impact codes page for some free stuff you may be missing.

#4103. What are we all playing this weekend?

My scares should have been reserved for today, what with it being All Hallows' Eve and all, but my fright came on Thursday.

It was a dark October night and I was returning from work. A storm had blown through earlier in the week, so the evening was unusually crisp and clear. I walked between the terrace houses, feeling the eyes of work-from-homers on my back. I turned the key in the door to the communal hallway, climbed the creaky stairs, and tried to keep my footsteps light as I passed my rude neighbour's flat. My head was wholly absorbed by the prospect of the risotto I had waiting in the fridge/

I unlocked my front door and started up the internal staircase to the kitchen, not even bothering to turn on the lights. Out of the dark, something jumped down the stairs at me, hitting me in the stomach. I flicked the lights on in a panic and saw a small brown thing with a long tail bolting back up the staircase. A mouse. In my house.

Terrifying stuff, I'm sure you will agree. It almost put me off my risotto. Anyway, this is what the rest of the team will be up to this weekend..

OllieI've settled into a very comfy rhythm of playing the latest Trackmania campaign and also a bit of Factorio, both with my brother. When I've a bit of time to myself I'm also interested in trying out Queen's Domain. Heard good things!

JeremyI continue to chip away at our Castlevania walkthrough as it chips away at my soul. Such is the transactional bargain of dealing with Dracula during Halloween, no? However, as I answer the door for trick-or-treaters, I may partake in what is becoming an annual tradition - watching an old game playthrough on YouTube as I hand out sweets. I'm thinking I will watch the 1994 SNES game Nosferatu this year, which is not related to Castlevania but does feature a bold guy going to beat up Dracula and all of his minions with nothing but his feet and fists.

JamesMy previously mentioned attempts to play Mortal Shell 2 have been thwarted this week by, in chronological order, work, social obligations, brownie making, Deep Rock Galactic, and more brownie making. We go again.

EdwinI'm helping with a house move this weekend, so I doubt I'll have much time for your foolish computer entertainments, but I'd like to crack on with Queen's Domain and also, try out Danchi Days, a sorrowful comedy about trying to revive a summer festival in a 2000s-era Japanese neighbourhood.

CallumSuspiciously, Callum has been making squeaking noises in meetings. Is this a sign he planted the mouse? Perhaps he was the mouse. Surely, it's not a coincidence. There's no such thing as coincidence when it comes to mice.

MarkI want to finish Virtue and a Sledgehammer, having started it the other night. I really dug The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood, one of Spanish studio Deconstructeam's previous games. Thus far, VaaS is hitting just as hard in terms of emotional beats, but in a manner that's more haunting than charming. We'll see where I land on it by the end.

JulianAs well as searching my flat for mouse hidey holes, I will be (touch wood/cross fingers/make a sacrifice to Bob the Builder) finishing the DIY I started last weekend. Alcove bookcases and a painted living room are in my future, I just have to manifest it.

Besides that, I've been dipping my toes into Titanium Court. I like it but I don't so far love it. It's witty, the presentation is excellent, but I feel like it is also keeping me at arm's length and I want to be drawn into its world, not kept at a distance. It may just need more time. I will also be trying hard not to sweep the moon.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

#4102. "It's Terrific" - Take-Two Boss Acknowledges Zelda Remake's High Score Ahead Of GTA VI Launch

There's been a lot of conversation online about the Zelda remake and Grand Theft Auto going head-to-head this month.

GamesBeat has now asked the Take-Two Interactive boss Strauss Zelnick what he thinks about this and Ocarina of Time's current Metacritic score of 96/100.

He politely responded, stating the game's score is "terrific" and Nintendo should be "very proud of the title".

As for the idea of the two games competing against each other, the CEO of Rockstar's parent company didn't really acknowledge any direct "competition", but more broadly, believes "you compete against everything and nothing" in the entertainment business.

"In the entertainment business, you compete against everything and nothing. Everything because there’s so many ways consumers can spend their time, and nothing because if there’s nothing good out there, people don’t need to consume any of it. It’s like food; like food could be bad, but you still are going to be hungry. But in the case of entertainment, it’s not a must-have; it’s a want to have. So it’s our job to make the best entertainment on earth. When we do that, people will show up for it.”

In his words, if it's the "best entertainment on earth", then "people will show up for it".

While Zelda's Ocarina remake has done tremendously well for Nintendo, and early reports suggest its sales are off to a positive start in certain locations, Grand Theft Auto VI (at least for now) has been labelled the most anticipated launch of all time. Presales of the new entry have already exceeded expectations, and it's a digital-only release, with retail copies sold as a "code-in-a-box" release.

And if you're wondering about the possibility of a Switch 2 version, Nintendo of America's president has recently said it's a "conversation for Take-Two and Rockstar". Earlier this week, Rockstar also confirmed GTA VI will run at 30fps on PlayStation 5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X|S. It will be available on Xbox One through Xbox Cloud Gaming, too.

#4101. Poll: Is GTA 6 Being Stuck at 30fps on PS5 a Dealbreaker?

Your (potential) nightmare has become a reality: GTA 6 runs at just 30 frames-per-second on PS5 and PS5 Pro.

The target frame rate was confirmed earlier today by Rockstar Games itself, prompting an outpouring of relative disappointment from those who were banking on a silky 60fps experience.

Of course, 30fps isn't the end of the world — as long as it's nice and stable — but there's no getting away from the fact that the vast majority of games on PS5 offer some form of higher frame rate.

Most AAA releases, for example, provide a choice between a 30fps 'quality' mode, which trades frames for increased visual clarity, and a 60fps 'performance' mode, which usually sacrifices resolution for smoother gameplay.

News GTA 6 PS5 Pro Features Revealed, 30fps Target on Both Consoles

Improved clarity and ray traced shadows on PS5 Pro

GTA 6 will offer no such compromise, presumably because it's so beefed up in the graphical department.

Indeed, early tech analyses have pointed out that this could be one of the most graphically intensive games ever made; an open world effort that goes beyond anything the genre's seen up until now.

The bottom line here is that you'd like to think Rockstar knows what it's doing. If it had to keep the frame rate capped at 30 to deliver on its vision of a modern Vice City, then that's the long and short of it.

Although having said that, I'm sure there are plenty of people out there who would have happily taken a graphical hit to have GTA 6 run at 60fps. I might be one of them!

But is GTA 6's lack of 60fps a dealbreaker for you? Might you actually avoid playing it now that only 30fps is confirmed? Vote in our polls, and then move at a higher frame rate in the comments section below.

Guide GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

@NavalHistorian It's kind of both: the CPU handles everything that happens on and off screen, but from a logic standpoint. Imagine you close your eyes and an agent from the game's Matrix starts narrating everything that's happening at any given moment. This is the CPU. Now, imagine that there's another agent that listens to that description and simply paints the frames without really thinking about the logic. That's the GPU.

If the CPU agent can't describe the action quickly enough for the GPU agent to render it, then it doesn't matter how fast the GPU is. You're CPU-bound.

And to answer your second question, the reason Sony opted for a rather small performance bump on the Pro's CPU side is probably a mix of compatibility/stability/reliability and cost. I mean, they could have moved to a better manufacturing process node and got a bigger frequency bump, but that would have made the console much more expensive. Or they could have moved to a newer architecture, which would dramatically increase R&D costs and ultimately raise the price as well, while posing compatibility risks with existing games.

You see, the GPU is way easier to scale, which explains why Sony (and Microsoft) opted for proportionally beefier GPU bumps for the PS4 Pro, the Xbox One X and the PS5 Pro.

#4100. Mystic Messenger's most loyal players are getting banned in droves for seemingly playing the game too much

With the 10th anniversary of Mystic Messenger nearly upon us, the dating sim has inexplicably begun issuing wide-spread bans for its most active players.

Mystic Messenger, arguably one of the best dating sims around, has been dormant for about seven years. Despite not receiving new content or any meaningful updates in all that time, the game remains popular with its core fans, many of whom just woke up to some shocking news about their accounts.

The free-to-play mobile dating sim has started banning players with seemingly too many Hourglasses - the game’s virtual currency - saved up in their accounts. So far, it looks like players with 1,000 or more have been targeted, but others with far fewer hoards have reported getting the axe, too.

The news exploded on the Mystic Messenger subreddit overnight, with over a dozen reports from players logging in to play normally, only to receive an in-game notice that their accounts had been banned.

The message players received is identical, and doesn’t mention the specific reason for the ban. “Your account has been banned because abusive behavior has been detected from your account,” it reads, ending with a support email address the affected user can contact if they believe they’d banned in error.

It didn’t take a while for players to realise that most, if not all of the bans are for players with thousands of Hourglasses in their accounts. The virtual currency can both be acquired in-game just by playing, as well as through direct real-money purchases.

For a nearly ten-year-old game that stopped receiving content three years into its life, it’s easy to see how a dedicated group of players would be able to acquire so many Hourglasses by simply playing regularly for so long.

When contacted by the affected players, Cheritz, the developer and publisher of the game, has instructed them to send receipts of how they acquired Hourglasses (assuming they were purchased) to verify whether or not they’d been fraudulently obtained.

Considering that Mystic Messenger has practically been abandoned by its developer, certain exploits have emerged over the years that allowed players to farm Hourglasses faster than intended, but those instances have always been dealt with then and there.

The blanket and sudden nature of this ban is what’s spooked players, especially those who’ve been logging in for years and never thought accruing in-game currency from playing the game too much would make them the target of a ban.

The running theory is that most of the bans are unintentional, and may be the result of a new automated security system that’s been implemented. It’s entirely possible, especially if its’s AI-based, that the new system simply couldn’t distinguish between those who have earned (or bought) their Hourglasses fairly, and those who used exploits.

The timing of the ban wave is also suspect. With the game’s 10th anniversary coming up in July, it could be that Cheriz is preparing to release a large update for Mystic Messenger, which may include new content. If most of the playerbase is already sitting on massive amounts of in-game currency, they may simply use that to fast-track their way to unlocking the new content, which would greatly affect the developer’s bottom line.

This is a problem that other live service games have run into in the past. Just recently, extraction shooter Arc Raiders added a cap to the amount of Cred players can hold in their accounts very quickly after its launch. That currency is used to buy cosmetic sets in the store, so the logic is easy to follow.

All of that has certainly put a damper on the enthusiasm of the game’s most active players, many of whom were excited to get together in person for the coming 10th anniversary, participate in community nights and so on to celebrate.

It’s also disheartening to see a fanbase so loyal; playing a game as regularly for so long without new content, to be treated so poorly. Even without knowing what the game is, it’s impressive that so many people have kept the flag of their favourite game flying for so long.

#4098. Horror-steeped card game Forbidden Solitaire shows how a strong theme can elevate even decade-old mechanics

Like a tag team of oiled snakes that have entered a wrestling contest, theme is a difficult quality to pin down. A game can be well designed, but if it lacks a coherence between those mechanics and its appearance, narrative, and its framing, there is a dissonance that can be hard to ignore. I realise I've just stepped into an old argument by using the word 'dissonance', but Hocking was right, games that don't cohere can be jarring. A developer may desire that sensation of discomfort, but often it is accidental and unwanted.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

(Much like opening an article with a simile about wrestling snakes when there is nothing connecting that image to a game about solitaire. It might be a good line, but it doesn't smoothly connect with the rest of the article to elevate its argument.)

Anyway, what does this all have to do with Forbidden Solitaire, a game in which you're delving deeper into a dungeon filled with horrors, progressing by clearing screens of cards? Well, it's an excellent example of how well-handled theming can raise a game into something more than its parts.

I've been playing Grey Alien Games' work since they released Regency Solitaire in 2015, and their games often revolve around the same core, Solitaire-inspired mechanics. Each level is a screen filled with stacks of playing cards, and you must clear the screen by picking cards that are one higher or lower than the one currently in your hand. In addition to standard playing cards, you may find padlock cards which can only be cleared with a matching key card, special cards that reshuffle all the stacks, or ones that change cards into suits or numbers that may help you. Except, in each of their games – Regency Solitaire, Shadowhand, Ancient Enemy, and now Forbidden Solitaire - the scenario for those mechanics changes, and in doing do, they show the power of recontextualising.

In Forbidden Solitaire, you're playing a game within a game. Although it's set in 2019, your character is playing a 1995 CD-ROM they found in a second-hand shop. It's one you vaguely remember from your childhood, if mainly for the controversy it caused at launch. The game sees you breaking into an old dungeon and exploring its depths. Each locked door that blocks you, labyrinth that puzzles you, or enemy that challenges you is tackled with the mechanics of Grey Alien Games' previous releases: screens of stacked cards to be cleared. Even familiar special cards, such as the one which shuffles all the cards before you, make a return. As you progress through Forbidden Solitaire's dungeon, you're interrupted by messages from your sister in the present, who is researching the game and the controversy surrounding it, sending you links to police reports, old news clips of the secretive developer, and hidden documents on a centuries-old group of cultists.

Yet, despite the mechanical familiarity, it's this fresh theme that elevates Forbidden Solitaire into something special. For new players, the 1995 game framing device immediately gives an allowance for the simple card mechanics, and allows them to sink into the kitsch horror story of cult members developing haunted video games. But, for returning players like me, I can see all the neat ways the old tools have been adapted to fit this new world. When you find a person marked for sacrifice tied to a bed, for instance, the level to free them is filled with locks that only disappear when you match enough cards of the same suit. It's a pairing of unlocking mechanics that have been in Grey Alien Games' work for at least the past decade to a moment in the story where you are untying a character. The action dovetails with the narrative perfectly.

Anyway, when I realised the role that theme had to play in Forbidden Solitaire, I was feeling extremely smart and smug. Then I reread Adam (RPS in peace) and Pip's (RPS in peace) Regency Solitaire verdict from 2015.

Adam: I think the whole game is a superb example of how a decent design can be elevated by a strong theme. It’s not even particularly overindulgent - flourishes throughout but no extended dialogues or huge slabs of exposition. It’s a few attractive backgrounds (though with an inaccurate non-pebbled Brighton beach, I’m told by RPS chatroom stalwart and Brighton denizen Alec Meer), a handful of characters and miniature conversations to set the tone. But it’s all done so well. It seems to be aware of its own posture in a way that allows it to be well-mannered, well-meaning and not at all over-bearing.

If it had been pixies or space marines, I don’t think I’d have been particularly interested at all - and that’s not to say the actual card game isn’t well-constructed because it is - but even though the story is slight, it’s a great reward at the end of a few hands.

Pip: I'd agree with that, particularly about the setting. It's a game that has a good understanding of its own size, scope and the tone which suits it.

Those absolute cads. Still, go play Forbidden Solitaire anyway. It's a far better time than trying to get an oiled snake into a three-piece suit.

#4097. The Sunday Papers

Sundays are for looking upon my DIY works and despairing. Strewn sawdust, spilled paint, and hunks of broken MDF litter my living room kingdom. When will it be over? When will I be free? When will I be able to reassemble my sofa, sit down with a cup of tea in hand, and admire my books, unpacked and arranged on perfectly fitted alcove bookshelves?

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

"Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

Inside our Gchat walls, there is a growing exhaustion with genAI stories. Every day another gaming boss talks about the inexorable march of the tech before putting out a trailer filled with blurry text and six-fingered characters. I don't doubt the tech is getting better, but it's not inevitable. As such, Rob Fahey's latest GI column is something of a balm:

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.

A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

Doesn't it feel like everything — especially everything Big Tech touches — is getting worse? Generative AI, not merely content with robbing humans of our craft and jobs, has escaped containment into physical reality in the form of shitty event flyers and small business signage. Hugely profitable industries like video games and film are being torn apart by the financialization of the economy as shareholders seek ever-increasing short-term profits. Algorithmic pricing of rent and groceries threatens to further punish the working class for the crime of not being born rich.

But in the heart of despair, we must reach for that which is good and pure and — dare I say it — better than it used to be. Karaoke is one of those things. And it is better not because of the disruption of tech giants, but, as is often the case, thanks to the work of enterprising maniacs toiling in obscurity, purely out of the love of the game.

I've been playing Forbidden Solitaire this week, where FMV sequences starring Xalavier Nelson Jr as an obsessive fantasy-author-turned-video-game-developer are played for laughs. So it was with a minor sense of whiplash I read Ashley Bardhan's piece for This Week In Video Games. Bardhan speaks to horror developers inserting themselves into FMV games to confront and explore violence against women.

Cara Cadaver uses her own photos and videos to represent multiple victims of sexual violence and murder in her unflinching 2025 game Vile: Exhumed. She tells me over email, “Being a woman is inherently a horrifying and violent experience, any way you slice it. One of my inspirations for making games in general is pulling from real-life experience and telling stories that most every woman has lived in some way; that’s real horror.”

“Horror in general has been a major outlet for me while dealing with trauma, and so much of horror as a genre goes back to women,” Cadaver says. “Women’s stories belong in horror — and that has been the case as long as horror has existed.”

Over at RPS-but-it's-The-Fade, Brendan's run through what made Bioware games great (and also terrible).

Bioware established romance as a must for any blockbuster RPG worth its frost salts (and not just RPGs).

Kissing your friends on the mouth is everywhere in mainstream and indie games today. It's a verb now. Characters are "romanceable". I played Nivalis Nights last month and could not get away from the swarms of horny NPC citizens trying to jump my noodle serving bones. Baldur's Gate 3 launched with a bug that made your companions fuckable in just a few nights, and people didn't even notice. They thought: that's normal and right, I should shag everyone, gender and orientation be damned. See that mountain? You can fuck it. And that's (at least partially) thanks to Bioware.

GTA is an unignorable thing. It is one of those breakout cultural objects that has its own gravity, drawing in attention and comment from politicians, mainstream press, parents, schools, comedians, columnists, footballers, taxi drivers, and hairdressers. In all the weight of it, I hadn't yet really seen it as a game. Simon Parkin's Edge cover feature may not reveal many new details about the game but it has made me appreciate it as a game (and maybe even get a little bit excited for its eventual PC release.

Nelson, grave-faced but friendly, wearing all black, with grey-flecked stubble, settles into a leather-and-chrome Eames chair while we perch on a burnt-orange sofa facing a pair of expansive wall-mounted TVs. In the past, Rockstar has carefully stage-managed encounters such as this. For previews of previous GTAs, one team member played the game while a publicist read from a pre-prepared script, further evidence of the paranoia that can take hold when an artist is working on something the entire world is desperate to see.

Today, however, Nelson has no script and, apparently, no plan. For the next 90 minutes he simply plays the current build, following his nose, confident that the game's systems will hold together wherever he pushes them, that this world's glories will glint and shimmer no matter which angle he approaches from. It is an extraordinary demonstration not of paranoia but of trust – in the game, in the team that built it, perhaps even in us.

Nelson picks up the controller and lets Grand Theft Auto VI speak for itself.

I am guilty of forgetting and looking away, but the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has not ended, it is deepening. Writing for the LRB, Selma Dabbagh bluntly captures the ugly events of the past two years :

In January 2025 Donald Trump described Gaza as a ‘demolition site’. ‘You’re talking about probably a million and a half people,’ he said, ‘and we just clean out that whole thing.’ The number is closer to two million people – not a ‘whole thing’ but two million individual human beings – who have been driven into an area that’s less than a third of the densely inhabited land they lived on. Their cities and arable lands – palms, olives, coriander, citrus and pomegranate trees – have been obliterated.

I'd like there to be a big reason for this week's music recommendation, but really it's just a little victory lap. I managed to nab some tickets to see This Is The Kit, so give Bashed Out a listen, yeah?

#4095. Forza Horizon 6 explodes on Steam even before it's officially out

Forza Horizon 6 looks to have easily delivered the most successful launch for any game in the series on PC, with record-breaking player numbers.

Steam is abuzz this week with a couple of long-anticipated launches, but in Forza Horizon 6’s case, at least, the game isn’t even out for what will be most of its players. The anticipated sequel in the open-world driving game series doesn’t officially launch until May 19, but owners of its most expensive version - the Premium Edition - can play it right now.

That version of the game includes more than just a few days of early access, of course, but you’d think the $120 price tag would’ve only been palatable to a small group of players. Not the case with this game.

Forza Horizon 6, which has spent 16 weeks in Steam’s global top sellers list, currently occupies the number two spot, having jumped up three spots this week in anticipation of the launch. The game has also naturally been popular with players, so popular in fact that it has already overtaken the player counts of all other Horizon games on the platform.

At the time of writing, the game has peaked at 128,157 concurrent players on Steam alone (via SteamDB). The figure has already climbed several times during the writing of this story, so you can only imagine how much higher it’s going to get deeper into the weekend.

All of that, of course, days before the official launch on Tuesday, when, theoretically, the majority of the game’s audience will be able to start playing. In just a few short hours, Horizon 6 has already gone well above Forza Horizon 5’s peak concurrent of 81,096, as well as Forza Horizon 4’s peak 75,689 players.

Steam is the only platform that publishes player numbers, of course, but it’s easy to see how similar the enthusiasm is going to be on Xbox. Though the game is not yet part of the Game Pass line-up, those who don’t want to wait could buy the Premium Edition Upgrade to get the included content, and play it right now.

Game Pass, and Xbox / Windows Store numbers don’t factor into Steam’s, which is another thing to consider when viewing the numbers holistically. Indeed, given how successful Forza Horizon 5 has been on PlayStation 5, Horizon 6’s upcoming release on Sony's console is bound to be even bigger.

Forza Horizon 5 has been off to a similarly flying start in the first few days of its own advanced access launch, so it’s obviously not surprising to see Horizon 6 do better there. In case you missed it, check out our review of Forza Horizon 6. In short, we really liked it, even if we expected more.

#4094. Poll: Xbox Turns 25 This Week, But Which Console Generation Had The Best Launch Titles?

This Sunday, Xbox will celebrate 25 years of great games and console experiences. Without giving away just how ancient we are, Fraser and I have been Xbox players since the beginning, enjoying each new generation of Xbox consoles and the games that launched alongside them.

With November 15th drawing closer, we thought we'd look back on each generation's launch lineup and ask for your verdict: which Xbox console had the best launch titles?

Was it the original Xbox, with Halo: Combat Evolved, Project Gotham Racing, and Fuzion Frenzy? How about the Xbox 360, with Condemned: Criminal Origins, Kameo: Elements of Power, and Call of Duty 2? Perhaps the Xbox One, with Ryse: Son of Rome, Dead Rising 3, and Forza Motorsport 5? Or is it the Xbox Series X|S, with Gears Tactics, Forza Horizon 4, and Sea Of Thieves?

We all have our favourite games from each console generation, but which one had the best launch lineup? That's for you to decide by voting in the poll below. Before you do, though, here's a closer look at each Xbox generation's launch titles:

#4093. The Outer Worlds 2 PS5 DLC Split into Two Parts, First in December

Obsidian still wants to carry out its post-launch DLC plans for The Outer Worlds 2, having lost 25% of its workforce in a recent round of layoffs. It's today announced an expansion called Side Effect Guaranteed will release in two parts: the first launches for PS5 on 2nd December 2026, and then the second arrives in Spring 2027. See it in action in the trailer.

The new DLC takes place just before the end of the main game, so if you've already finished a playthrough, there'll be a new option on the starting menu screen that lets you access the content through a new character.

A distress signal beckons you and your crew of the Incognito to a derelict ship, where you discover the ship’s crew in suspended animation. All signs point to foul play, especially the puddle of what was most likely a person that you recover a video message from. It was left by the captain of the vessel, who explains that the crew has been contaminated with something while on a heist that will cause explosive cell death unless they find a cure. And by explosive cell death, she means more like a… “liquefaction”.

Side Effect Guaranteed adds a new region to explore called Elysium Valley, another recruitable character, a level cap increase to 36, more than 15 new perks, four extra flaws, and additional gear (weapons, armour, and outfits). You can also look forward to an additional 20 songs.

The expansion costs $14.99, or if you bought the Premium Edition of the game, you'll gain instant access to the DLC.

Review The Outer Worlds 2 (PS5) - Mechanically Fantastic RPG Struggles to Be Memorable

It'll work to expand and improve an RPG we thought was pretty good at release, awarding it a 7/10 rating. "The Outer Worlds 2 succeeds in being a bigger and better sequel, buoyed by an even greater emphasis on player choice and freedom. Its RPG mechanics are largely fantastic, and there are key improvements to both combat and exploration," we said at the time. "However, despite Obsidian's clever writing, there's an underlying dreariness to the property that it just can't seem to escape."

Are you returning to The Outer Worlds 2 for its expansion? Let us know in the comments below.

#4092. It looks like footage of a Persona 1 remake has leaked, and if it's legit I really hope you don't hate the colour purple

I'm sure the artist formerly known as Prince would have loved it, at least

In this genAI world, every single leak that makes its way out into the world should be seen as more of a "leak" until proven otherwise. With that said, it does kind of seem like a remake of the first Persona game is on the way, with some footage supposedly leaking and showing it in action.

The leaked footage was shared yesterday to the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, originally uploaded to the file-sharing site Gofile on Halloween, i.e. yesterday, i.e. October 31st. You will not at all be surprised to hear that, stylistically, it's incredibly in line with the vibe of contemporary Persona, a la the visual design established with Persona 5 that's been carried through to the Persona 3 and 4 remakes.

There's not a whole lot of footage to actually look at, just shy of two minutes all told. One bit shows the game's protagonist walking through a school at night before starting a battle. Again, the battle system looks like what you'd expect from Persona, being turn based and whatnot. The colour theme for this one is overwhelmingly purple, too, which at least lines up with the series' 25th anniversary artwork. What's perhaps slightly odd is that Persona 2's protagonist can be seen in battle; not sure if this is implying a combination of the two games, if two remakes are being made in tandem and it's a temporary use of assets, or if it's just an odd placeholder.

Persona 1 and 2 remakes wouldn't exactly be much of a surprise. Ashley interviewed series producer Kazuhisa Wada not too long ago, and he literally said "Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too." A knowing tease from Wada, perhaps? Who knows! Either way, the gameplay on display here looks believable, and Sega's leakier than a broken faucet (various Persona bits have leaked in the past too), so, something to keep an eye on at the very least, even if best taken with a pinch of salt.

#4091. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.3 will take us deeper into the World in Canvas and make Mortenax Blade playable

Honkai: Star Rail's next big outing will see the continuation of the Planarcadia story, and it's going to be with us soon.

HoYoverse has today delivered full details on the next major update for Honkai: Star Rail. Version 4.3, dubbed The Lethe Below the Living, will be available for all players on June 1. The upcoming update adds a new chapter to the Planarcadia arc, and introduce a new playable character.

The new narrative chapter will also unveil more about Mortenax Blade, the Trailblazer themselves, and the husk of the Aeon.

Mortenax Blade is the hero of this chapter, and he’s going to step into the World in Canvas. The goal is to - by borrowing the power of Voracity - excise Shuhu from his body and end the curse.

The Trailblazer goes on a trip of their own in Version 4.3, this time to Inkford Hermitage, right on the edge between the World in Canvas and the real world. They’re going to undertake this journey to warn Graphia of the Asat Pramad threat.

In case you hadn’t already guessed, Mortenax Blade is this version’s new playable character. The 5-Star Fire-Type swordsman is on the Path of Nihility. Blade’s Ultimate allows him to enter an enhanced state by deploying a special Bounded Field.

While the field is active, all enemies receive more DMG. Entering this state is also how Blade unlocks his skill, which uses a Sword Formation to deal more damage. This is then used to essentially unlock a second, more powerful Ultimate for him.

The benefits of Mortenax Blade’s kit extend to his teammates, too. Any ally who attacks an enemy with him on the team, they inflict a debuff on them. This also builds up a special Charge that Blade can later use with his Skill.

Version 4.3’s launch arrives alongside the Gift of Tempered Blade event. Through it, you can claim a new Trailblazer Outfit piece for free, but only after getting Mortenax Blade from Warping. The first phase’s rerun will be Yao Guang, and the second phase will bring back both Cyrene and Phainon.

You can also expect the Wispae Amusement Park to arrive within the World in Canvas, which you’ll get to design. You can plan where the rides will go, pick the different themes, set visitor routes and more.

Starward Mode is another new addition, which can be found in Memory of Chaos, Pure Fiction, and Apocalyptic Shadow. Starward will see you take on three different stages, which you’ll need three teams for. Clearing each challenge with full stars will reward you 100 Stellar Jades extra per chase.

There’s more coming down the line, too. A new Fate/Stay Night [Unlimited Blade Works] collaboration will arrive in a content up this summer. The event will give players a chance to earn Gilgamesh or Archer for free by logging in.

#4090. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

If you're excited to jump in tomorrow, be sure to check out these Free Monopoly Go Dice Links before you dive into the new content.

#4089. New Details Revealed About The Physical Edition Of GTA 6 For Xbox Series X|S

Double-sided poster, shipping dates & more

Everyone already knows about the code-in-a-box situation for GTA 6's physical edition on Xbox Series X|S and PS5, but we've also come to learn a few extra details in recent days about what to expect from the boxed copy of the game.

So, when you open up GTA 6 for Xbox Series X|S in physical form, you'll be presented with a code that will allow you to redeem the game on the Microsoft Store - essentially converting your physical purchase into a digital one.

Rockstar Games mentioned a shipping date of November 12th for the physical version a few days ago, but we've spotted some retailers saying they'll start shipping on the 11th instead, while a very small number of people even seem to have their copy already.

Once you've got the physical version in your hands, you'll be able to preload GTA 6 in full, although you can technically also do that from tonight by installing the game via the Xbox mobile app.

As you can also see from the tweet above, the physical edition is now confirmed to come with a double-sided A3 poster (at least if you buy from certain retailers). This poster appears to include the game's main artwork along with some character art on the back, so that's at least a nice little bonus to ease the pain of a disc-less release.

But what about a map? Well, Rockstar Games is handling the map a bit differently this time around, making a digital version available to download for free at launch. Alternatively, physical maps will be available to buy from the Rockstar Store "shortly after launch" for $0.99, but we reckon those will be in extreme demand and quickly sell out.

Of course, none of this really changes the fact that the physical edition of GTA 6 is kinda pointless for any platform as things stand, but it does at least make for a good display piece, and it'll be popular for gifting purposes this Christmas.

What's even weirder about this is that Rockstar is supporting GTA 6's launch with various other physical releases, such as an official soundtrack album and all kinds of merch, but it seems there's little hope for a disc version right now.

Let's start with the bad news: Final Fantasy 14: Evercold has been delayed. The good news, that doesn't matter all that much, as it's only a delay of roughly a month, and a release date has been set in stone too: February 23rd, 2027. It's cutting it a bit close to the seasons shifting towards spring, making the game seasonally inappropriate, but hey ho, February is still winter!

That release date was revealed during this week's Final Fantasy 14 Fest Fest held in Tokyo. It was paired with a big ole cinematic that'll open up the expansion when you do actually get to play it. You can watch that down below if you fancy, that'll just depend on whether you want to go into the expansion knowing as little as possible. Looks pretty at least! I like the big dragony ship we've seen previously.

The expansion's second new job has been revealed too. It's called Zephyr, a physical ranged DPS that uses a crossbow and comes with its own avian familiar to assist you in battle. Seems like a pretty good option for folks afraid of getting in close but want to get some damage in. The bird friend you get is neat too. I hereby request that every other job gets a bird friend! I don't care if it doesn't make sense!

Most annoyingly, for me personally as someone that's only managed to play A Realm Reborn and doesn't really have time to go through a ridiculous number of hours and expansions just to get to this one, a preview for the Evangelion collab alliance raid was shown off rendered in the style of the original anime's post-credits, next episode teaser reels. Anyway, don't forget to mark your calendars, February 23rd! Be there or be, uh, anywhere else I guess. I'm not your boss.

#4087. It's Official, Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Has Sold Over 5 Million Copies In 4 Days

Nintendo has announced that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has sold a total of 5.2 million units in just four days.

This number includes 810,000 copies sold in Japan alone, and makes Ocarina of Time the fastest-selling Nintendo-published Switch 2 game since the console's launch. For added context, the N64 original sold an overall total of 7.6 million units, according to Video Game Sales wiki.

This also makes it the second highest-selling Switch 2 game, with initial sales putting it above Donkey Kong Bananza's lifetime sales at 5.05 million (as of 30th September 2026). The best-selling Switch 2 game remains Mario Kart World at 16.48 million.

It's not clear what the digital/physical split is at the time of writing, though we should have a slightly better picture of this once Famitsu releases the Japanese boxed charts later this week.

Nintendo Co., Ltd. (HQ: Kyoto, Minami-ku, Japan; President and Representative Director: Shuntaro Furukawa, “Nintendo” hereafter) announced that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 sold over 5.2 million units worldwide (including 810,000 units sold in Japan) in the first four days following its launch on November 5, 2026.

This is the highest global sales for any Nintendo-published Nintendo Switch 2 game in its first four days.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2, released worldwide on November 5, is a full remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, originally released for Nintendo 64 in 1998. Link travels between two time periods, as Young Link and Adult Link, making use of different abilities and items available in each period to progress through his adventure. Developed for Nintendo Switch 2, the game features reimagined visuals and enhanced playability, while preserving the experience of the original game.

The game also supports ZELDA NOTES, a service available within the Nintendo Switch App for compatible smart devices. By using ZELDA NOTES, players can access a variety of features that support gameplay.

In the UK, it was confirmed that Ocarina of Time was the second biggest physical launch in series history, coming in just behind Tears of the Kingdom. It stormed to the top of the charts to become the biggest physical video game launch of 2026 (so far – hi, GTA).

As for our review, we awarded Ocarina of Time a 9/10, stating it to be "the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time":

"Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time."

#4086. Sony Cancels Fairgames After Years of Work on PS5 Live Service Shooter

PlayStation has officially cancelled Fairgames, the PS5 and PC live service shooter it had in production at Haven Studio.

The news comes from Bloomberg journalist Jason Schreier, though it's been sourced from an internal email distributed to PlayStation employees, and a company spokesperson has commented on the story.

That spokesperson told the outlet that Haven Studio will remain open following the cancellation, and it won't suffer any job losses. The developer, originally headed by Jade Raymond of Assassin's Creed fame — who left about a year and a half ago — will now become a support team within PlayStation Studios.

In the email to PlayStation employees, it's said a recent test of Fairgames didn't deliver the results the company wanted.

It said: "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set. Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

Announced more than three years ago, Fairgames was one of the headline announcements from the infamous PlayStation Showcase that properly pushed Sony's live service efforts — it was also where Concord and Helldivers 2 debuted.

Since then, absolutely nothing official from the game has been made public except for studio departures.

The game has reportedly done poorly during pre-launch and private tests, which has now been confirmed in the email to employees this week. There were rumours Fairgames would be brought back with a new name, Break In, around the summer season of games conferences earlier this year, but it never materialised.

It's yet another failure from PlayStation's first-party efforts during the PS5 era, which has seen many cancellations to the likes of The Last of Us Online, Payback from Bungie, live service titles from Sony Bend and Bluepoint Games, and Twisted Metal. You might as well throw Concord in there too, because while it did actually release, it was taken offline permanently after just two weeks.

Let's hope the PS6 generation doesn't follow in these footsteps.

@EfYI It’s a bit more complicated than that. Cancellations are a part of the business. Always have been, always will be. There are ideas that sound feasible on paper or in a trailer but just don’t come together in practice, That has always been the case in commercial art industries in general (including but not limited to movies, tv shows, music and books) and videogames in particular. IMHO it’s more of an issue nowadays because of lengthening development cycles and coteries of gamers on the internet that get very invested in behind the scenes stuff. Don’t take my word for it. Below is a snippet from an interview with Yoshida.

https://www.gamesradar.com/games/former-playstation-boss-shuhei-yoshida-canceled-so-many-games-including-a-new-ip-from-god-of-war-dev-santa-monica-studio-these-days-a-usd25-million-cancellation-is-nothing-special/

While canceling games isn't unusual for Yoshida, he says he usually tried to do it before $25 million worth of development resources had been spent. "I canceled so many games," he says. "No one knows most of the games, because we canceled early enough. We tried to try a new idea, do the prototype, and if it's good, continue. If it's not good, rework or stop. So early cancellation doesn't cost us much. However, if the game was kind of making progress, and very promising vision went on and on, after $25 million it was a really hard decision. But I think in that case, Santa Monica Studio by themselves, was like, 'probably we have to stop.'"

————What of that other $25 million project Yoshida mentioned previously? He offers less in the way of specific details there, but apparently it was in development at one of Sony's European studios. "There were many, many good games from Europe," Yoshida says. "But one game was a big-budget project [that] didn't, in a similar way, have the core game anyway. These are the two large cancellations. But these days, a $25 million cancellation is nothing special."
