#4050. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

#4048. "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight

"I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it"

Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

#4047. Mini Review: Barbie Rewind (PS5) - Fab Outer Layer Brings This Retro Ensemble Together

Version Reviewed: PS5 (Standard) / European

The only Barbie title I've played, prior to Barbie Rewind, is a PC game named Fashion Designer, in which you choose clothes based on particular themes, then apply patterns, accessories, and colours. You could print them out and put them on real Barbie dolls — a nice idea.

Sadly, Fashion Designer isn't among the games included in Barbie Rewind, but what is in this retro compilation is similarly simple and enjoyable, for the most part.

16 old school games starring the iconic doll feature here, from 1991's simply-named platformer Barbie all the way to 2007's Barbie as the Island Princess, basically a handful of mini-games.

Some of the included titles don't hold up particularly well nowadays, but it's still interesting to see the gaming legacy of the character, which spans a surprisingly wide range of experiences. There are sports, horse riding, detective adventures, and more.

While it's obviously great to have all these games gathered — especially with the inclusion of the previously unreleased Barbie Vacation Adventure — the best thing about Barbie Rewind is actually the way it's packaged.

You can play the classic games at any time, but tying it all together is an in-game DreamHouse that you can freely decorate as you unlock more items.

Completing basic challenges in the retro titles unlocks new rooms as well as more furniture and accessories, giving you somewhere to return to and kit out as you see fit.

It's a really neat way to encourage you to play all the games, making the collection feel nicely cohesive. It's also an entertaining thing to noodle around with in its own right, with hundreds of items and several rooms to decorate.

The way it's presented reminds me of Unpacking; it doesn't have that game's wonderful wordless storytelling, but placing down objects just how you want them has a similar appeal here.

On top of that, there's the Catalog, which is the museum style mode with lots of old documents and materials to look through regarding Barbie as well as the games themselves.

It's another great effort from Digital Eclipse, and I think going the extra mile with the DreamHouse really lifts the whole thing. If you're nostalgic for Barbie games or are just curious about their history, this is a lovely way to experience them.

#4046. Marathon To Add New Co-Op Roguelite Mode, Social Spaces, And Other Major Features In December

It's beginning to look a lot like Destiny

Bungie isn't prepared to let its extraction shooter go quietly. Instead, Marathon's upcoming 'Symbiosis' update arrives on December 8, bringing a whole host of new PvE and PvP modes. Having just finished watching the new gameplay trailer above, I've got to say, It's giving off plenty of Destiny vibes.

I'm a big, big fan of Marathon, but that's not to say I don't think the game needs a shake-up. It clearly needs something to keep things ticking along. I can't help but feel extremely hyped now that Bungie has shared a first look at all the new content coming next month.

The most interesting addition of the bunch is 'Limbo': a new social space. This is where runners can hang out, chat, test weapons at the firing range and challenge each other in the duelling pit. It reminds me of The Tower from Destiny 2.

Social spaces play a huge role in fostering a sense of community in games, and Bungie knows all about that. Just look at the time Destiny players gathered at The Tower en masse to mourn the passing of Lance Reddick, the voice of Commander Zavala.

Beyond that, 'Expedition' is a new co-op PvE roguelite mode. No PvP, just you and your crew going against new threats. PlayStation.Blog shared an official description of the the new mode:

"Expedition: Phase 1 of a new PvE-only mode built around a three-run series. Play solo or with a crew, face new combat and environmental challenges without PvP threats, and use Flash Boosts to shape your build during a run."

If battling it out against other runners is more your style, Marathon is getting it's first PvP mode, Deathmatch (Beta) pitting quick 3v3 matches against one another. Personally, I think this is a great way to let players get used to the game's arsenal of weapons and gadgets without the time commitment that comes with extraction.

There are a few other new bits and bobs coming to Marathon in December, including a new runner shell, which we'll cover below:

To coincide with the Symbiosis update, Bungie will also be hosting an Open Play Week starting December 8, allowing new players to download and play Marathon for free.

News Lance Reddick, The Voice Of Commander Zavala In Destiny 2, Has Passed Away

What do you think PXers? Are you fussed about Marathon? Let us know what you think in the comments below.

Craig is a Staff Writer and former Video Producer at Pure Xbox, where he covers the biggest games in the world of Xbox.

It's a special day today, because Skyrim is now 15 years old. Yes, I know - my back hurts too. This wondrous anniversary had people wondering whether Bethesda might do something to mark the occasion, such as revealing more The Elder Scrolls 6 news. Alas, that much definitely won't be happening.

Speculation was gaining momentum because, aside from the community's own hopes the company would mark a landmark birthday for Skyrim, podcast Kiwi Talkz teased a reveal of some sort. "There is an awesome announcement happening in the next two days that gamers will be happy about," Kiwi Talkz host Reece Reilly posted on Twitter on November 9.

He clarified soon afterward that this had nothing to do with The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel or Mass Effect, ruling out the big topics people were hoping for. Bethesda itself then stepped in to quell anticipation.

"We aren't going to have any big announcements tomorrow," an official account for the studio wrote on Reddit yesterday. "We're excited you’re excited but we will not be sharing anything new on Sentinel for some time."

Disappointing as this may be, I feel the need to remind people that this is the same company that took eight years to go from revealing that The Elder Scrolls 6 is in development to giving us the title and logo. And we've had a single crumb of lore around the game otherwise.

We're coming up on season three of Amazon's Fallout TV show, and there hasn't been a peep about when we might get big remasters of Fallout 3, 4, or New Vegas, never mind Fallout 5. Bethesda's notoriously quiet, and it's better to err on the side of hearing nothing than to set yourself up for disappointment.

If anything is revealed, it'll be a Skyrim remaster following Oblivion's. But even that seems unlikely. Maybe there's a surprise port literally in GTA 6 or something. At this point, I wouldn't count it out.

#4044. Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.

In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?

Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.

Developers are turning to buffs over the old XP-to-gold conversion mechanic

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Blizzard is meeting gold-starved World of Warcraft: Forever players halfway by making more quests more generous regarding the resource. That said, an old feature that plenty used to grind gold is staying gone.

When WoW: Forever launched, players racing to level up as swiftly as possible found that the XP-to-gold conversion for quests completed at max level was no longer present. If you'd like a quick history lesson, Blizzard added the feature to OG WoW before Burning Crusade launched, and it worked simply – once you're at max level, you get gold instead of XP.

The decision not to include that feature in World of Warcraft: Forever hasn't been popular. As such, Blizzard has made an appearance online to explain some of its rationale.

"We left that functionality in place in Classic Era in 2019, but we decided that for WoW: Forever, we would remove the XP-to-Gold conversion, as it created an incentive for players to hold a full quest log worth of completed quests to hand in after hitting level 60 for maximum gold returns," community lead Randy "Kaivax" Jordan explains in a forum post. "Under those conditions, the optimal way for players to level to 60 was to simply grind creatures for XP and not hand in quests at all, which is not a design we want to retain in WoW: Forever."

Jordan continues by explaining that one thing Blizzard did not account for, however, is that only 25% quests in the original World of Warcraft actually provide raw gold rewards. So on that front, Blizzard is saying, yeah, actually you might have a point if you think the MMO is being stingy.

But hopefully not any longer. Blizzard has now released a World of Warcraft: Forever patch that ensures most quests at level 48 and above now additionally reward gold. That said, don't expect the return of XP-to-gold conversion, as "it would be inappropriate" to have players keep hold of quests rather than hand them in.

"This change brings high-level quests in line with the rest of questing in WoW: Forever, with the goal of giving players a good reason to complete those quests while leveling up to 60 and thereafter," Blizzard explains in a new patch post. "Quests that were not affected by this change include those that already reward valuable items, repeatable quests, and those that don't provide significant rewards because they're quick, easy, or trivial to complete."

#4041. Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic's next DLC is set to expand the city building sim into the one place not corrupted by capitalism: SPACE

Following not the inherent liberal capitalistic framework of city builders like SimCity but instead a revolutionary (sorry) interpretation of planning and logistical simulation that prioritises centralisation and minute detail, Hooded Horse and 3DIVISION's Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic offers a tense, socialist look at what a citybuilder could be. Fellow contributor Sin Vega, in her 1.0 review, described it like this: "You have to build things to demolish things. That might be Workers & Resources in a nutshell. You're not managing budgets (money is exclusively for imports/exports), you're organising stuff." Now, having previously expanding out of the Soviet Republic and across the globe with the World Maps DLC, the next step for socialist citybuilding is, of course, space. Our Edwin outright predicted this two years ago, correctly calling that "the logical endgame here is to go to space." Good on him.

The Space Program DLC, set to release on November 23rd, will add a variety of new technologies and types of industry to the builder. It looks like it'll focus on not only the actual rockets that get into space, and the spectacle of it all, but also the huge amounts of science and industry that get to the point of rockets not exploding upon takeoff. For example, while it's all well and good for Space Program's scientists to be able to design rockets that are capable of remaining together for long enough to land safely, the designs they dream of still have to be built, meaning that industrial pipelines must be effectively centralised to ensure that every single component is of high quality and arriving in the required quantity.

The update also specifies the Sputnik and Vostok programs as elements of the expansion, implying a close historical aspect to it — though, elsewhere, "an unprecedented duel with nature" is mentioned, which is referring to either the simple harshness of space or aliens. Jury's out. A 1960s campaign will be a star feature of the DLC, which is described as a place for players to learn the new mechanics "in relative peace, surrounded by a happy, healthy, and economically stable utopia." What an idea.

#4039. Square Enix Sees Huge Increase in Digital Game Sales, Upping Its Financial Forecast

Much like Capcom, Square Enix is seeing a significant surge in digital game sales, as opposed to physical, with the latter now in steady decline.

In fact, Square Enix's latest financial report is pretty eye-opening. It makes for a positive assessment of the company — something of a rarity over the last several years — and it's primarily down to the aforementioned increase in digital purchases.

The publisher reveals that digital sales have practically exploded, jumping from 5.83 million to 8.19 million year-on-year. It cites healthy numbers for Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth's Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox ports, and The Adventures of Elliot — the action RPG that was released back in the summer.

In total, a whopping 89% of all Square Enix's sales were digital over the last six months, while physical sales dropped from 1.09 million units to 1.01.

So while there's still some demand for boxed games, the slice of the pie is only getting smaller.

All of this has led to the Japanese company upping its financial forecast for the rest of the fiscal year, going from ¥298,000 million to ¥310,000 million. While not a massive jump, it's still a good sign, given the publisher's recent struggles.

Of course, all eyes will now be on Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, which launches on the 8th April. It'll be the first game in the trilogy to release on multiple platforms — a move that Square Enix thinks could make a big difference after Rebirth couldn't come close to matching Remake's initial sales.

What do you make of Square Enix's current situation? Is the publisher finally on the up? Wait for some digital discounts in the comments section below.

#4037. I'm sad that the Like A Dragon creator's new studio is closing, but I wish their now-cancelled debut Gang of Dragon wasn't just LAD again

Less than a year after the announcement of their first game, and only four years after the studio's creation, Gang of Dragon developers Nagoshi Studio have been dissolved by a shareholders' resolution (thanks, Gematsu.) That also means a premature end for Gang of Dragon, which was announced at last year's Game Awards with a flashy trailer featuring Like a Dragon-esque realistic visuals, combat and exploration through Kabukicho, a couple new elements like actual gunplay and car chases, as well as the star power of actor Ma Dong-seok (a.k.a. Don Lee). Following reports in March that NetEase, the studio's source of funding, would be pulling said funding in May due to ballooning costs reaching around seven billion yen, the time has sadly come for Nagoshi Studio, having not found any alternative funding sources in the time since.

Gang of Dragon looked very much to be 'just Like a Dragon again', which I find to be something of a depressing fate for a studio headed by the original series' creator. Having left Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio following Judgment and Yakuza: Like a Dragon, two of its most innovative games both with new protagonists and one entirely new turn-based gameplay style, it feels indicative of the industry that Nagoshi was granted funding seemingly on the condition that the studio makes something that just looks like the rest of the Like a Dragon series. I love Ma Dong-seok as an actor, but his presence was one of the more blatant, 'look, we got that guy!' castings of the LAD archetype, which is saying something considering Infinite Wealth had fucking Danny Trejo in a prominent role. The trailer closing with a shot of Dong-seok framed by Kabukicho's torii gate, maybe the most famous image from the Like a Dragon series, put a sour taste in my mouth as being just more of the same brand recognition (yet, for a new IP!) to prioritise safe return on investment.

I'm unfortunately not that surprised to see Gang of Dragon and Nagoshi Studio lost to time, though I am sad about it. I have some conflicted feelings on Nagoshi as a person/auteur, but I don't think he, or his studio, deserves to have funding pulled before they could even release anything as a result of NetEase deciding to pull investments out of non-Chinese companies over time. It's unknown what Nagoshi and the team will be attempting next, but I truly hope they can eventually make something. No More Heroes studio Grasshopper Manufacture was able to detach themselves from NetEase very recently and possibly avoid a similar fate, so it might not be impossible.

#4036. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel teaser all but confirms Hammerfell setting and means we can finally stop using that eight year old header image with the hills

Say hello to sandy scroll screengrab for the foreseeable future

Praise Talos and whatever other Elder Scrolls deities you might worship. We here at RPS and in the wider gaming press finally have new material to use when hunting for images to symbolise The Elder Scrolls 6. No more will we be limited to that shot of some hills from the 2018 teaser, because Bethesda have shown off an elder scroll covered in sand while revealing the new game's subtitle and all but locking in a setting. As a recent report from The Verge claimed, it's called The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel and looks to be set in Hammerfell.

These details were revealed in a short teaser at the end of a Todd Howard-fronted video celebrating Bethesda Game Studios' 40th anniversary. As such, the majority of the video is the Toddinator recapping the studio's history by touching on each of the games they've put out since 1986's Gridiron. Then, he looks to the future. "You know, everybody’s always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," the Toddfather said. "And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."

Cue a shot of an elder scroll buried in sand, followed by the The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel in fancy logo font. Then, a quote attributed to a moth priest called Yazar. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." OOH, CRYPTIC. In all seriousness, between the subtitle, the sand, and Yazar being referred to as a moth priest in service of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell, the Verge report's assertion that the game will be set in Hammerfell is essentially set in stone by this teaser even if his Toddliness didn't spell it out himself.

Sentinel's the name of both a kingdom and city in the Redguards' province. The inclusion of an elder scroll in the teaser and the quote from Yazar also lend credence to the Verge report's claim that the game will make a big thing out of unravelling secrets linked to the provenance of these mysterious bits of paper. As for the quote's yammering of lost futures and undone victories, I'll venture to speculate that it could turn out to be reference to the player character thwarting a Thalmor victory, since Skyrim seemed to set up the elves as being on the verge of conquering Tamriel as the Cyrodillic empire fractured and fell.

That may or may not be the case, but we do know for sure that this teaser likely means a huge downturn in use of the header image below. It's eight years old, pulled from The Elder Scrolls 6's infamous 2018 teaser. All these years on, the game's finally on the way. You've served us well, screengrab of some hills. Talos guide you to wherever less regularly used images go.

Elder Scrolls teasing aside, it's worth bearing in mind that Bethesda parent company Microsoft have spent the majority of this year gutting their workforce with mass layoffs and studio ditching. Microsoft are also still currently subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

Here is an overview of the game, via Devolver Digital:

Freely customize and modify your cards and units or craft and mutate every individual soldier to create wildly different builds and strategies in every run. Explore combinations between different characters, factions, cards, and battlefield setups to create devastating armies!

#4034. Mobile Suit Gundam Battle Operation 3 has been announced, marking another attempt at a free-to-play team game after Gundam Evolution's unfortunate fate

Bandai Namco have released the initial announcement trailer for Mobile Suit Gundam Battle Operation 3, a free-to-play team action game and a sequel to 2018's Battle Operation 2. The trailer is very, very pretty, showing off Gundam units clashing in large-scale battles and infantry fighting beneath the colossal mechas' feet (kinda like Titanfall, in having both human and mecha players in the same match). I'm sadly not yet enough of a true Gundam fan to recognise many of these units on sight other than the RX-78-2, but there's a real variety shown off here.

MOBILE SUIT GUNDAM GUNDAM BATTLE OPERATION 3　Announcement Trailer Watch on YouTube

While there's no release date specified in the trailer, Bandai Namco have confirmed that there will be a network test in Japan through November 20th-22nd, with an open network test planned for the future (thanks, Gematsu).

Following the fate of Gundam Evolution, a 2022 attempt at a hero shooter featuring Gundam units, it's nice to see another shot at taking the Gundam series into a team format. Evolution suffered from the all-too-common trappings of heavy microtransaction inclusion, with several playable Gundam units with unique abilities only available through paying real cash. It was rightly criticised for this, and since Bandai Namco seemed to have had high hopes for the revenue it could make from said microtransactions, the lack of money made meant it shut down just a year later.

Contrastingly, from what I can see, Gundam Battle Operation 2 was received fairly well on its release. While little is actually known about the third game at this point, let's hope it has a better chance than the series' last big release. I will quickly note that the trailer does close with a "*Some content may require purchase" note, so it'll likely have some form of microtransaction in itself — hopefully not to the same degree as Evolution. And, while we're on the topic of Gundam, there's also 2027's Gundam Rogue Orbit, a drastically different game that seems closer to a Devil May Cry-esque action title (though, unlike Battle Operation 3, will begin life as a timed exclusive to PS5). Now, if we could get a Gundam game that plays something like Armored Core, and god willing a proper PC release, I would be a very happy girl.

#4033. Hardware Review: Astro A50 X Lightspeed - The Ultimate Gaming Headset, But Not Suited to All

The Astro A50 X Lightspeed is a pair of headphones I’ve been looking forward to trying out for a while. This is a high-end headset that actually utilises HDMI passthrough rather than the traditional dongle connection.

This is by far the most expensive headset I’ve ever tested, so let’s see if that moolah translates to a genuinely great audio experience.

The Astro A50 X Lightspeed is a pair of wireless gaming headphones from Logitech. They operate out of a base station, which both charges the headset and enables you to switch sources between PS5, PC, and Xbox.

It’s rocking Pro-G Graphene drivers, a 48kHz flip-to-mute mic, Lightspeed wireless technology for quick connections, a playsync button that allows you to switch sources, a game and voice chat audio balancer on the right earcup, and Bluetooth, which can be used simultaneously with the wireless HDMI connection.

In total, this headset will set you back £309.99/$399.99, and is available in White, Black, and Mars Red variants.

Within the Astro A50 X Lightspeed box, you have the headset itself, the charging station, the power cable, and connecting USB-C to A connectors.

Truth be told, setting this thing up is a bit of a headache, and it requires what seems like a lot of wires. So in my setup, I’m connecting the headset to both my PS5 and my PC. With that, I need the power cable running to the station, but it also splits and runs to the PC.

I also have a USB-C to A cable connecting to my PS5. Then you have the HDMI cables, which aren’t provided. You need one running from your PS5 to the station, and another running from the station to the TV or monitor.

In total, that’s four cables running out of the back of that station (one splitting off to power and PC), and it could be more if you decided to connect an Xbox too. It’s far from the tidiest setup, and it took me a little bit to ensure my desk wasn’t a complete mess of cables.

Before we get to the sound, we have the headset itself, which is a lot lighter than I expected. It features a plush fabric headband and ear cups, which is a little different from the usual faux leather designs of other gaming headphones.

The first thing I thought when I noticed this was, “I wonder if it gets hot?” and sadly, it actually does. Don’t get me wrong, these things are very comfortable; however, if you’re in a hotter room, or maybe you’ve been wearing them for extended sessions, your ears will get warm. The Sony INZONE H9 IIs also utilised fabric around the earcups, but were quite breathable by comparison.

However, heat aside, I loved the feel of these headphones. They are quite flexible and are easy to find the right fit for your head. If you’re in a cool room, you’ll be able to wear these things for hours on end without feeling any discomfort.

The right earcup, which houses most of the controls, thankfully isn’t overcomplicated with tons of buttons – something that’s annoyed me in some other headsets. Instead, you have a volume rocker, which actually controls the sound with accuracy – not something every headset gets right – a Bluetooth button, the playsync button to change sources, and the power button.

Switching sources is one of the big features of this headset, and I loved being able to easily do so at the touch of a button. This might not be something that the average person is utilising all of the time, but as someone who regularly switches between recording gameplay on my PS5 and then writing some video scripts, I actually found it super useful.

An interesting quirk of this HDMI setup, however, is that you must select your PS5 as your source through the headset for it to play through the television or monitor; otherwise, it’s as if there is no video source. However, the charging station does support HDMI 2.1, meaning you can utilise passthrough of games running up to 4K 120Hz, allowing for 24-bit high-resolution audio.

On the side of the right earcup, you also have a game and chat audio balancer, which is really easy to use and doesn’t get muddled up with any other controls.

On the left side, you have the flip-to-mute mic, which is also quite flexible. It’s claimed that this is producing “broadcast quality” comms. I doubt I’d go that far, but the mic on the Astro does sound fantastic and is much better at cutting out those additional room sounds like breathing.

I was actually playing games online with someone else who was using the same headset and found it actually runs a little loud, but this is something you can easily fix in the party settings, or by adjusting your own mic gain on the PS5.

Logitech claims you can get around 24 hours of playback on this headset. It’s not something I really got to properly test out, however, and I doubt you will either. Because the base station also acts as a charging station, I was always just quickly dumping them there at the end of a session. It meant that battery life became a complete afterthought for me, which is really what you’re looking for.

The station itself will showcase how much charge the headset has, as well as the source that’s currently selected, and whether Bluetooth is active. As well as being handy, I think this station looks really nice, and it quickly blended into my desk setup.

The only main complaint I really have with this setup, and it’s maybe personal to me, is that the headset isn’t very mobile. Where most dongle headsets can be switched to another PS5 in another room, or taken out of the house if you’re taking your PS5 somewhere else, the Astro A50 X Lightspeed is very much a stationary headset.

I suspect for most people this is a non-issue, but as someone who has a PS5 in my office and then one in my living room, I wasn’t easily able to bring this headset downstairs.

The audio experience is really what you’re here for, and on that front, the Astro A50 X Lightspeed does not disappoint. These headphones have spectacular range.

I’ve used them to play quieter games like Zero Parades and it picks up all the little minutiae of dialogue and environmental sounds. I've also played bombastic games like Modern Warfare 4, where explosions are brought to life with powerful bass. Then, switching that source, I’ve spent countless hours listening to music and even taking part in calls, and the quality persists.

The Astro A50 X Lightspeed is a jack of all trades headset, but it may also be a master of all. I was thoroughly impressed with the audio quality on display, which, to be fair, is expected with the price tag attached to this headset.

The one curious omission from this headset is active noise cancelling. It’s not featured at all, so you’re still going to hear your own voice or the surrounding sounds during your gaming sessions.

Maybe as a byproduct of that, I did find the headset a little quiet. I tend to like my headsets to run loud, so I often felt like I wanted a bit more in terms of pure volume – although I’m sure my ears will be glad that isn’t the case.

If the out-of-the-box experience isn’t quite right for you, then there is a Logitech app, on both mobile and desktop, which allows you to further customise your audio profile to get the right fit for you.

There’s no getting around the fact that the Astro A50 X Lightspeed is an incredibly expensive headset. With that, I’d really only be happy recommending it to people who know they’ll get the full use of its features, namely that of source swapping.

As someone who regularly splits my time between PC and PS5, being able to switch sources with the touch of a button is a Godsend. It’s really the thing that differentiates this headset from the rest.

However, strip that away, and you still have a solid headset that masterfully balances the audioscape of both quiet and explosive games, thanks to HDMI-passthrough 24-bit audio. On top of that, you have a mic that’s a cut above the industry standard, and a flexible, lightweight design that does run a little hot for me, but is still incredibly plush.

It might not be the right headset for everyone, but if this sounds like it would work for you, you can’t get much better than this.

#4032. Microsoft Announces Last-Minute Restock Of The Xbox Series X25 Console

Available at launch through the Microsoft Store and participating retailers

Ever since the Xbox Series X25 console first became available for pre-order in August, it's become hard to get your hands on one. The "Limited Edition" system quickly sold out, and became a target for scalpers within 24 hours as well.

If you were hoping to add the Series X25 to your collection (or the accompanying controller, for that matter), you might still have a chance - Microsoft says that a "limited" restock will be available on November 12th to mark the launch.

This apparently goes live at "midnight local time", which we assume means November 11th going into November 12th (although the tweet doesn't make this fully clear):

As you can see, the restock will be available on the official Microsoft Store / Xbox Store, but also at other participating retailers that have yet to be named. We assume most of them will be the ones that carried the original pre-order.

You can feel free to go back to our pre-order guide for the Xbox Series X25 console if you want easy to access to various links and pricing info, but just be aware that things might be a bit different for this restock, so it's worth searching around at midnight local time if the Microsoft Store version sells out quickly.

Are you hoping to get your hands on one of these? Let us know down in the comments section below!

#4030. The Outer Worlds 2 DLC ‘Side Effects Guaranteed’ launches December 2

Publisher Xbox Game Studios and developer Obsidian Entertainment will release The Outer Worlds 2 downloadable content “Side Effects Guaranteed” on December 2 for $14.99, the companies announced. It is also available with the Premium Edition or Premium Edition Upgrade for The Outer Worlds 2.

Here is an overview of the content, via Xbox Game Studios:

“Side Effects Guaranteed” is the first chapter of a two-part expansion for The Outer Worlds 2. A distress signal beckons you and your crew of the Incognito to a derelict ship, where you discover the ship’s crew in suspended animation to keep themselves alive, as they’ve been infected with something that causes explosive cell death. The hunt for a cure leads to Elysium Valley, a brand-new region on Eden.

Two Sub Rosa agents have very different plans for saving or sacrificing the crew which involve a Protectorate settlement and the future of Sub Rosa, and they want your help. The fate of settlement, the crew, and Sub Rosa itself are yours to decide. (Side effects may vary.)

The Outer Worlds 2 is available now for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, and PC via Steam and Microsoft Store. It is also available via Game Pass.

#4029. Venom-toothed Noxious Terminids are soon to infest Helldivers 2, and it's your noble job to sterilise the galaxy for Super Earth

Helldivers 2 isn't slowing down any time soon, and according to Edwin's recent interview with Arrowhead CCO Johan Pilestedt, it'll continue to be Arrowhead's main priority for the future. As if Helldivers 2 wasn't full of enough horrors for our brave Super Earth Helldivers to shoot at for the betterment of galactic democracy, its next update is due to add an entirely new Terminid subspecies, the Noxious Terminids.

First up on are the Noxious Scavengers. These horrible little (see: huge) things skitter around at high speed and are loaded with deadly poison, but are thankfully at least fragile. Liberal use of area-of-effect weapons such as flamethrowers, explosives and flamethrowers are recommended to avoid being overrun by these horse-sized insects. Then there's the Noxious Spewer, which is not only fast like its smaller brethren despite its larger size, but also equipped with a web projectile which locks a Helldiver in place, vulnerable to a fatal bite. Oh, and if you dare shoot its soft underbelly, it violently explodes, with the same web fluid covering a wide area around it. The poison inflicted by these creatures' bites is a new damage over time effect that can blur vision, slow movement, eat away at your health, and make you fear this may be the end for you — so it's a bit like getting the flu (get your jabs!)

HELLDIVERS™ 2 | A Cleaner Galaxy Starts With You Watch on YouTube

This update also makes the change that bug caves can be found across many more worlds across the galaxy, leading troopers down tunnels with limited visibility and claustrophobic dead ends. Super Earth's propaganda, sorry, I mean, guidance, describes the galactic sterilisation program quite simply: locate the invasive species, identify the horrific monsters at the barrel of your flamethrower, and sterilise (burn to cinders). The guidance also, hilariously, includes the line: "Super Earth reminds you that ammunition is cheaper than antivenom." Now, get out there and rid our beautiful democracy of this vile pestilence.

#4028. Frostpunk 2's The Surge DLC keeps the wintery apocalypse and adds in faction-clash-inducing electricity and sets a seasonally appropriate December release date

For the time being, the world of Frostpunk remains a hypothetical, even if it's one that seems just that little bit more likely than I'd like it to be given who's in charge of the world. But at the very least, there are pockets of hope to be found in Frostpunk 2, namely with its newly revealed next bit of DLC, The Surge, a name that has been bequeathed to it for incredibly obvious reasons. Oh, you need me to explain them? Fiiiiine.

You and your probably not so merry band of survivors have been trekking across the UK, when you end up at a "mysterious valley." Apparently some rumours have been going round about a "marvel left behind by history’s greatest mind - a relic with the potential to reshape the world itself." So you go off to look for it, and it essentially seems like this relic lets you use a whole bunch of electricity. Only, despite how useful this is for automating a bunch of work, various factions disagree over how it should be used, "while the secrets hidden within the valley prove far more difficult to uncover than anyone expected."

In terms of what you should expect from this DLC, for starters there's a new scenario to check out "set in an entirely new region, far beyond the borders explored in Frostpunk 2 so far." This relic is also implied to have come from the mind of one Nikola Tesla, you know, the electricity guy. There'll apparently be ways to utilise the Great Storm that's ruined the planet to "turn catastrophic whiteouts into valuable, harvested and stored resources." And you'll have some hidden treasures to find and mysterious to uncover in various nearby caves and ruins.

All sounds neat enough! And it's not too far away either. The Surge is currently slated for a seasonally appropriate December 14th release date. Let's hope no real world environmental disasters get in the way of that, 'ey? While you wait for it, you can wishlist the DLC on Steam.

#4027. GTA 6 Preloading Is Causing Major Download Traffic Spikes in Europe

If you needed another clue as to how big GTA 6 is going to be, internet service providers in a number of countries are reporting inflated traffic figures in the wake of preload access.

Millions of eager fans have pre-ordered the open world action title on PS Store — in fact, it's the most pre-ordered game on the digital storefront ever — and ahead of its launch, they're able to download the game to their PS5s to ensure it's ready to roll come 19th November.

This process, which sees people trying to download a game that's roughly 212 GB in size, is causing inflated traffic in several European countries.

A German ISP, 1&1, has said (thanks Golem) that connections to PlayStation Network and Xbox Live were 10 times higher than usual "during the night of November 9th to 10th." Vodafone also reported a spike in the same period.

Over in Sweden, Philip Wagrowski, business manager at GlobalConnect Sweden, has stated an increase in traffic of 50 per cent on the night when preloading began. Danish and Estonian ISPs report similar findings too.

In the UK, Virgin Media O2 reports that the 10th November saw record-breaking data volume and traffic thanks to preloading GTA 6.

In short, then, a lot of people have been downloading the game this week, and it's made a pretty significant impact on the ISPs.

Over in the United States, Spectrum is currently running a promotion in which qualifying users can take advantage of a temporary boost to 1Gbps, or 2Gbps if they're already on the 1Gbps plan. This comes at no extra cost, and is expressly for the purpose of downloading GTA 6 as fast as possible.

It's pretty interesting to see the reactions from global ISPs; the game really is setting up to be a massive moment when it finally drops next week.

DCU fans fear we may never see John Cena's Peacemaker again

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With James Gunn and Peter Safran stepping down as DC Studios co-CEOs, the future of the DCU is truly up in the air. But to make matters worse, Gunn seems to have already nailed the coffin shut on one DCU hero.

Underneath Gunn's DC Studios exit statement on Instagram, one fan commented, "We're never going to see Peacemaker again." Though Gunn didn't outright confirm the statement, he liked the comment, which pretty much tells us that the fan is right.

Not long after Skydance acquired Warner Bros. earlier this year, the company has already started to make major changes to the conglomerate, starting with replacing Gunn and Safran with former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham, starting on December 1, 2026. Though Skydance, which owns Paramount, has yet to reveal what its intentions are with the DCU, reports suggest the company plans to "dismantle" Gunn's DCU Chapter One.

This would seemingly mean that DCU characters such as John Cena's Peacemaker, David Corenswet's Superman, Milly Alcock's Supergirl, and more would cease to exist and be replaced, just as the DCEU's characters were the last time around. Seeing Peacemaker on the chopping block wouldn't be too surprising, as he is a character who has been championed by Gunn from the start, first appearing in the director's 2021 movie The Suicide Squad, and later given his own HBO show.

But there may be light at the end of the tunnel for some characters, as Gunn's statement states that although he is "relieved" to be stepping down and going back to "pure filmmaking," that's not to say that he and Safran are "immediately done with DC or superheroes," adding that "the characters we set up will live on."

The good news is that titles already deep in development, such as Man of Tomorrow and The People v. Gorilla Grodd, are still happening. But another show seemingly in danger is Lanterns, which, despite becoming one of HBO's most successful new shows ever, has yet to be renewed. Showrunner Chris Mundy says a second season is a 50/50 coin toss right now, but Variety reports that Skydance doesn't think that the show is capturing the zeitgeist, which may be why it hasn't been officially greenlit.

For more, check out our guide on how to watch the DC movies in order, and keep up with upcoming DC movies and shows announced before Gunn's departure.

#4023. Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

The greatest compliment I can give the Legend of Zelda-inspired Twilight Sword RPG is "I have no idea how they weren't sued while making this." It distills everything that makes Ocarina of Time, Wind Waker, and the rest so beloved before lacing that knowledge into a D&D-style game.

I was able to get my hands on a physical copy early, and as a lifelong Legend of Zelda fan who also happens to adore the best tabletop RPGs, believe me when I say that Twilight Sword is entirely my jam. It may be the closest we'll ever get to riding across Hyrule at our tables, and it's immediately gone onto my to-do list once I've finished my current D&D campaign.

Twilight Sword has just hit shelves. You can either pick it up straight from publisher Free League or, if you're based in the UK, grab it for a discount via Wayland Games (which tends to be a good source of reduced tabletop RPGs or bargains on the best board games).

Twilight Sword wears its heart on its sleeve. Between a Breath of the Wild-esque cover and monsters that feel as though they've been plucked from Hyrule field, this RPG isn't ashamed of its roots. It's a love-letter celebrating all things Legend of Zelda (up to and including the recent Ocarina of Time remake), from a world map using the classic wheel and spoke structure to formatting that wouldn't look out of place in Tears of the Kingdom. There's even a corrupted castle at the center of everything, covered in a familiar red glow reminiscent of Calamity Ganon.

In other words, this game wants to be the Legend of Zelda RPG – and after spending some time digging through it, I think the development team at Two Little Mice deserves their flowers. Its muse may be obvious, but the result isn't usually slavish; even though some references fly incredibly close to the sun (more than one enemy looks like their Nintendo equivalent with the serial number filed off), Twilight Sword skillfully identifies and leverages the tropes that make Zelda so beloved. Whether that's noble kingdoms fallen into ruin or cheerful woodland spirits who always seem to be getting themselves into bother, it understands what makes the franchise tick.

Despite being close enough that they feel drawn from a lost Zelda game, I'd argue this extends to the RPG's take on monsters like Moblins or Lizfalos. They're an iconic part of the franchise, so removing them from this tribute would strip away something crucial.

You could modify Twilight Sword to set it in Hyrule, of course, but its bespoke world of Radia does have a lot to offer. Besides proving some truly whimsical and novel locations, there's a sense of discovery – of plunging into the unknown – that you couldn't get with a true Zelda tie-in, or the best Legend Zelda merch. There's also joy to be had in exploring a world that's new yet strangely familiar.

Twilight Sword shares a lot of DNA with D&D but is simpler on the whole. You still have numbered stats like Strength or Charisma that vary based on how good you are at that particular ability, but your aim here is to roll less than your score with a d12 to succeed. (As an example, rolling a 1 is the best possible result here.) Resources like Stamina points play a big role too, and they can be used to activate certain abilities such as the 'Feats' that differentiate your class – here called a 'Way.'

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

When you factor in your health by measured by hearts, Twilight Sword feels a lot more arcade-y than many tabletop RPGs… and considering its video game roots, that's nothing if not appropriate.

With any luck, this game will go from strength to strength just like its inspiration. And considering how it just launched a new crowdfunding campaign for a Monster Book on Backerit (which has already hit €306,254 in funding after just a few hours, well over the €30K goal), that seems more than possible.

This game feels like Zelda with a dash of Final Fantasy. If you'd prefer one that emphasizes Final Fantasy instead, try the excellent Break!! (currently available via the official store, or on Amazon UK if you're based across the pond).

I've been writing about games in one form or another since 2012, but these days you'll find me managing GamesRadar+'s tabletop gaming and toy coverage (I spend my time here handling everything from board game reviews to the latest Lego news). I've also been obsessed with Warhammer since the 1990s, and love nothing more than running tabletop RPGs like D&D as a Dungeon Master.

#4021. Fairgame$ canceled

Sony Interactive Entertainment has canceled development subsidiary Haven Interactive Studios‘ May 2023-announced multiplayer shooter Fairgame$, according to a Bloomberg report.

A spokesperson for Sony Interactive Entertainment told Bloomberg there will be no job cuts as a result of the cancellation, and that Haven Interactive Studios will move to support other studios within the organization.

In an email to employees today, which was reviewed by Bloomberg, Sony Interactive Entertainment executives Sean Decker and John Doyle said a recent playtest with thousands of players—likely the “Project Espresso” playtest we reported on in September—did not deliver on the results the organizations expected.

“While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness, and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,” the email reads. “Combined with challenging market conditions in the [player-versus-player] shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game.”

Fairgame$ was planned for release on PlayStation 5 and PC.

#4020. Silica, an FPS and RTS hybrid that mixes a smidge of Dune and Helldivers together, has left early access and entered 1.0

The concept of fusing an RTS and an FPS always sounds like a fun one, and since 2023 Martin Melichárek has been trying to make a new take on the combination under the watchful eye of DayZ devs Bohemia Interactive through Silica. Today marks the day that Silica leaves early access and enters 1.0, fully fleshing out its hybrid and mish mash of Dune's Arrakis and Helldivers' Terminids.

Digging into Silica a touch more deeply, it is a sci-fi shooter set on a planet where there's a fancy resource you're trying to mine that definitely isn't the spice. There are two warring factions competing for said resource, when, uh oh! Some bug-ish, giant aliens aren't very happy you're doing all that. So, you can either join the fray on the ground with some classic first-person shooting alongside your friends, or you can take the role of commander and dictate your artillery from above.

The 1.0 update obviously comes with a few additions, namely the Centauri Campaign, a "story-driven single-player experience set in the war for Baltarus. It opens with a cinematic intro and features fully voiced mission briefings and in-game dialogue. Between missions, a 3D planetary globe tracks the war as territory changes hands." Commanding your army should be a better experience now too, with the ability to "arrange units into formations, issue more precise movement and attack orders, and quickly select all units of the same type. Improved AI targeting and vehicle movement also help your armies operate more effectively in large-scale battles."

Beyond that, 1v1 matchmaking has been added in, where you can fight against another commander. The Steam Workshop sandbox tools have been expanded for building your own scenarios and sharing them with others. And there are a whole bunch of bug fixes, quality-of-life improvements and additions, and more. You can read about some of those in more detail in this handy little blog post. If you like what Silica is putting down, then you can pick it up on Steam.

#4019. Feature: What Sony Live Service PS5 Games Are Still Alive?

All the cancelled projects and those that remain

Video games are cancelled internally all the time, but never in PlayStation's personal history have those cancellations had to happen in such a public manner. The current PS5 generation has seen the platform holder try to win the live service space, and a few years later, it's having to cancel most of the projects it revealed in attempting to achieve that.

To try and get a piece of the Fortnite pie, Sony made a hard and deliberate push into the Games as a Service space at the start of the PS5 generation. It acquired Destiny 2 studio Bungie to have it help the manufacturer do so, and at the height of the initiative, PlayStation planned to launch 12 live service games in just a few years.

The latest victim is Fairgames from Haven Studio, a developer set up to create the heist co-op title. It was announced in 2023, and three and a half years later, it's now been cancelled after failing to impress in a new round of private tests.

Times have changed, and company executives are finally learning you can't set out with the intention of making the next Genshin Impact or Apex Legends; it has to happen more naturally. Sony has learnt that the hard way, with many graves dug for its failed projects.

But what's still left of the push and remains in active development at PlayStation?

I'm going to document all the live service PS5 games from Sony that have been cancelled, released, and are still set to come (for now).

Here are all the PS5 games and projects Sony publicly announced or acknowledged that have now been cancelled:

Here are all the PS5 games Sony released that are considered live service:

Here are all the live service PS5 games Sony still has in the works:

By my count, that's nine game cancellations for projects Sony either confirmed or commented on publicly, six titles that have actually released, and four more that are currently in development. The disaster that was Concord means it can basically be discounted from the released list, despite the fact it did actually come out.

Then, the list of PS5 live service games currently in development could lose another title as soon as next month.

Horizon Hunters Gathering is currently being reworked into a more traditional co-op title, but if it doesn't impress in an evaluation planned for December, then it's getting cancelled too.

News PlayStation Scaling Back Horizon Live Service PS5 Game as Sony Failures Continue

Guerrilla has until December to impress Sony execs

Despite the consistent failure in the space, with only one big win to its name in the form of Helldivers 2, Sony has stated it's going to persist with live service titles. Back in June, boss Hideaki Nishino said the game model "attracts users on a global level".

He continued: "The genre itself is relatively new, and I think many people are trying various things, so we also want to continue to take on challenges within that context."

From Sony's perspective, those live service games aren't going anywhere despite the track record and industry shifts.

#4018. Xbox Brings Halo's Iconic Pelican To Microsoft Flight Sim 2024 As Limited-Time Freebie

Act fast and claim the combat dropship for free!

Asobo Studios is commemorating the 25th anniversary of Halo by introducing the iconic UNSC Pelican into Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

Over the years, the combat dropshop has seen a plethora of talented pilots don its cockpit: Carol 'Foehammer' Rawley, the reluctant Fernando Esparza, and now you!

"Designed and built by Misriah Armory, the D77 Pelican has a typical crew of three (pilot, copilot, and crew chief) and can carry up to 14 fully outfitted infantry and their equipment. A vehicle can be carried in the external hardpoint clamp for immediate deployment. It has a lifting body design powered by four high-efficiency fusion thrusters with secondary positional / stability augmenters. The wings have three hardpoints each, which can hold sensors, cargo pods, or weapons."

Halo turns 25 alongside Xbox this Sunday, on November 15. So, we've seen iteration after iteration of the sci-fi shooter's most recognisable ship, which has traditionally only been pilotable in the previous MSFS and Halo 4's 'Shutdown' mission. There are other, more difficult means, to cheese your way into flying the Pelican across other Halo games, but now you don't have to.

The D77-TC Pelican in Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 offers:

Personally, even though MSFS isn't my cup of tea, getting to roleplay what it'd been like to ferry Master Chief across the ring is something I'm definitely interested in trying. I really do enjoy when Halo vehicles show up in other games. From time to time, I stick on Halo 2's scorpion mix, hop into Forza Horizon 5 and take the Warthog for a spin. Just for the vibes.

If you're keen to fly the Halo Pelican in Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, you'd best act quick, because it's only free between November 10-17, and then $9.99 afterwards.

#4017. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#4016. ‘Mega Man Legends – New Media’ listing appears on ACTRA Toronto current projects page

A listing for “Mega Man Legends – New Media” has appeared on the “What’s Shooting” page of ACTRA Toronto, the union representing performers in the film, radio, television and digital media industries in Ontario, Canada. The entry notes a production window spanning from September 14, 2026, to December 1, 2026.

The discovery could suggest that a new Mega Man Legends game, remake, or a collection of titles is in development. Notably, the English dub for the original Mega Man Legends was also recorded in Canada.

Mega Man Legends originally launched for PlayStation in Japan in December 1997. It spawned a sequel, Mega Man Legends 2, and a spin-off, The Misadventures of Tron Bonne. A long-awaited third entry, Mega Man Legends 3, was announced for 3DS in September 2010 before being canceled in 2011.

The Rings of Power season 3 has debuted to a respectable Rotten Tomatoes score

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Rings of Power season 3 is finally here – and it has debuted to a Rotten Tomatoes score that is solid, but lower than the previous two installments.

This season of the Lord of the Rings TV show revolves around Sauron and his quest for the One Ring, while the Elves continue to struggle against him.

The show has debuted to a score of 79% on Rotten Tomatoes, which, while very decent, is lower than season 2's 85% and season 1's 84%. But, season 3 so far only has 29 reviews counted on the site compared to season 2's 173 and season 1's 487.

Our own The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 review awarded the show 3.5 stars, with our verdict reading: "With Sauron's terrible might threatening Middle-earth and the forging of the One Ring at hand, The Rings of Power season 3 is a dark, thrilling installment – but one still mired in dense, dragging subplots."

The Rings of Power is set to run for five seasons on Prime Video, which means there are still two seasons remaining. The show is set in the Second Age, long before the events of the Peter Jackson movies, and will take us up to the events of the Fellowship of the Ring prologue.

You can stream four episodes on Prime Video now, and keep up to date with the rest with our The Rings of Power season 3 release schedule. For more, see our roundup of all the other most exciting upcoming TV shows.

#4014. Shrek 2 Remastered Has No Official Reviews Yet, But The User Reviews Are Quite Bizarre

It has a high score on Xbox right now, but a Mixed one on Steam

Yesterday marked the launch of Shrek 2 Remastered on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S (along with other platforms), and if you're wondering why nobody seems to be talking about it, it's because there are no official reviews yet.

It seems codes were only sent out at launch for this one, which means it's going to take a while for the critics to catch up and share their thoughts on this remaster of an original Xbox cult classic.

We can at least see what the initial user reviews are saying about it though, and if you look at the Xbox Store, everything seems to be pretty rosy. Shrek 2 Remastered has a 4.3/5 rating on the US Xbox Store as things stand, with 76% of people giving it a 5-star review, while most of the (minimal) grumbles are focused on bugs and crashes.

The Steam reviews for Shrek 2 Remastered are quite bizarre though. Over there, the game currently has a "Mixed" average rating based on over 350 user reviews, with 46% of people rating it "Positive" overall.

If you look at the "Most Helpful" reviews that appear first, there are multiple people suggesting it's not a great port, highlighting issues with bugged cutscenes, a lack of settings options, and even claims that the CPUs are less intelligent than they were in the original game (although others debate that it plays "exactly the same" as it used to!). There are also multiple accusations that the remaster might have been partially put together using generative AI, although this is just speculation and not confirmation by any means.

Some people are totally put off by all these issues, while others are still really enjoying their time with the game.

Satan Claus on Steam: "Shrek 2 was one of my favourite games growing up, and I honestly can't explain how happy I am to have the chance to play it again after all these years. It's just as special as I remember, and seeing it brought back with changes that do the original justice is wonderful. Even better, being able to enjoy it on modern hardware, especially the Steam Deck, feels like a dream come true. Some childhood memories are worth revisiting, and this is absolutely one of them."

Mikey on Steam: "I was really hyped for this remaster since this game is a game I grew up playing with my sister, but I am sort of disappointed with the state it is in right now. Lots of camera bugs, cutscenes ending aprubtly, missing skybox textures, characters looking woody and uncanny and lots more. It's like they just threw a paint bucket on it and called it a day. I'll wait for patches, since there still is hope."

As mentioned, Shrek 2 Remastered is getting a much better reception on Xbox than Steam right now, so perhaps we ended up getting the better version (or Xbox fans are more lenient), and you can check it out for yourself at the price of £22.49 / $26.99 for Series X and Series S if you're interested.

We do actually have a review copy of the game that we'll hopefully be able to check out soon, so stay tuned for our impressions in the near future. We'll also keep an eye out for raw Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S footage comparisons so you can get an idea of how it plays across both consoles.

For now though, we'll leave you with some basic gameplay from Shrek 2 Remastered down below.

#4013. Skyrim Celebrates 15th Anniversary with Creation Club DLC Bundle, Big Sales, and More

The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim is officially 15 years old today, having originally launched on the 11th November, 2011.

And no, Bethesda doesn't have a new re-release lined up or anything like that, so the memes will have to be put on hold for now.

But that doesn't mean the developer's forgotten about its most successful RPG. To celebrate the occasion, it's reduced Skyrim: Special Edition's price by 80% on PS5 and PS4, cutting it all the way down to $7.99 / £6.99.

Buyers can then upgrade to the Anniversary Edition, which, as far as I can tell, still costs $19.99 / £15.99. Anniversary Edition is the one that bundles all of the Creation Club stuff into the deal.

If you somehow haven't played Skyrim before, or you've just never got around to it on PS5, it's a decent discount — although it's also worth pointing out that the Special Edition is currently available through a PS Plus Extra subscription as well.

Next up, Bethesda's curated a Creations (premium mods verified by the developer) bundle for the anniversary. It throws together five of the most highly rated Creations available at a heavily discounted price.

If you were to buy all of these Creations separately, they'd set you back 3,000 credits — roughly $28 / £27, since you have to buy separate 'Creation Credits' packs.

This bundle is going for 1,500 credits, which amounts to buying 500 and 1,000 Creation Credits at $15 / £14.

Obviously Skyrim's fan-crafted DLCs aren't everyone's cup of tea, but some of them really do fall in line with what you'd expect of an official release. Legacy of Orsinium in particular is a borderline expansion, and it's got a lot of fans.

Beyond all of this, The Elder Scrolls Online is unsurprisingly getting in on the action. You can unlock Skyrim-themed rewards by taking part in the MMO's current 'Golden Pursuit' campaign.

"Fans can also expect a week full of giveaways, community spotlights, and social content," Bethesda's press release adds.

When was the last time you played Skyrim? Dare I ask if you'll be venturing back to its snowy lands for this anniversary? Shout at something in the comments section below.
