Final Fantasy 7 Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi talks hitting the slopes in the trilogy's final chapter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The original Final Fantasy 7 might have featured heaps of command battles and a dense, complex mythos, but it's more than its ecologically-forward story that connected us to the game's world. Filled with a whole planet of towns to explore and people to chat with, Cloud and his RPG party frequently take time to embed themselves in these communities. Taking part in activities and minigames is a huge part of that. Who among us didn't spend whole afternoons just chilling at the Gold Saucer like we were taking a real theme park break?

One of the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy's greatest strengths is understanding this appeal and building upon it as the perspective moves from an abstracted top-down view into a more realistic scale – and Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is aiming to take that even further with its scope of activities. While some people might be eager to see what the final game in the series will reveal about Aerith's fate, or just what is going on with the formerly deceased Zack Fair, we have more urgent questions for director Naoki Hamaguchi. What about snowboarding? What about my precious cards?!

"The snowboarding minigame is just essential to FF7 as a whole," says Hamaguchi. He's totally correct. Cloud dealing with emotional trauma and delving deep into haunting research notes before tearing down a mountain while grabbing sick air is a vital part of the PS1 classic's identity. "I feel like that's what fans are expecting," he says, and the team are keen to deliver on that promise.

With the remake trilogy drawing to a close early 2027, we get ready for the epic conclusion with our Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Big Preview across hands-on impressions, dev access, and deep dives into the whole adventure so far.

"It's not just going to be a minigame you access through the Gold Saucer," confirms Hamaguchi. "It's actually going to be involved in the main story as well." While this detailed remake and pseudo-sequel trilogy dig deeper into some of the story's themes and seriousness, it's historically not been afraid to show its sillier side. If how the team expanded on Wall Market in Final Fantasy 7 Remake is anything to go by, there's every chance snowboarding here will be played straight while adding plenty of flourish.

"In terms of when exactly you're going to play it during the game in the main story, I'll say I hope you stay tuned!" adds Hamaguchi. Though these remakes alter the events of the original game at points, most of the main beats are intact, so it'll be interesting to see if this tease means it'll shift context slightly. Going off the PS1 original, I'd expect to see it fairly early in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation. Yet, I could imagine it becoming a fist-pumping sequence closer to a climax instead. Who's to say there even will be a traditional fight against Sephiroth instead of Cloud and the silver-haired villain settling their differences by shredding the slopes?

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is boasting even more content than its already stuffed predecessor and middle-entry in the trilogy, Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth. Able to hop in the Highwind airship to explore a planetary-sized open world, that'll likely mean plenty of returning activities and minigames for Cloud and the cast to check up on – especially back at the Gold Saucer.

Rather than resurrecting minigames from the original FF7, though, a card game that stole our hearts in FF7 Rebirth will be returning in FF7 Revelation. Taking cues from the series' history with card-based side-activities – most notably Triple Triad across Final Fantasy 8 and Final Fantasy 14 – Queen's Blood is a lane-based monster-slinging card game that saw us taking on all manner of opponents throughout the last adventure, including a cruise ship tournament and a mysterious conspiracy. The best Final Fantasy games usually have some sort of side-diversion I become obsessed with.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

"Ever since the launch of FF7 Rebirth, we've [had] a lot of warm, positive reception specifically to the Queen's Blood minigame. We saw a lot of people saying, 'Oh, are you guys making a standalone game for Queen's Blood?' or 'Oh, it's going to be in Part Three, right?'," laughs Hamaguchi. Other RPGs with card games have indeed made that standalone leap – and with the recent The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered I've been hooked on Gwent once again. Soon enough, Queen's Blood will have me equally hypnotized.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation boss doesn't want to hear your Rebirth minigame discourse: "I don't think that discussion really gets to the heart of the matter"

"We saw a lot of those [comments]. So, from early on, there really was no other option for us – like, yeah, we've definitely got to put it into Part Three, so that was a given from the start!" says Hamaguchi. This time around, the wolf-like party member Red XIII will take the lead in the new Queen's Blood storyline, building on his role as the enigmatic challenger on the cruise in FF7 Rebirth.

The new storyline will seemingly be its own self-contained activity with rewards that just feed back into the deckbuilding so those who don't like it can safely move on. It's a shift in the reward system that stops players who are only interested in certain types of play feeling strong-armed into completing everything if they don't want to, which wasn't the case with FF7 Rebirth. For FF7 Revelation, "what's important is communicating to the player, making it very easy to see what you're going to get for going through that content, what kind of rewards you can expect," says Hamaguchi.

Besides the new narrative content taking Red XIII through his Queen's Blood matches, the card game will also be receiving updates. "The gameplay of Queen's Blood, it was really good – we felt that it was in a pretty good state, and a lot of fans were pretty happy about it too – but we didn't want to just rehash the same exact thing. We did polish the system again. We are implementing new rules and mechanics into [it]." says Hamaguchi.

Aspects like balance have been a big point of discussion on the team, with a lot of tweaks throughout development to get it right. "We are pretty confident that we're able to show, like, a new side of Queen's Blood that fans did not see in Rebirth." Say no more. Just deal me in!

#3984. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#3983. PUBG live-action series in the works at Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct and star

PUBG is being turned into a live-action series for Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct, write, executive produce, and star.

Krafton announced the adaptation on 30th October, adding that Glover's brother Stephen, his writing partner on Atlanta, will join the project as a writer and executive producer.

The series will also be executive produced by Michael Schaefer for Neon TV, Fam Udeorji for Gilga, and Taeseok Jang and Sujin Lee for LV3H. LV3H is Krafton's entertainment arm, and it's involved in both developing and producing the show.

There's no word yet on a release window, plot, or who else will star.

Glover is a two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner, best known for Atlanta and Community. Krafton calls PUBG "one of the world’s most enduring gaming franchises", and says the game, which is credited with popularising the battle royale genre, holds seven Guinness World Records.

Earlier this month, Krafton revealed it was ending development of PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction shooter spin-off announced nearly a year ago. The publisher’s other games include Subnautica and InZoi.

With the help of a separate Arduino computer to manage temps.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In what they describe as "just a proof of concept", one Redditor has gone further than your average custom looper to help keep their game room cool, by routing the liquid cooling in their gaming PC outside to a radiator sat in the cold winter air.

The setup involves slapping a Bykski water block on their Nvidia RTX 4070 Ti and direct-die cooling on the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus using a Thermal Grizzly 1851 Mycro Pro water block, after de-lidding the CPU, of course.

The two blocks are hooked up to each other, and the custom loop can feed water through a radiator outside through holes in the wall when needed.

Part of the reason for doing all this, the Redditor claims, is that their room gets warm when they game:

"My room gets warm when I game and it's -4 outside. Free cooling right? The catch is if the water going into the PC gets too cold you get condensation on the parts, and water dripping on a 4070 Ti Super is not the vibe. So the whole thing is built around keeping the water cold, but not too cold."

"The pc loop runs like normal. When it needs extra cooling, the second pump sends some of the water out to the rad outside and back in.

"A Python script starts on startup and it connects to the Arduino, takes over from the Arduino's own auto mode, and it connects to HWi and Fancontrol so i get total control over the dynamics."

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Yep, that's right; the loop also involves a secondary computer system managing everything. Part of the calculations the Arduino boards handle involves keeping temperatures above the "dew point", ie, above the point at which a difference in temps might make condensation form on the electronics. Because, y'know, that thing about water and electricity not mixing.

Although part of this was to keep the gaming room cool, I'm sure another part was pushing these components for performance. And on this front, there are some great results, including keeping the GPU running around 48 °C under load and the CPU at 52 °C under load. While playing CS2, the GPU stays at 34 °C and the CPU stays between 45–50 °C.

Given this is just a "proof of concept", there's more to be achieved, and the Redditor says: "I'm coming for that number two spot in Steel Nomad for 4070 Ti Super." In other words, they're trying to beat out some top records for that 3DMark benchmark. Let's hope for a nice and chilly winter, then.

#3981. Don’t Fret launches December 8

First-person psychological horror game Don’t Fret will launch for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, and PC via Steam and Microsoft Store on December 8, publisher Digital Pajamas and developer Scary Kid Studios announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

Don’t Fret is a first person psychological mascot-horror puzzle game, where music and horror intertwine in ways never before seen by the indie gaming community. Navigate the hallways of Harmonic Heights as “Fret,” a young talented guitar who is in search of finding a way back home.

Meet Fret, a sentient guitar trapped in a nightmare of music and madness. Navigate the decaying halls of Harmonic Heights, uncover its secrets, and confront the horrors in a music world.

Step into the visually stunning world of Don’t Fret, where every instrument, hallway, and shadow is alive with purpose. The game’s bold art direction blends psychological horror with musical surrealism, creating an unforgettable atmosphere that sets it apart from every other indie horror title.

Shattering the boundaries of traditional indie horror with an expansive world spanning dozens of handcrafted environments—from classrooms and underground tunnels, to outside courtyards, gondola rides, and more.

Every area in Harmonic Heights is designed to keep you engaged at every turn.

Don’t Fret delivers a story-driven horror experience that unfolds through audio logs, inspectable items, and cinematic cutscenes seamlessly woven into gameplay. Unravel a tale of exploitation, performance, and identity as you descend into the nightmare of Harmonic Heights.

Your guitar tuner doubles as a diegetic HUD, displaying your health, stamina, and battery levels—and even detecting nearby enemies through sound. As you progress, upgrade your tuner with new abilities to aid you on your journey.

Every encounter in Don’t Fret demands creativity. Some enemies are drawn to sound and movement, forcing you to be stealthy. Others are relentless, fast, and unpredictable, attacking from any angle. And some cannot be fought at all. You’ll need to observe, listen, and adapt to survive.

Musical Puzzles and Interactive Instruments

Music is more than atmosphere—it’s the key. Don’t Fret features a range of instrument-based puzzles, from pianos to percussive drum riddles, to guitars and harps. At the center is the G-PAD, a guitar-inspired lock mechanism requiring you to perform under pressure at every turn.

Don’t Fret is truly one-of-a-kind adventure that you can’t miss!

#3980. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.

Shift Up says Stellar Blade: Blood Rain is making solid progress toward reaching the quality highs the developers expect, and that more will be revealed "in stages." And if that doesn't get you excited, The Weeknd has played it and is a big fan.

As part of a new financial briefing to investors, the top brass at Shift Up has been taking questions about what's currently going on behind the scenes. One of which is, simply, how is Stellar Blade: Blood Rain getting on?

"Development of Stellar Blade: Blood Rain is progressing toward our target quality level under the principle of securing sufficient development time to deliver the highest level of completeness," Shift Up says, "and we plan to disclose information about the game in stages."

That means it's going alright, if you were wondering. Shift Up has previously spoken about setting a high bar and ensuring what the devs are making clears it with flying colors before putting a game in the public's hands. It's all pretty common speak when it comes to investor reports, though what comes next is anything but.

"Recently, global pop star The Weeknd visited our headquarters during his trip to Korea, toured the development floor, played the build in development first-hand and shared his affection for Stellar Blade," Shift Up continues. "This shows that Stellar Blade is establishing itself as a global IP drawing attention beyond gaming into the wider cultural sphere, and we will do our utmost in developing Stellar Blade: Blood Rain to live up to this interest."

I ain't here to tell people what they should like or not like, but it's the first time – and maybe last? – I've seen The Weeknd mentioned in an investor report. You know, those reports that are filled with numbers and are put together for people who are mainly interested in labor costs and ask why you can't just release more games to make more money while spending less money.

Anyway, I wonder if our Star Boy has played Goddess of Victory: Nikke. Much to ponder.

#3978. Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition launches 12th November and a demo is out tomorrow

Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition will launch on 12th November, bundled with a new mode called Dandori Academy.

Nintendo confirmed the date during yesterday's surprise Pikmin Day Direct, which also revealed that a demo will land on the Nintendo eShop on 2nd November. Any progress you make in the demo will transfer to the full game if you buy it.

Dandori Academy is a timed exam mode. The Direct showed off one of its exams, Gargantuan Garden, which challenges players to collect gold nuggets before time runs out (thanks, Insider Gaming).

The Switch 2 Edition will also let you give voice commands to Oatchi, the game’s dog companion. If you already own Pikmin 4 on the original Switch, you can buy an upgrade pack from the eShop.

Nintendo had warned ahead of the broadcast that there would be no new game announcements. Instead, Shigeru Miyamoto introduced Japanese actor Fuka Koshiba as a new ambassador for the series, and Nintendo confirmed that 1st November, today, is now Pikmin Day.

Pikmin 4 originally launched on Switch in July 2023. The Switch 2 Edition is one of two big Nintendo releases this month, alongside The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on 5th November.

Legendary Nintendo developer Shigeru Miyamoto - who directed classic games such as Super Mario 64 and produced The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - recently argued that the rise of generative AI tools won't necessarily replace human talent.

#3977. Roguelite action RPG Conan: The Black Pyramid announced for PC

Publisher Grindstone and developer Games Farm have announced Conan: The Black Pyramid, a roguelite action RPG “where sword and sworcery meets cosmic horror.” It supports two-player online cooperative play, and will launch for PC via Steam in 2027.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

The Black Pyramid calls to warriors across time. Conan has answered.

Conan: The Black Pyramid is an action roguelite RPG where sword and sorcery meets cosmic horror. Fight alone or with a friend in two-player online cooperative play. Shape your build with every run, turn chance to your advantage, and return with new ways to challenge the darkness.

Explore the distant lands of Robert E. Howard’s shared universe and take control of such iconic heroes as Conan, Solomon Kane, Dark Agnes, and more. Descend into eldritch chambers of the Black Pyramid, a mysterious and dangerous place that defies the logic of space and time. Confront the shadows of the champions themselves and piece together the dark secrets of their past.

Choose your own path through the shifting labyrinth of ancient ruins, ravaged kingdoms and occult halls ripped from different eras of time. Slay nightmarish monsters, savage beasts and bloodthirsty fanatics, and face off against challenging bosses that guard every layer of the Black Pyramid.

Every run presents new routes, new combat possibilities and new story events that move you closer to learning the truth: who summoned you here?

Choose from five distinct characters and weave crushing melee blows, precise swordplay, ranged gunfire and magical attacks into powerful combos. Dodge away from danger and stagger enemies with precisely timed parries to unleash brutal executions, or wear them down with dangerous status effects. Switch weapons and relics to adapt to every combat situation and outsmart your opponents.

Discover multiple Warrior Memories for every character, each with their unique combination of weapons and abilities that drastically change the playstyle. Define your build with ancient artifacts that grant new devastating effects, introduce new combat mechanics, or save you from a fatal blow. Combine them with upgradable Combat Masteries to create your own version of the unstoppable champion. Become even stronger with every attempt as you level up your heroes and unlock permanent upgrades with Wakestones.

As you search the Pyramid for perfect items for your build, you collect dice that increase your chances of better loot. Add more dice to your result and unlock additional rewards now, or save them for later when the stakes are higher.

Fight the nightmares of the Pyramid alone or with a friend in 2-player online co-op. Share the journey, earn individual rewards and keep your progression. Experiment with different characters and build combinations to truly dominate the foe, side by side.

#3976. "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"

Unionised workers reiterate call for a "solid offer" for Arkane Lyon's future

Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Published by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - one of two unions who represent workers at Arkane, the other being Printemps écologique, who didn't issue a similar message - the official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine". It maintains that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. The writers then take Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuse the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 11th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.

The suite of GFX13 patches aren't particularly exciting in themselves, but they do suggest there might actually be some new GPUs next year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD's next-gen graphics architecture has popped up in a graphics driver for the first time, with a suite of GFX13 patches going live in an AMDGPU Linux kernel graphics driver. This has first been reported by Michael Larabel at Phoronix, who spotted a series of eight patches being posted by AMDGPU maintainer, Alex Deucher.

The RDNA 4 GPUs, the Radeon RX 9070 XT et al, were all noted under the GFX12 codename in previous patches, so it is only natural to expect that GFX13 refers to the next generation of AMD graphics cards featuring the RDNA 5 architecture.

The timing of these graphics driver patches would suggest support for the new GPUs is going into the upcoming Linux 7.5 kernel release. With Linux 7.0 dropping earlier this year, and the 7.4 version currently in release candidate testing at the moment, it is expected that the 7.5 kernel release will occur sometime in early 2027.

Wee side note for you... that's not the only interesting thing happening in Linux 7.5, however, as it will also mark the end of an era for Intel. The multimedia extensions it introduced in the Pentium era with MMX will have their last vestiges of optimisations removed in the upcoming kernel release.

At the moment, the current expectation on the actual AMD GPU release schedule itself would see one mid-range RDNA 5 card coming out in 2027, using silicon under yet another codename: AT2. That would tally neatly with the architecture's appearance in this new Linux kernel.

As for the actual code that's been dropped in this series of driver patches… it's not particularly exciting. There is a lot of code, and I am absolutely not smart nor Linux-savvy enough enough to be able to discern anything special from them, but Larabel has himself noted that as far as he can tell there isn't anything in there that reveals tasty new tidbits about the potential future RDNA 5 feature set.

But that's not to say further patches won't do that, so it will be worth keeping an eye on these updates going forward as potentially more functionality-based patches get dropped into the upcoming kernel.

#3974. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.

#3973. Dune: Awakening's free Blood and Ice expansion swaps sand for snow on 1st December

Funcom's survival MMO Dune: Awakening is heading north with a free expansion that trades the deserts of Arrakis for a frozen new map.

The expansion, called Blood and Ice, will release on 1st December. Funcom said it adds "around 35 hours of new progression", along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialisation traits. It's coming to PC, PS5, and Xbox.

The new map, called the Polar Sink, turns the game's usual survival loop upside down. Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm, upgrading your gear with resources found only in the Polar Sink.

The map is split into two biomes, the tundra and the ice cap. You'll start in the tundra, where wealthy water shipper families have built lavish strongholds, before trying to get into the heavily guarded ice cap. Once you're in, you can harvest ice to cool your base equipment and speed up production.

According to Funcom, the expansion "brings the focus back to ground-level survival, with traversal, temperature management, and combat all playing important roles in your progression". The studio also said future updates will add more reasons to go back to the region.

Blood and Ice also brings a new Events tab to the main menu. Shortly after the expansion launches, a new event called Water Crisis will follow the current one, The Scourge. Funcom says every event can be completed in both single-player and multiplayer, and that it plans to run them more often, each with new stories and free rewards.

Funcom has also launched a cosmetics store, which it says will help fund continued development and free updates. The store will start with a rotating selection of items, including looks taken from the Dune films to coincide with Dune: Part Three's release in cinemas this December. The plan is to eventually make the full catalogue available at all times.

Several of the community's most-requested features are also on the way. Offline single-player is due this month, and from January 2027 you'll be able to copy characters from multiplayer servers to single-player, and from single-player to select private or self-hosted servers on PC. Full cross-play will also arrive in January 2027.

"We're far from done," Funcom said, adding that it has "ambitious plans for the year ahead", including major free updates in 2027. The studio says more than a million new players have joined since the game launched on consoles, alongside a rebuilt endgame, three DLCs, and the conclusion of the game's first story arc, Book One.

Just a couple of weeks ago, Norwegian developer Funcom, creator of Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles - and many other games - confirmed it was entering a period of restructuring and bracing for layoffs as a result. You may remember the company making a similar move this time last year, months after the initial PC release of Dune: Awakening.

#3972. The Road of Dust and Sorrow delayed to February 19, 2027

Publisher Silver Lining Interactive and developed Painted Black Games have delayed cozy survival horror adventure game The Road of Dust and Sorrow from its previously planned December 3, 2026 release date to February 19, 2027. It will be available for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, Switch, and PC via Steam. A physical edition will be available for PlayStation 5.

Here is an overview of the game, via Silver Lining Interactive:

Dive into a story-driven survival horror adventure inspired by classics like Resident Evil and Silent Hill. A cure designed to end famine became humanity’s ruin. The failed experiment twisted people into feral creatures called Dusters, driven by primal hunger. Katherine and her daughter Ava roam the remnants of civilization, searching for a safer future. Their journey draws the attention of a Preacher and his mysterious cult, driven by an ancient hunger, they see humans as fertile soil.

Streets lie abandoned, buildings rot from the inside out, and vegetation is growing back at an accelerated rate. Traces of the past linger, in homes—barricaded for protection, offices with supplies scattered, and stores picked clean of supplies. Humanity is shaped by desperation, how far will you go to survive?

Claw your way through decaying streets, bloodthirsty monsters, locked rooms, and forgotten corridors. Solve environmental puzzles, uncover hidden paths, and survive encounters with feral Dusters for a chance to reach safety. Proceed with caution every door can lead to salvation… or devastation.

Protect Ava at all cost. The world can die but she must live. Every step draws you deeper into a place that wants you gone. No one will save you, but you can fight. You can run. You can try to get her to safety.

#3971. World of Warcraft: Forever review: "A love letter to the MMORPG I fell for over 20 years ago"

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

World of Warcraft: Forever is a love letter to why we all fell for it in 2005. It still has a familiar charm but it adds on extra areas, extra quests, and a plethora of fantastic user interface improvements which makes it feel far more modern than before. It's everything that veteran players have longed for.

A beautiful reinvention of a much-loved MMO

User interface changes and tweaks are improvements

It's still World of Warcraft at heart, so it won't convert naysayers

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

As I created a Hunter in World of Warcraft: Forever for what must be the 100th time by now, the saying 'the definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results' rolled around my head a lot. I've played this game before. A lot. Is Forever truly sufficiently different to be so obsessed again? Well, yes. It's this lovely, warm, flawed, wonderfully infuriating dose of nostalgia. It's simultaneously far improved from the original World of Warcraft and, more recently, World of Warcraft Classic (we'll get into the differences shortly), while leaving you with questions of 'why would you leave that in?'.

Will it convert those who never liked WoW in the first place? Of course not. I don't think that's the point of World of Warcraft: Forever. Instead, it brings home all those slightly lost souls from 20+ years ago (AKA millennials like me who want to return to familiar comfort once more), but with some core improvements. It does that incredibly well and given it has brought back a record number of lapsed players, so far it's succeeding.

I've been playing World of Warcraft since the closed beta days in 2004. I've reviewed many World of Warcraft expansion packs (including my WoW: Midnight review this year), played Classic substantially, and have now skipped meals and sleep in favor of playing Forever. I've played seemingly every other mainstream MMO you can think of too, and should probably learn to step away from the PC more often but the allure of WoW remains too strong. – Reviewer Jen Allen

Release date: November 4, 2026Platform(s): PCDeveloper: In-housePublisher: Blizzard Entertainment

Before I dive too deep, let's sum up the differences between World of Warcraft, World of Warcraft Classic, and World of Warcraft Forever so you actually know why the game's important. Retail is best seen as an entirely different beast to Forever. It's very fast-paced, throws nearly as many unlocks at you as a standard game of Fortnite, and is all about leveling up as fast as possible to get to the next part of the story. Getting from level 1 to the level cap of 80 can take just 10 hours if you know what you're doing. It has its place for sure and I really like it, but it's far removed from World of Warcraft's launch years, which is where Classic comes in.

Classic took the game right back to the start and has gradually introduced expansion packs in chronological order. It has a linear progression path, while its leveling process is slow-paced. Each level is richly earned and you'll spend around 200 hours or more playing to reach the level cap of 70. Crucially, not much has been done to spruce anything up. There are some odd UI choices, it looks increasingly dated, and it feels old. It's familiar and fun but also fairly rough around the edges once you start looking.

World of Warcraft: Forever takes what many loved about Classic, but with some key quality-of-life improvements. Player level is permanently capped at 60 with horizontal rather than vertical progression. Oh, and there's a new race called the Skyborne and a bunch of new race/class combinations. You'd be forgiven for thinking Forever still sounds a lot like Classic from this brief overview. It kind of is. But, it's better. This feels like a take on World of Warcraft Classic fans like me wanted, truer to the original experience but willing to remix its approach to deliver new sensations as well.

I spent dozens of hours playing the World of Warcraft: Forever beta, and I've already put dozens more into the full release. I'm not alone either. Friends are excited about it again and the servers are packed. I've yet to see them prohibitively packed though. Forever uses a new layering system whereby players pick how they want to play the game (Normal, PvP, or Roleplay) and that's it. There are no pesky issues with 'oh no, my friend chose a different server to me and now we can't play' with the game shrewdly keeping an eye on its layers and moving people around as and when that layer gets full to the point it would degrade the play experience.

It mostly works. Early on, friends and I found that we had to manually reset the layer by logging out and back into the game, but after the first day, it worked seamlessly. Such a move is an early example of how Forever is designed to be far more accessible for all.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Right from the start, you're actually guided through the game with a helpful early tutorial teaching you how to move, attack, and what to do when you die for the first time. As a veteran player, I didn't need it, but I could see the substantial benefit. Retail has a tutorial, but Classic never bothered with one. Another point in favor of this iteration.

Diving in is a beautiful experience once more, especially if you roll one of the new Skyborne race characters. Affectionately referred to as blue Smurfs, these elves are wondrous. They look great amongst a game with improved looking models but none that can rival this new race. You can play either as Alliance or Horde with the Skyborne, with Druid, Hunter, Rogue, and Warrior available for all, while Horde and Alliance have Mage and Shaman classes at their disposal respectively.

There are specific Skyborne racial abilities which are useful too. Walk on Air allows you to glide in the air for 10 seconds which I found a great timesaver when wanting to fall from high distances. There's also Skysight for Horde which boosts run speed by 10%, while Alliance can activate a ley line and gain 100% increased health and mana regeneration for a time. Throughout my time playing WoW, I tend to forget to use my racial abilities – but these are the kind of skills I didn't want to miss out on.

Skyborne also has some delightful new animations such as a unique dance, a cute cheer, and a more appealing jump than most. Druids get new forms as well. It all feels very fresh once more. After extensively leveling with Skyborne, I didn't want to go back to the legacy races. The Skyborne starter zone of Zephras Isle is luscious. It has that typical World of Warcraft feel to it but it's sprawling, colorful, and a gorgeous reflection of how far games have come.

The water effects across the game are more realistic with waves moving naturally, and the lighting reflecting how it should be compared to real life. Even the audio is slightly muffled when you're underwater, although I found I needed good headphones to absorb this fully. There are some great looking weather effects too. Seeing The Barrens on a hot summer's day then the next day encountering bad storms and fog is special.

None of this would matter much if Forever wasn't fun but it is so much fun. Right now, everyone in-game is as welcoming as they were during the original days. I easily found pickup groups but also I'd have random players resurrect me just because they could, or toss me a heal at a key moment. Another time, I was boarding a zeppelin outside of Orgrimmar and the ship was full of shamans in wolf form dancing and encouraging everyone else to join in.

The ship was full of shamans in wolf form dancing and encouraging everyone else to join in.

After years of World of Warcraft feeling lonely and more of a solo MMO, Forever has united players again. At points, I'd be in a silent group, but at others, we'd chat and share our experiences. My Hunter teamed up with a Druid for one quest, and even though neither of us spoke the same language so we communicated through emotes. It was a beautiful moment when we succeeded.

There are new dungeons too covering all level ranges. Hall of Thanes is an early addition for levels 13-18 and it isn't just a matter of 'run and smash' with a bit more strategy easing you into the dungeon mentality, before hitting Ruins of Lordaeron at 15-20, Excavation Site: Wetlands in the 20s, and more beyond that. There's a rich variety here with experience bonuses varying a little while Blizzard balances things. I don't live in dungeons but I've enjoyed diving in to break up the exploration side of the game.

Forever also encourages community spirit with its campfire system. Feeling delightfully RPGish, you can plonk down a campfire and share some buffs with other players. It ties into cooking well, but ultimately it gives you a moment to reflect. While exploring, I've come across plenty of players just camping and chilling. It's a nice reminder that you're playing an MMO, an active world full of players making their own way.

There are still predictable moments of tedium, of course. While Forever has much faster respawns than other versions of the game (sometimes too fast to keep up with in quieter areas), quest item drops can be very hit and miss. At one point, I spent a disproportionate amount of time trying to collect satyr horns from mobs. I needed 16. They only seemed to drop about every 10 mobs despite me being able to see the horns on the satyrs. A boring reminder that sometimes, you'll still be simply grinding away in-game rather than absorbing those beautiful moments of unity.

After 22 years, World of Warcraft: Forever has finally sold me on Blizzard's undying MMO – now I never want to leave

Combat is mostly much how it's always been. There's autoattack via one key press (or button on the action bar) and then you choose other actions such as casting a particular spell, buff, or special attack.

There's now gamepad support which has opened the game up to unofficial Steam Deck support via a few tweaks. I found this worked well enough. Much like Final Fantasy 14's implementation of gamepad support on console, I wouldn't fancy my chances using a gamepad during more intense moments such as dungeons or raids. It's just not quite as precise or as speedy as a traditional mouse and keyboard setup. It is handy for casual play though, and for those times you don't want to be hunched over your keyboard. Ultimately, more choice is only ever a good thing.

Curiously, while Forever has made the game smaller by not implementing expansion packs, it also feels much bigger as exploration is mostly conducted on foot until you can afford a ground mount (no flying mounts here) but it means everything you achieve feels richly earned.

For the most part, Forever is a wondrous success. The game I'm itching to play more of even though it's all I've done for days. There are so many good tweaks that make it better than Classic. A recent ally alert pops up next to players you've recently grouped with, there's Discord integration which was previously only on Retail, and the quest limit is now up to 40 from 20 (incredibly convenient if you're like me and stockpile quest hand-ins).

The promised 1,000 or so new quests are interspersed nicely with many of the early ones linking together zones more cohesively, and introducing professions and other valuable skills well. Some simply provide you with good gear like bags or a weapon that helps you feel strong for a few levels. All the new quests I've experienced feel like they deserved to be there rather than feeling like filler to pad out the experience.

I'm curious about what will happen further down the line for the game. There's a roadmap lined up for new raids in December before we get even more new raids, dungeons, and quests in 2027, so the next 12 months should be pretty exciting. From there, who knows? WoW: Forever focuses on horizontal progression so we won't see a level cap increase but that makes sense for a game that's all about the journey rather than the destination.

As in life, it's a smart move to enjoy the ride rather than think too far ahead and I haven't had this much fun with World of Warcraft in decades. Sometimes that's all you need. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have a Skyborne Hunter seeking my attention. I want to make some new gear for my guild and get raid ready. The good times are finally back.

World of Warcraft: Forever was reviewed on PC, with a code provided by the publisher.

#3970. You can now play Pillars of Eternity and Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire with a controller on PC from start to finish, thanks to a new update open for testing

Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also gotten a makeover

After gifting Pillars of Eternity a turn-based mode for its tenth anniversary, Obsidian have now rolled out full PC controller support for both the RPG and its younger sibling Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire. The support, along with some tweaks to Deadfire's turn-based mode, are currently out in public test form.

"You can now play the whole of either game with a controller, from character creation to the end credits (and, in Deadfire, all the way out to naval combat), in both real-time with pause and turn-based mode," the studio wrote in their announcement of the public test going live. "Deadfire’s support builds on the controller scheme from the console editions. Prefer to switch things up? Pick up your mouse and keyboard at any time, and the game follows right along."

"Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also been reworked with the improvements we made for Pillars of Eternity’s turn-based mode: turns now follow each character’s speed, combat is more lethal, and swapping weapons or drinking potions no longer costs your action. You can now switch turn-based mode on or off during a playthrough, and the update brings a long list of fixes across combat, quests, audio, and the interface."

Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are included in the support, along with the Steam Deck and Steam's Big Picture mode. Radial menus have been worked in to allow rapid firing of abilities, spells, and party commands, with the interface also popping up the right button prompts for your controller of choice.

These additions are all part of Patch 1.3.10.0, the full notes for which can be found in the post I've embedded above, alongside instructions on how to get into the public test. The patch also does things like ensure "the description of Fulvano’s Boots is no longer fragmented". I'm glad Obsidian have saved those soles.

The studio haven't put a concrete end date on the test at this point, instead noting it "will run for some time as we continue to update it in preparation for a full release". As it's a test, those jumping in should expect bugs and other funkiness.

#3969. Footage of a Persona 1 remake has seemingly leaked online

Almost two minutes of footage from what appears to be a remake of the original Persona has leaked online.

The clip, which seemingly gives the remake the subtitle Be Your True Mind, was shared on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit. It was uploaded to file-sharing site Gofile on 31st October under a Japanese filename that translates as "Megami Ibunroku Persona Remake".

Interestingly, the footage looks a lot like Atlus' more recent entries. It shows off stylish menus and a brief look at combat that closely resembles Persona 5 and Persona 3 Reload. There's also a short social link cutscene in a noticeably different, almost graphic novel art style.

Fans digging through the clip believe they have spotted several details that lend it credibility. These include what looks like Unreal Engine debug text in the top left corner during battle (Atlus switched to Unreal Engine for Persona 3 Reload), a new remix of the original PlayStation game's Pandora theme, and the protagonist being referred to as "Boy With Earring", which is how he is named in Persona 2: Eternal Punishment.

Atlus has not announced a Persona 1 remake, and we can't verify the footage, so treat all of this with the usual caveats.

How do you solve a problem like Persona 4? At Gamescom, we sat down with series director Kazuhisa Wada to talk about the Persona 4 Remake, and ask about how Atlus is approaching the original text for the remake.

Valve opens up the doors to the data it's been collecting.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Steam Deck is the most popular handheld gaming PC, and no doubt a lot of you own one already. It's also far from the most powerful handheld on the market, meaning devs have to get optimisation just right to allow the Deck to maintain 60 or even 30 fps. Now, Valve is letting everyone see exactly how well those optimisations are made by listing average Steam Deck frame rate data on game store pages.

Valve explains that this applies to any game that's been tested for Steam Deck compatibility, not just Verified ones. It applies to 'Verified', 'Playable', and 'Unsupported' ones. Apparently that means thousands of games right now.

The data is based on what different users have opted in to provide, which, despite only being for opt-inners, presumably still gives a big sample size. We've known about Valve collecting this kind of data since at least February this year, and we heard about Valve handing it over to game devs just last month.

Now, Valve is letting us all get in on the action. To look at a game's average frame rate data, go to its store page, look on the right-hand side for where it lists its 'Steam Deck Compatibility', and click 'Learn more'.

Once there, you're shown the average fps, and if you click the down arrow, you can view a "framerate histogram... breaking down the percentage of data samples at each framerate." The bigger a particular bar, the more of the game session (on average) is enjoyed at that frame rate.

I checked the Elden Ring data, for instance, and found that the Steam Deck OLED averages 42 fps and the Steam Deck LCD 38 fps. The latter seems mostly split between 60 fps and 30 fps, with most at 30 and little in between, leading me to believe most players lock their frame rate for more stable gameplay.

The biggest benefit, though, will probably just be the ability to quickly view the average frame rate. It will mean less guessing exactly how well a game should perform on your Steam Deck before you decide to purchase. And that can benefit other handheld gamers, too, as if you have a more powerful handheld, you'll know you can achieve at least that frame rate or higher.

Here's where you need to go to complete Heart of the Fist in Phantom Blade Zero

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Phantom Blade Zero Heart of the Fist side quest is a very simple one, tasking you with finding the grave of the Iron Fist Master and leaving some incense there for the Iron Fiend. Unfortunately, the only hint that the game gives you is that the grave is in the Mirrorwood. Thankfully, it's not very far at all and you will have walked past the grave at least once or twice while playing through Phantom Blade, so this is where to find it.

The Iron Fist Master's grave is very close to the Burial Grounds Bell on the eastern side of the Crimson Forest. Fast travel to this location, then head over to the large grave in the middle of this icy clearing.

Interact with this grave and you'll see a cutscene of Soul burning some incense to honor the fallen master. You'll then immediately be rewarded with the Fist Fragment: Shell item which automatically combines with the Fist Fragment: Core you got after fighting the Iron Fiend the first time. They form the Worldbreaker Fist, which is the necessary item for Soul Tempering the Iron Gauntlets Phantom Edge.And that's the end of Heart of the Fist! Now you should carry on exploring the frozen parts of the Crimson Forest. I recommend going back to the Sha-Chi Tower and sparring with the Jade Dancer and Iron Fiend for the 'Use It Against Them' quest if you haven’t already, as this is how you get the Soul Tempering item for the Fiend Saws dual swords. Then you can finish off the Phantom Blade Zero Triple Threat quest by getting to the end of the forest and facing the Phantom Blade Zero Three-Faced Puppet once again.

#3966. Goddess of Victory: Nikke's PC launcher suffers potential malware infection, with its publishers suggesting folks who've booted since late September do a security check

A cruel twist for the Shift Up-developed epic shooter RPG of cruel humanity destiny

Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a gacha shooter/RPG developed by Stellar Blade makers Shift Up, has suffered a "security incident" which has seen its PC launcher potentially be infected with third-party malware. Thankfully, it seems a patch to make the launcher safe again has been quickly dished out, but publishers Level Infinite are still advising players who've booted the game up since September 27th to do some security checks.

"We have identified that some files in the NIKKE Windows PC launcher were recently tampered with by a third party, potentially allowing malicious programs to run when the launcher was launched," the developers of the game with anime girls who - judging by the promo art - breast boobily announced yesterday. "As a result, your PCs and account information may have been exposed to security risks.

"We are continuing to investigate the extent of the potential damage and review appropriate response measures. We are also conducting a thorough review of our network security environment, including our CDN, to determine how the PC launcher files were compromised. We will take all necessary precautions to prevent further damage and ensure that this issue does not happen again. We deeply regret that this security incident has caused Commanders significant concern and distress, when our responsibility should have been to provide a safe gaming environment."

In order to try and help players "scan for and remove the malicious programs distributed in this incident", publishers Level Infinite have added a feature to Nikke's official PC client that does just that. They're advising that anyone who's booted up the game at least once after September 27th at 15:41 (UTC+9) use that or perform a manual security check.

Once that's done, affected players are advised to change the passwords for any accounts they've used on the PC they used to boot the launcher, as well as generate new API keys and access tokens. "We take very seriously the possibility that this incident may have affected not only your gaming experience but also your PC, accounts with external services, and personal assets," Level Infinite added. "If you believe you may have been affected by this issue or suffered from any loss, please contact our customer support team. We will review each inquiry carefully and respond as promptly as possible."

Going forwards, they plan to improve their monitoring "so that any unauthorized file modifications or security threats can be detected early and addressed promptly", as well as "establish an integrity verification system for external resources accessed by the PC launcher" and ensure the launcher only requires "the minimum permissions necessary".

Here's hoping the studio are able to keep things more secure in the future and that affected players are able to get rid of any malware with minimal suffering or inconvenience.

You can finally see The Devils in all its uncensored glory.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than fifty years after it was banned in numerous countries and received a scarlet letter X-rating in Britain and The United States, The Devils is finally getting seen in all its glory. An uncensored director’s cut of the religious horror film returned to theaters on a limited basis earlier this year, and it’s now getting a full 4K UHD release next year in all its debaucherous glory.

The Devils has largely faded from the collective cultural memory, but the conversation around it was inescapable in the early 1970s. Directed by Oscar nominee Ken Russell, the film stars Vanessa Redgrave and Oliver Reed and follows a charismatic priest and a repressed nun who is sexually obsessed with him. His lurid behavior leads to accusations of witchcraft and some truly wild behavior from nuns, townspeople, and witch hunters.

Russell’s original version of the film required heavy censorship to even get an X-rating. An infamous scene, nicknamed The Rape Of Christ, allegedly involved naked nuns provocatively touching a statue of Jesus, while a priest looked on and masturbated. It had to be removed entirely. Another scene of a woman using a human femur to pleasure herself was significantly shortened along with other scenes of torture that were deemed far too graphic for general audiences. After a lot of back and forth, it eventually got the X-rating.

Typically the X-rating drives audiences away, but in this case, the significant controversy actually led to a solid box office run. The Devils made more than ten million dollars worldwide, which was a respectable sum in 1971. It also earned some of the most divisive reviews in history, as it got 0 stars from Roger Ebert and many other prominent critics who called it pornographic, while simultaneously winning awards at Venice and getting recognized by the US National Board of Review.

Prior to his passing, Russell worked on a director’s cut of the film. It was screened on a limited basis in the early 2000s but never released without heavy censorship. In recent years, Warner Bros. did a full 4K remastering of the film, and earlier this year, they brought it to Cannes for a screening. It was well received, and the film later got a more limited release in some artsy theaters in the US and Europe, this time with the modern NC-17 rating. It did quite well for a re-release.

You probably already know if you’re the type of person who can handle the full-blown version of The Devils. If you read this article and walked away feeling like it’s something you want to experience, you’ll be able to screen the movie at home when it’s officially released on April 20, 2027. It’ll include Russell’s Director’s Cut, as well as the other versions that were released over the years, plus hours of interviews, featurettes, and other bonus materials.

#3964. Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has much worse input lag than PS5

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has noticeably worse input lag than on PS5, which could put Nintendo players at a disadvantage in multiplayer.

Digital Foundry's tech review measured multiplayer latency at 81ms when docked and an average of 100ms in portable mode, against 49ms on PS5. Testing used wireless controllers on both consoles (a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a DualSense), and portable results ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst.

Digital Foundry said "responsiveness here simply isn't as good as on other consoles", and described the lag in portable mode as "actually deleterious to performance" (thanks, IGN).

Beyond the lag, Digital Foundry is fairly positive about the port. Multiplayer runs at 60fps most of the time, and if your TV supports VRR, you'll notice the drops less. The campaign is capped at 30fps and resolution is dynamic.

Docked with DLSS on, the game targets 900p, but Digital Foundry saw it drop to 450p in busier scenes, such as the Paris vehicle chase. In portable mode, the target is 720p, with drops to 360p.

It's been 13 years since a Call of Duty game last appeared on Nintendo hardware, with Ghosts on Wii U in 2013. The series' return is the result of a 10-year deal Microsoft offered Nintendo while it sought regulatory approval for its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

Yesterday we reported that Activision has apologised to the bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it will remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

#3963. Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim

Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

In a new episode of Nightdive's Deep Dive podcast releasing later today, legendary voice actor Stephen Russell spoke about his experience portraying the protagonist of the Thief series, Garrett. We also got final confirmation of something Nightdive had been teasing for awhile: Russell will be reprising the role in the new Tarnished Mirror expansion coming with the Thief remaster on December 3.

I don't think I realized before this interview that Thief was Russell's very first videogame role. Before working with Looking Glass, he had experience in theater, radio and "medical reads" where he had to pronounce complex disease names in an even, doctorly cadence.

Russell said that he felt able to let loose for the first time as Garrett, channeling Clint Eastwood to nail the rogue's singular noirish rasp. Russell hadn't been much into games, with his main frame of reference being simple arcade and educational fare, so he was struck when he first saw an early build of Thief, still remembering "the incredible claustrophobia they had created."

Recalling the creative ferment of Looking Glass in the '90s, Russell said that he had "never seen so many sleep-deprived people in [his] life." He also affectionately recalled the studio's habit of pulling devs out of their office chairs to fill out games' VO roles alongside the professionals: "Having got my start as an actor in community theater, it felt very familiar," Russell quipped. "You're not painting the sets today, today you're playing the lead role!"

Even after a long career appearing in the likes of Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, and Dishonored, Russell still counts Garrett as one of his favorite roles, and said that playing both the protagonist (Garrett) and antagonist (Father Karras) in Thief 2⁠—and having so few people realize he was voicing Karras⁠—remains one of his proudest acting achievements.

And Russell seems chuffed to be returning to the role of Garrett so many years later. "The writing this time around is just as strong as the first time and honors what was created originally," Russell said, adding that it was "great to be back with the old guy."

It's honestly just lovely to see how much this role still means to Russell, and that he's as happy to be returning as Garrett as we will be to hear him. Tarnished Mirror is shaping up to be a real "our powers combined" sort of project, as development was headed up by the team behind the beloved Thief: The Black Parade mod from 2023. You'll be able to listen to the full interview on Nightdive's YouTube channel later today, and you can wishlist Thief Remastered on Steam.
